meta.title: MMI Practice Circuit — content pack
meta.audience: Thai M6 students (female, 17–18, CEFR B2–C1) preparing for Multiple Mini Interviews in Thai university admissions
meta.contents: Everything the app shows: station guidance for interviewees, prompts for interviewers, scoring criteria for observers, and 3 scenarios per station per profession.
notes: Scenario data tables are illustrative practice data, not real statistics.
professionOrder is fixed and FULL: report codes store the profession index in 4 bits (0–15). Never reorder. Adding a 17th profession requires a new report-code version.
v1.1 changes are listed in CHANGES.md. Report codes and session codes are unchanged from v1.0.

0.label: n/o
0.meaning: Not observed — excluded from the score

2.label: Developing
2.meaning: Some evidence, but inconsistent or only after prompting

globalScale.prompt: Compared with a successful applicant, how suitable was this performance overall?
globalScale.calibrationNote: Most practice answers sit between 3 and 5. Keep 6 and 7 for answers you would be happy to hear in a real interview.

clockHints.before: Get into your seats. Interviewees: don't look at the prompt yet.
clockHints.read: Interviewee reads the door. Interviewer reads the notes.
clockHints.feedback: Interviewee speaks first, then the interviewer, then the observer shares the report.
clockHints.rotate: Roles move one seat. Get ready.
clockHints.done: Well done. Check My reports for your feedback.
clockHints.idle: Press Start when your group is ready.

settings.bandNote: Bands follow the 1–4 scale: all 2s = Developing (33%), all 3s = Strong (67%), mostly 4s = Outstanding (85%+).

uiText.noStrengths: No clear strengths were rated yet. Focus on the framework for this station.
uiText.noReportsYet: No reports yet. After each station where you are the interviewee, type the code your observer gives you.
uiText.noGivenYet: Codes you create as an observer are listed here, in case the interviewee needs them again.
uiText.rateMinimum: Rate at least 3 station criteria and 8 criteria in total first.
uiText.invalidSessionCode: That session code isn't valid. Check the board: it looks like 0945F2 or 1010CA.
uiText.invalidReportCode: That code doesn't match. Check each character with your observer.
uiText.concernBanner: Concern raised. {flags}. In a real MMI this could outweigh a good score.
uiText.storageNote: Reports are saved on this device only. Use 'Copy report as text' to keep them somewhere else, such as your notes app.
uiText.copyFailed: Copy isn't available here. Select the code and copy it manually.
uiText.raterGap: Your two raters' global ratings differ by {gap} points. Ask each of them what they noticed.
uiText.checklistGlobalMismatch: The checklist score and the global rating tell different stories. Ask your raters what the checklist missed.
uiText.selfPrompt: Before you open it: how would you rate your own performance?
uiText.selfHigher: You rated yourself higher than your raters did. Ask them for one concrete example of what to improve.
uiText.selfLower: You rated yourself lower than your raters did. You may be underselling yourself: note what they saw working.
uiText.selfClose: Your self-rating was close to your raters'. That's good self-awareness.
uiText.scanHint: Interviewee: scan this with your phone camera to save the report, or type the code.
uiText.deepLinkInvalid: That link doesn't contain a valid report code. Ask your observer for the code.
uiText.lessonTooLong: This plan runs {total}. That leaves little time for teaching in a {lesson}-minute lesson.
uiText.readingTight: Station 5 has data tables. Consider 2 minutes of reading time.
uiText.concernsNote: One concern can be a slip. The same concern twice is a pattern to fix before interview day.

roles.label: Interviewee
roles.summary: Answers the station as a real candidate.

phaseInstructions.before: Sit facing your interviewer. Don't look at the scenario yet.
phaseInstructions.read: Read the door prompt. Name the station type, choose its framework, note 2–3 key points.
phaseInstructions.interview: Phone face down. Look at your interviewer. Answer first, then explain. Think aloud. It's fine to pause.
phaseInstructions.feedback: Speak first: one thing that went well, one thing you'd change. Then listen, and scan or type the report code.
phaseInstructions.idle: Press Start when your group is ready.

roles.label: Interviewer
roles.summary: Reads the opening question, asks follow-ups, plays the character in role-play stations, and gives a 1–7 global rating.

phaseInstructions.before: Get ready to read the examiner notes.
phaseInstructions.read: Read the opening question, follow-ups and (Station 4) your actor brief while the interviewee reads the door.
phaseInstructions.interview: Read the opening question, then stay quiet and let them talk. Use the timing guide.
phaseInstructions.feedback: Let the interviewee speak first. Tell the observer your 1–7 rating, then give one thing that worked and one thing to work on.
phaseInstructions.idle: Press Start when your group is ready.

conduct: Keep a neutral, friendly face. Don't help, hint or nod constantly.
If the candidate stops early, wait 5 seconds, then ask the next probe.
Use the pressure probe only if the candidate is doing well or being vague.
In Station 4, stay in character until about 70% of the time has passed, then step out and ask the follow-ups.
Choose your global rating on your own, before you hear the observer's scores.

roles.label: Observer
roles.summary: Scores the 13-criterion checklist, ticks key points and red flags, records both global ratings and creates the report.

phaseInstructions.read: Read the scenario key points so you know what to listen for.
phaseInstructions.interview: Tick key points and rate the station criteria as you hear them. Leave Communication and Presence for the bell.
phaseInstructions.feedback: Let the interviewee speak first. Get the interviewer's rating, create the report, then show the QR code or report code.
phaseInstructions.idle: Press Start when your group is ready.

roles.label: Observer 2
roles.summary: Only in a group of 4. Scores the same checklist as the Observer (producing a second report) and also keeps time, calling the 1-minute warning.

phaseInstructions.read: Read the scenario key points so you know what to listen for.
phaseInstructions.interview: Score what you see and hear, and call 'one minute' when 60 seconds remain.
phaseInstructions.feedback: Let the interviewee speak first. Create your report and show your QR code or report code too.
phaseInstructions.idle: Press Start when your group is ready.

standard.text: Read the opening question. Then stay quiet and let them talk.
Follow-up 3: push further or change the situation ("what if…").
Pressure probe if they're doing well or being vague.
Final follow-up. Stop when the bell goes.

roleplay.text: Read the opening question aloud, out of character. Then say your first line in character.
React naturally. Follow the 'how to react' notes.
Step out of character: "Thank you. Let's talk about how that went."

interviewer.timingNote: Times = atFraction × interview length, rounded to the nearest 30 seconds.

generalRules.title: Use your reading time
generalRules.text: Identify the station type, choose its framework, and note 2–3 key points before you walk in.

generalRules.title: Answer first, then expand
generalRules.text: Give a direct one-sentence answer, then your reasons. Check you answered the question that was asked.

generalRules.title: Think aloud
generalRules.text: Assessors score your reasoning, not a 'right answer'. Let them hear how you weigh things up.

generalRules.title: Pausing is allowed
generalRules.text: 'That's a difficult question. Let me think for a moment.' A short pause is better than a rushed answer.

generalRules.title: Admit what you don't know
generalRules.text: Bluffing is a red flag. A Ramathibodi candidate passed the 'pressure station' by honestly saying she didn't know, then linking to her own experience.

generalRules.title: Each station is a fresh start
generalRules.text: Different examiners score each station. A weak station does not sink you, unless you carry it into the next one.

generalRules.title: Be real, not rehearsed
generalRules.text: Examiners push with follow-ups until memorised answers fall apart. Prepare stories and ideas, not scripts.

generalRules.title: Know your Thai context
generalRules.text: Health and social systems, current issues in your field (AI, ageing society, PM2.5, rural shortages), and your target programme.

generalRules.title: Know your portfolio inside out
generalRules.text: Expect deep questions on any project, including the ones that failed. Be honest about what went wrong.

generalRules.title: Body language counts
generalRules.text: Smile and greet at the door, sit upright, keep your hands calm and visible, and keep natural eye contact.

anchors.4: Smooth, organised, well signposted

feedback.whenLow: Signpost your structure ('There are two sides to this…') and use 'Let me think about that' instead of silence.
feedback.whenHigh: You spoke fluently and organised your ideas clearly.
feedback.followUpAction: Record a 2-minute answer daily; listen back and count the long pauses.

anchors.4: Precise topic & profession vocabulary

feedback.whenLow: Use precise words from your profession list instead of general words like 'good', 'bad', 'thing'.
feedback.whenHigh: You used a good range of precise, profession-specific vocabulary.
feedback.followUpAction: Learn the 15 words in Toolkit › Vocabulary for your profession and use 5 in your next answer.

anchors.4: Varied structures (conditionals, modals), mostly accurate

feedback.whenLow: Use the station's grammar focus: conditionals for hypotheticals, modals for obligation, present perfect for experience.
feedback.whenHigh: You used a range of grammatical structures accurately.
feedback.followUpAction: Write 5 sentences using this station's grammar focus and check them with your teacher.

anchors.1: Hard to follow; too fast or too quiet
anchors.4: Clear, well paced, good stress and volume

feedback.whenLow: Slow down slightly, stress key words, and keep your volume up at the end of sentences.
feedback.whenHigh: You were clear and easy to follow.
feedback.followUpAction: Shadow a 1-minute English interview clip, copying the speaker's pace and stress.

anchors.4: Upright, open, calm hands

feedback.whenLow: Sit upright, feet flat, hands relaxed and visible. Avoid playing with hair, pens or sleeves.
feedback.whenHigh: Your posture and body language looked calm and professional.
feedback.followUpAction: Film yourself answering one question and note one body-language habit to change.

anchors.1: Looks down or away most of the time
anchors.4: Natural, steady eye contact

feedback.whenLow: Hold natural eye contact about 60–70% of the time. Look away briefly to think, then come back.
feedback.whenHigh: You kept natural, confident eye contact.
feedback.followUpAction: Practise with a friend: hold eye contact through a full 2-minute answer.

anchors.4: Calm under pressure; recovers from mistakes

feedback.whenLow: When challenged, pause, breathe and say 'That's a fair point. Let me think about it.' Then answer.
feedback.whenHigh: You stayed calm and composed, even under pressure.
feedback.followUpAction: Ask a partner to use the pressure probe on you; practise one calm recovery phrase.

anchors.1: Answers a different question; ignores follow-ups
anchors.4: Answers exactly what was asked; builds on follow-ups

feedback.whenLow: Listen to the whole question and answer it directly in your first sentence before expanding.
feedback.whenHigh: You answered exactly what was asked and built on each follow-up.
feedback.followUpAction: Practise 'answer first': respond to 5 questions with a one-sentence direct answer, then expand.

anchors.1: Finished far too early or rambled
anchors.4: Concise answers; used the time well

feedback.whenLow: Aim for 60–90 seconds per answer, then stop and let the interviewer guide you.
feedback.whenHigh: You managed your time well with concise, complete answers.
feedback.followUpAction: Time your answers at home; aim for 60–90 seconds each.

redFlags.label: Dishonest or unethical choice (e.g. faking a document, breaking confidentiality)
redFlags.followUpAction: Honesty and confidentiality are non-negotiable in every profession. Redo a Station 2 scenario and choose the honest option, explaining how you'd do it kindly.

redFlags.label: Disrespectful or judgemental language
redFlags.followUpAction: Describe behaviour, not people: 'she made a poor choice', not 'she is a bad person'.

redFlags.label: Blamed others / took no responsibility
redFlags.followUpAction: Make sure every story in your story bank includes something you would do differently.

redFlags.label: Sounded memorised or scripted
redFlags.followUpAction: Prepare bullet points, not scripts. Practise telling the same story in three different ways.

redFlags.label: Avoided the question or never decided
redFlags.followUpAction: End every answer with a clear decision or a one-sentence summary.

redFlags.label: Bluffed instead of admitting uncertainty
redFlags.followUpAction: It's fine to say 'I'm not sure, but I'd find out by…'. Bluffing is a bigger risk than not knowing.

reflectionPrompts: Which part of the framework did you forget?
Which phrase from the Toolkit could you have used?
What would you say differently to the hardest follow-up?

commentFields.label: Best moment (quote them if you can)

observer.redoActionTemplate: Redo Station {station} at home with Scenario {nextVariantLetter}: record a 6-minute answer, then self-score it with the observer checklist.

feedbackGuide.text: One thing that went well, one thing you'd change.
Tell the observer your 1–7 rating. Give one strength and one target.
Create the report. Read out the top strength and the top priority.
Scan or type the report code before you rotate.

scoringGuide.during: Tick key points as you hear them, rate the station criteria and mark any red flags.
scoringGuide.atBell: Rate Communication & English and Presence, then give your global rating.
scoringGuide.honesty: Score what you saw, not your friend. An honest 2 now helps her more than a kind 4.

stations.name: Motivation & Insight
stations.purpose: Why this field? Assessors check that your motivation is genuine, informed and realistic. 'I like science' or 'my parents want me to' is not enough.

steps.label: Spark
steps.text: The specific moment or experience that started your interest.

steps.label: Steps
steps.text: What you did to test it: shadowing, projects, reading, volunteering, talking to professionals.

steps.label: Reality
steps.text: Show you know the hard parts (workload, pressure, pay, Thai-specific challenges) and why you still want it.

steps.label: Fit
steps.text: Link your strengths to the profession and to the programme you are applying for.

phraseBank: What first drew me to … was …
That experience made me realise that …
To find out whether it really suited me, I …
I've since spoken to / shadowed …
I'm aware that the job also involves …
What I find most rewarding is …
One thing that surprised me was …
I think my strengths in … would help me to …
In the long term, I'd like to …
Rather than …, what really motivates me is …
interviewee.grammarFocus: Present perfect for experience up to now (I've volunteered at…); past simple for the specific story (Last summer I shadowed…); would like to / hope to / plan to for the future.
traps: Clichés like 'I want to help people' with no example
Prestige, money or family pressure as the main reason
Saying nothing negative about the job
Not knowing what the programme or university actually offers

anchors.4: Personal, specific reason backed by a real story

feedback.whenLow: Replace general reasons with one specific moment that sparked your interest, and say what it made you realise.
feedback.whenHigh: Your motivation sounded personal and specific, anchored in a real experience.
feedback.followUpAction: Write your 'Spark' story in 80 words, then tell it aloud in under 60 seconds without notes.

anchors.4: Knows the hard parts and the Thai context, still committed

feedback.whenLow: Show you know the realities (workload, pressure, pay, a current issue in Thailand), then explain why you still want it.
feedback.whenHigh: You showed a realistic, informed view of the profession, including its challenges.
feedback.followUpAction: Read one Thai news article about your field this week and note 3 challenges professionals face.

anchors.4: Clear examples: shadowing, projects, reading, talks

feedback.whenLow: Mention concrete steps you took to test your interest: people you talked to, things you read, made or volunteered for.
feedback.whenHigh: You gave concrete evidence that you have actively explored this field.
feedback.followUpAction: List 3 things you've done to explore your field; for each, write one thing you learned.

anchors.1: Can't link own strengths to the field
anchors.4: Links specific strengths (and weaknesses) to the role and programme

feedback.whenLow: Name two strengths with evidence and connect each to something the profession needs.
feedback.whenHigh: You linked your own strengths clearly to the demands of the profession.
feedback.followUpAction: Research your target programme and find 2 features that match your strengths.

stations.name: Ethical Dilemma
stations.purpose: There is usually no single right answer. Assessors score how you reason: do you see all sides, apply clear principles and reach a fair decision you can defend?

steps.label: Problem
steps.text: Name the conflict in one sentence: 'This is a conflict between loyalty to a friend and honesty.'

steps.label: People
steps.text: Who is affected? Include people who are not in the room.

steps.label: Principles
steps.text: Honesty, safety, fairness, confidentiality, autonomy (a person's right to choose), the law, professional rules.

steps.label: Possibilities
steps.text: Give 2–3 options with their consequences, from mildest to strongest.

steps.label: Decision
steps.text: Choose one, justify it, and say what would change your mind.

phraseBank: The central issue here seems to be …
On the one hand …; on the other hand …
I'd want to find out more about … before deciding.
The people affected include …
It would be wrong to … because …
The least harmful option might be to …
I would start by talking privately to …
If that didn't work, I'd have no choice but to …
My first priority would be …'s safety.
I'd only change my view if …
interviewee.grammarFocus: Second conditional for hypotheticals (If I were in that position, I would…); modals of obligation and possibility (should, have to, might, could); hedging (It seems…, It may be that…).
traps: Jumping to a decision in the first 10 seconds
Choosing the 'kind' option that breaks the law or a rule (e.g. faking a document)
Judging people harshly ('he is a bad person')
Sitting on the fence and never deciding

anchors.4: Names the competing values clearly at the start

feedback.whenLow: Open by naming the conflict in one sentence: 'This is a conflict between X and Y.'
feedback.whenHigh: You named the central conflict clearly before answering.
feedback.followUpAction: Practise naming the dilemma in one sentence for 3 Station 2 scenarios.

anchors.4: Considers everyone affected, including people not present

feedback.whenLow: Before deciding, list everyone affected (including people not in the room) and how each might see it.
feedback.whenHigh: You considered several perspectives fairly, including people not present.
feedback.followUpAction: For one dilemma, draw a stakeholder map: 5 people affected and what each wants.

anchors.4: Uses honesty, safety, fairness, autonomy and law appropriately

feedback.whenLow: Use named principles (honesty, safety, fairness, confidentiality, autonomy, the law) to justify each point.
feedback.whenHigh: You used clear ethical principles to support your reasoning.
feedback.followUpAction: Learn the principles in Toolkit › Station 2 and use at least 3 in your next answer.

anchors.1: No decision, or an extreme one
anchors.4: Clear, proportionate decision; says what would change it

feedback.whenLow: Always land on a decision. Give options from mildest to strongest, choose one, and say what would change your mind.
feedback.whenHigh: You reached a clear, balanced decision and justified it well.
feedback.followUpAction: Record a 2-minute answer that ends with 'So, on balance, I would… because…'.

stations.name: Problem Solving
stations.purpose: You have more problems than time. Assessors want to see safe, logical, step-by-step thinking, and how you adapt when the situation changes.

framework.name: Triage thinking: Risk · Facts · Rank · Act · Tell · Review

steps.label: Risk
steps.text: Is anyone in danger? Safety comes first.

steps.label: Facts
steps.text: What do I know? What do I still need to find out?

steps.label: Rank
steps.text: Order the tasks by urgency and importance, and say why.

steps.label: Act
steps.text: What will you do first? What can you delegate or ask for help with?

steps.label: Tell
steps.text: Who needs to be informed, and when?

steps.label: Review
steps.text: Check the result, adjust, and prevent it happening again.

phraseBank: My first priority would be …, because …
Before doing anything else, I'd check …
Once that's under control, I'd …
That's less urgent, so it could wait until …
I'd ask … for help with …
The risk of doing that is …
An alternative would be to …
If the situation changed and …, I'd …
To prevent this happening again, I'd …
Looking back, I'd make sure …
interviewee.grammarFocus: Sequencing language (first of all, then, once, after that, meanwhile); would + infinitive for planned actions; cause and effect (because, so that, which means).
traps: Trying to do everything yourself
Giving no reason for the order you choose
Ignoring safety or the most vulnerable person
Freezing when the interviewer adds a twist

anchors.4: Puts safety first and ranks tasks with reasons

feedback.whenLow: Start with 'Is anyone at risk?' and rank the tasks by urgency and importance, giving a reason for each.
feedback.whenHigh: You prioritised safely and explained the order of your actions.
feedback.followUpAction: Take one Station 3 scenario and rank every task on an urgent/important grid.

anchors.4: Clear sequence with signposting

feedback.whenLow: Signpost your plan: 'First…, then…, once that's done…, finally…'.
feedback.whenHigh: Your plan was logical and easy to follow.
feedback.followUpAction: Learn 6 sequencing phrases from Toolkit › Station 3 and use them in a 90-second plan.

anchors.1: Tries to do everything alone; one option only
anchors.4: Asks for help, delegates, compares options and trade-offs

feedback.whenLow: Show you would ask for help or delegate, and compare at least two options with their trade-offs.
feedback.whenHigh: You used the people and resources around you and weighed alternatives.
feedback.followUpAction: In your next practice, name one person you'd ask for help and one alternative plan.

anchors.1: Freezes or repeats the same plan
anchors.4: Calmly re-prioritises with new information

feedback.whenLow: When the interviewer adds a twist, pause, restate the new situation and re-rank your priorities out loud.
feedback.whenHigh: You adapted calmly when the situation changed.
feedback.followUpAction: Ask a friend to add 'What if…?' twists to a Station 3 scenario; practise re-prioritising aloud.

stations.name: Communication Role-play
stations.purpose: Your interviewer becomes a character. Treat them as a real person. Assessors watch how you listen, show empathy and explain clearly. How you give the information matters more than the information itself.

steps.label: Hello
steps.text: Introduce yourself and your role, check their name, ask if it's OK to talk.

steps.label: Explore
steps.text: Ask open questions: what do they know already? What worries them most?

steps.label: Acknowledge
steps.text: Name the feeling: 'I can see this is really frightening.' Give them time.

steps.label: Respond
steps.text: Explain in plain language, in small chunks. Check understanding. Agree next steps. Never promise what you can't deliver.

phraseBank: Hello, my name's … and I'm … Is it OK if we talk for a few minutes?
Could you tell me what you understand so far?
What's worrying you most?
That sounds really difficult.
I can understand why you'd feel …
Let me explain that more simply.
Does that make sense so far?
I'm afraid I can't …, but what I can do is …
Would it help if …?
Is there anything else you'd like to ask me?
interviewee.grammarFocus: Indirect questions for politeness (Could you tell me what happened?); softeners (I'm afraid…, I wonder if…); present continuous for feelings now (I can see you're feeling…).
traps: Jargon and talking too fast
Giving lots of information without checking understanding
False reassurance ('Don't worry, it'll be fine')
Arguing with an angry character instead of acknowledging the feeling

anchors.4: Introduces self and role, uses their name, warm and respectful

feedback.whenLow: Begin with your name and role, check the person's name, and ask permission to talk.
feedback.whenHigh: You built rapport quickly with a warm, respectful opening.
feedback.followUpAction: Memorise one natural opening line for role-plays and practise it with different characters.

anchors.4: Asks open questions, names the emotion, lets them speak

feedback.whenLow: Ask what worries them most, then name the feeling: 'I can see this is really upsetting.' Let silence work.
feedback.whenHigh: You listened well and acknowledged the person's feelings.
feedback.followUpAction: Practise 5 empathy phrases from Toolkit › Station 4 until they sound natural, not scripted.

anchors.4: Plain language, small chunks, checks understanding

feedback.whenLow: Use plain words, give information in small chunks, and check: 'Does that make sense so far?'
feedback.whenHigh: You explained clearly in plain language and checked understanding.
feedback.followUpAction: Explain one technical idea from your field to a family member in under 60 seconds with no jargon.

anchors.4: Agrees realistic next steps; no false reassurance

feedback.whenLow: Avoid 'Don't worry, it'll be fine'. Agree a realistic next step and be honest about what you can and can't do.
feedback.whenHigh: You were honest and agreed realistic next steps.
feedback.followUpAction: Write 3 honest alternatives to 'Don't worry' that still sound kind.

stations.name: Data & Critical Thinking
stations.purpose: You get a table, graph or claim. Assessors want accurate reading, healthy scepticism and a careful conclusion. Reading every number aloud scores nothing.

steps.label: Describe
steps.text: The main pattern, with 1–2 precise figures.

steps.label: Doubt
steps.text: Sample size, how the data was collected, who paid for it, what's missing, correlation vs causation, the small print.

steps.label: Decide
steps.text: A cautious conclusion, plus the further evidence or action you'd want.

phraseBank: The most striking thing is …
… is roughly twice as high as …
This suggests that …, but we can't be sure because …
The sample is very small, so …
This shows a correlation, not necessarily a cause.
It's not clear how the data was collected.
I'd want to know …
A fairer conclusion would be …
One alternative explanation is …
Before acting on this, I'd …
interviewee.grammarFocus: Comparatives and approximation (nearly twice as many, slightly lower); trend vocabulary (rose sharply, levelled off); hedging verbs (suggests, indicates, may reflect); the passive for method (The data was collected…).
traps: Reading every number aloud with no interpretation
Believing the headline
Confusing correlation with causation
Ignoring the small print

anchors.4: Picks out the main pattern with precise figures

feedback.whenLow: Lead with the main pattern and quote one or two precise figures, not every number.
feedback.whenHigh: You picked out the key pattern accurately with precise figures.
feedback.followUpAction: Describe one chart in 3 sentences: main trend, biggest difference, one exception.

anchors.1: Accepts the data or headline uncritically
anchors.4: Questions sample, method, bias, causation, small print

feedback.whenLow: Always check: How big is the sample? How was it collected? Who paid? Is it correlation or cause? What's missing?
feedback.whenHigh: You questioned the data critically and spotted its limitations.
feedback.followUpAction: Make a 5-question 'Doubt checklist' card and apply it to one news headline every day.

anchors.4: Hedged, evidence-based conclusion

feedback.whenLow: Use cautious language: 'This suggests…, but we can't be sure because…'.
feedback.whenHigh: Your conclusion was careful and matched the evidence.
feedback.followUpAction: Rewrite 3 overconfident headlines as cautious, accurate statements.

anchors.4: Names what extra data or next step is needed

feedback.whenLow: Finish by saying what extra information you'd want, or what sensible action could follow.
feedback.whenHigh: You suggested sensible further evidence and next steps.
feedback.followUpAction: In your next data station, end with 'Before deciding, I'd want to know…'.

stations.name: Teamwork & Reflection
stations.purpose: Assessors want real examples. They want to know what YOU did, how you work with others and whether you learn from mistakes.

steps.label: Situation
steps.text: Set the scene briefly: when, where, who.

steps.label: Task
steps.text: Your responsibility, or the challenge.

steps.label: Action
steps.text: What YOU did. Say 'I', not 'we'. This is most of your answer.

steps.label: Result
steps.text: What happened, with evidence if possible.

steps.label: Learning
steps.text: What you'd do differently, and how you've used the lesson since.

phraseBank: A good example of this was when …
My role was to …
The challenge was that …
I decided to …
I suggested that we …
As a result, …
Looking back, I realise …
If I had …, I would have …
Since then, I've …
What that taught me about teamwork is …
interviewee.grammarFocus: Narrative tenses (past simple, past continuous, past perfect); third conditional for reflection (If I had listened earlier, we would have…); reflective phrases (In hindsight…).
traps: Hypothetical answers ('I would…') when asked for a real example
Saying 'we' all the way through, so your own role is invisible
Blaming teammates
A 'failure' that is really a disguised strength

anchors.4: Specific, real situation told with STAR

feedback.whenLow: Answer with a real story (Situation, Task, Action, Result, Learning), not 'I would…'.
feedback.whenHigh: You used a specific, real example and structured it well.
feedback.followUpAction: Build a story bank: write 4 STAR stories (teamwork, failure, leadership, conflict).

anchors.4: Clear 'I' actions and responsibility

feedback.whenLow: Spend most of your answer on what YOU did. Switch from 'we' to 'I' for your actions.
feedback.whenHigh: Your own role and actions were clear.
feedback.followUpAction: Retell one group story and count your 'I' statements; aim for at least 5 actions.

anchors.4: Honest reflection; shows how they have changed

feedback.whenLow: End with what you learned and how you've used it since. Try 'If I had…, I would have…'.
feedback.whenHigh: You reflected honestly and showed real learning.
feedback.followUpAction: For each story in your bank, add one sentence beginning 'Since then, I've…'.

anchors.4: Respect, responsibility, resilience and fairness

feedback.whenLow: Show respect for teammates, even difficult ones. Explain how you understood their side.
feedback.whenHigh: You showed respect and responsibility toward your team.
feedback.followUpAction: Think of a difficult-teammate story and retell it from their point of view first.

vocabulary.def: deciding the order in which patients are treated, based on how urgent their condition is
vocabulary.example: In the ER, triage means the most urgent cases are seen first, not the people who arrived first.

vocabulary.def: a patient's agreement to treatment after the risks, benefits and alternatives have been clearly explained
vocabulary.example: Before the operation, the surgeon must obtain informed consent in language the patient understands.

vocabulary.def: the duty to keep a patient's personal and medical information private
vocabulary.example: Posting a photo of a patient's X-ray on TikTok is a clear breach of confidentiality.

vocabulary.def: when bacteria and other microbes change so that medicines no longer kill them
vocabulary.example: Buying antibiotics over the counter for a simple cold contributes to antimicrobial resistance.

vocabulary.def: Thailand's public health insurance (the '30-baht scheme') that covers citizens not in other schemes
vocabulary.example: Most patients at community hospitals are treated under the Universal Coverage Scheme.

vocabulary.def: care that focuses on comfort and quality of life for people with serious or terminal illness
vocabulary.example: With an ageing society, Thailand needs far more doctors trained in palliative care.

vocabulary.def: having two or more medical conditions at the same time
vocabulary.example: Many elderly patients have comorbidities such as diabetes and high blood pressure.

vocabulary.def: a small district-level government hospital, often staffed by newly graduated doctors
vocabulary.example: Many new graduates spend their government service years at a community hospital.

vocabulary.def: making clinical decisions using the best available research together with clinical experience and patient values
vocabulary.example: Evidence-based medicine means I should check the research, not just trust an advert.

vocabulary.def: physical and emotional exhaustion caused by long-term stress at work
vocabulary.example: Long shifts and staff shortages put young doctors at high risk of burnout.

vocabulary.term: weigh up the risks and benefits
vocabulary.def: consider carefully the possible good and bad results before deciding
vocabulary.example: A good doctor weighs up the risks and benefits with the patient, not for them.

vocabulary.def: a professional's responsibility to act in a way that protects the people they serve from harm
vocabulary.example: A doctor has a duty of care to every patient, whatever their background.

vocabulary.term: act in the patient's best interests
vocabulary.def: make decisions that truly benefit the patient, even if it is not what is easiest
vocabulary.example: Prescribing the expensive brand because of a free trip is not acting in the patient's best interests.

vocabulary.def: report a problem to someone more senior when you cannot solve it yourself
vocabulary.example: If I noticed a colleague was unsafe, I would escalate my concern to the supervising doctor.

vocabulary.def: honestly admit what you do not know or cannot do
vocabulary.example: As a medical student, I need to acknowledge my limitations and ask for help early.

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are applying to a six-year Doctor of Medicine programme. Many healthcare professionals help patients every day: nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists, medical technologists and public health officers. The interviewer wants to understand why you have chosen to become a doctor specifically, what you have done to test this choice, and what you believe makes a good doctor in Thailand today.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Why do you want to study medicine, rather than another healthcare profession such as nursing or pharmacy?
followUps: What exactly does a doctor do that a nurse does not? Give a concrete example.
What have you done outside school to find out what being a doctor is really like?
What is one thing you saw or learned that surprised you, or made you doubt your choice?
If you were not accepted into medicine this year, what would you do next, and why?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Your parents are both doctors. How do I know this is your choice and not theirs?

keyPoints: Distinguishes the doctor's role (diagnosis, overall clinical responsibility, leading the team) from other roles without looking down on nurses or pharmacists
Refers to specific personal experience such as hospital shadowing, volunteering, a family illness or a medical camp, and reflects on what it taught them
Shows awareness of the realities: six years of study, long shifts, night duty, government service obligation, emotional stress
Gives a plan B that still shows commitment and maturity, not panic or indifference
Motivation centres on patients and service rather than status, salary or family pressure
warningSigns: Says 'I want to help people' with no explanation of why a doctor and not another profession
Speaks about nurses or other professions as 'less important' or 'for students who cannot get into medicine'
Motivation is mainly prestige, money or 'my parents want me to'

interviewee.doorPrompt: Most medical graduates in Thailand must complete several years of government service, and many are sent to community hospitals in the provinces. These hospitals often have too few doctors, long queues, and patients with chronic diseases such as diabetes and high blood pressure. Some young doctors pay the fine to leave service early. You will be asked about your understanding of a doctor's life outside Bangkok.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What do you think daily life is like for a young doctor working in a community hospital in a rural province?
followUps: Why do you think many doctors leave rural hospitals after their service ends?
What could the government or the medical schools do to keep more doctors in rural areas?
Would you be happy to be sent to a district hospital in Nan or Mae Hong Son for three years? Be honest.
If a friend of yours wanted to pay the fine and leave service early to work in a private hospital in Bangkok, what would you say to them?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Every candidate tells me they want to work in the countryside. Most of them leave as soon as they can. Why would you be different?

keyPoints: Describes realistic details: high patient numbers, on-call nights, limited specialists and equipment, need to refer patients, working with village health volunteers
Explains causes of the shortage (workload, isolation, lower income, family needs, training opportunities in cities) without blaming individuals
Suggests practical solutions such as better support, telemedicine, rotating specialists, recruiting students from rural areas
Gives an honest personal answer that balances commitment with realistic concerns
Treats the friend's choice with fairness, recognising both personal circumstances and the public duty behind the scholarship-style system
warningSigns: Has no idea that government service exists or what community hospitals do
Speaks negatively or stereotypically about rural patients
Gives an obviously rehearsed 'I will happily stay forever' answer with no awareness of the challenges

interviewee.doorPrompt: This is a 'pressure' station. The examiner is deliberately direct and may challenge everything you say. You will be asked about the future of medicine in Thailand, about this faculty, and about your own plans. Stay calm, think aloud, and be honest if you do not know something. Showing how you handle uncertainty matters more than having a perfect answer.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What major project do you think our faculty will be running fifteen years from now, and why?
followUps: You don't actually know what our faculty does now, do you? If you don't know us, why do you want to come here?
Many people say AI will diagnose diseases better than doctors within ten years. So why should Thailand spend six years training you?
With an ageing society and falling birth rates, which medical specialties will Thailand need most in 2040?
What will you personally be doing in fifteen years? What if that specialty is no longer needed?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Do you really want to be a doctor if you don't even know what you'll be doing? Maybe you just want the title.

keyPoints: Stays calm and polite under pressure; admits gaps in knowledge honestly instead of inventing facts
Links predictions to real Thai trends: ageing society, NCDs, PM2.5, AI and digital health, antimicrobial resistance, road traffic injuries
Argues that AI will support rather than replace doctors, mentioning judgement, communication, ethics and responsibility
Shows they have researched the faculty (e.g. its hospital, community programmes, research strengths) and can say why it suits them
Accepts that career plans may change and shows flexibility and lifelong learning
warningSigns: Becomes defensive, argues with the examiner, or freezes and gives up
Makes up specific facts about the faculty to sound impressive
Says AI makes doctors unnecessary or, the opposite, dismisses AI as irrelevant to medicine

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a newly qualified doctor working at a private clinic. Your cousin Krit is flying to Japan tomorrow for a work trip. The airline requires an official RT-PCR certificate, but Krit only has a negative ATK result taken at home this morning. Krit asks you to 'just write' a negative RT-PCR certificate on clinic paper, saying, 'You know I'm fine. It's only a formality, and the trip is important for my job.'

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do, and why?
followUps: Who could be harmed if you wrote this certificate? Think beyond Krit.
Krit says, 'Family helps family. If you refuse, I'll lose this contract.' How do you respond?
What if Krit's ATK was positive but Krit had no symptoms and still begged you?
Suppose you later discover a colleague at your clinic has been selling false certificates. What would you do?
interviewer.pressureProbe: It's a small thing that thousands of people did during COVID. Isn't refusing just being rigid and unkind to your own family?

keyPoints: Clearly refuses to falsify a medical document, explaining it is dishonest, illegal and a breach of professional trust
Identifies wider stakeholders: other passengers, the destination country, the clinic, the reputation of Thai medical certificates
Remains kind to Krit and offers a practical alternative, such as arranging a real RT-PCR test with a fast result or contacting the airline
Explains why doctors' signatures carry public trust, so the 'small thing' argument does not hold
Would report a colleague's systematic fraud through proper channels while being fair about gathering facts first
warningSigns: Agrees to write it 'just this once' because the test is probably negative
Refuses coldly with no empathy or alternative for the cousin
Says they would ignore a colleague selling false certificates because 'it's not my business'

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a junior doctor on night duty at a small community hospital near the border. A construction worker from a neighbouring country arrives with a deep, bleeding wound on his arm. He has no health insurance, no ID card and speaks little Thai. The hospital finance officer tells you, 'We already lose money on these cases. Just bandage it and send him away before the morning. He might also be illegal.'

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you handle this situation?
followUps: Is it your job as a doctor to think about the patient's documents or the hospital's budget? Explain.
How would you communicate with the patient if no interpreter is available at night?
What if the wound needed surgery that only the provincial hospital could do, and the referral would cost money no one can pay?
The finance officer says you are being naive about how hospitals survive. How would you respond respectfully?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Your idealism will bankrupt small hospitals. Who pays for your kindness?

keyPoints: States that emergency treatment must be based on clinical need, not nationality, documents or ability to pay
Assesses and stabilises the patient first (stop bleeding, check for nerve or tendon damage, tetanus) before discussing money
Uses practical communication strategies: a co-worker or employer to interpret, translation apps, simple gestures, written diagrams
Separates clinical duty from administrative issues, involving social workers or the employer, and mentions that migrant health insurance schemes exist
Treats the finance officer's concern as real and suggests raising funding issues through proper channels, not at the bedside
warningSigns: Agrees to send the patient away or give minimal care to save money
Talks about reporting the patient to the police as the first action
Dismisses the finance officer's concerns entirely as unimportant

interviewee.doorPrompt: A single donor liver has become available at a transplant centre. Two patients are a good medical match. Patient A is a seven-year-old child with a rare liver disease who has been on the waiting list for four months. Patient B is a 45-year-old father of three whose liver failed after years of heavy drinking; he has now been sober for eight months. Both will die within weeks without a transplant.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Who do you think should receive the liver, and how would you reach that decision?
followUps: Should the fact that Patient B's illness was partly caused by alcohol affect the decision? Why or why not?
What if the adult had a much higher chance of surviving five years after the transplant than the child?
Who should make this kind of decision: one doctor, a committee, the families, or a fixed system? Why?
If the child's family asked to meet you to understand the decision, what would you say to them?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Stop sitting on the fence. You have ten seconds. Child or adult? Tell me now.

keyPoints: Recognises that real decisions use transparent criteria (medical urgency, likelihood of success, time on list, compatibility) decided by a committee, not personal feelings
Discusses whether 'blame' for lifestyle-related disease is fair, noting addiction is an illness and the patient has stayed sober
Considers years of life gained, dependants and likelihood of success without claiming any single factor settles it
When pressed, commits to a reasoned position while acknowledging the moral cost of the choice
Shows compassion for the family who does not receive the organ and talks about honest, gentle communication
warningSigns: Instantly chooses the child because 'children are more valuable' with no further reasoning
Says alcoholics do not deserve treatment
Refuses to engage when pressed, or changes answer every time the examiner pushes

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a junior doctor in a busy emergency room in Khon Kaen. Your aunt arrives with a mild fever and a sore throat and wants to be seen immediately: 'I'm family, I don't want to wait two hours.' At the same moment, an unknown man is brought in by ambulance after a motorbike crash, unconscious and breathing poorly. Another doctor is busy with a cardiac arrest, and there is one nurse free.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do in the next ten minutes, and in what order?
followUps: How would you explain to your aunt that she has to wait?
What if your aunt then said she was having chest pain?
Should doctors ever treat their own relatives? What are the risks?
Later, your mother calls you angry that you 'ignored' her sister. How would you respond?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Your aunt raised you when your parents were working. You owe her. Doesn't loyalty matter at all?

keyPoints: Immediately prioritises the unconscious crash victim based on clinical urgency (airway, breathing, circulation) and calls for help
Delegates appropriately, e.g. asks the nurse to check the aunt's vital signs and reassess her
Explains triage to the aunt briefly and kindly without showing favouritism
Recognises that new symptoms like chest pain change the priority and require reassessment
Discusses the risks of treating relatives (lost objectivity, confidentiality, family conflict)
warningSigns: Sees the aunt first because she is family or because she is louder
Tries to manage the crash victim entirely alone without calling senior help
Is dismissive or rude to the aunt

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are the only doctor on night duty at a 30-bed district hospital. At 2 a.m., five things happen at once: (1) a nurse reports a diabetic patient's blood sugar is very low; (2) a mother calls about a child with a mild rash; (3) a relative complains loudly about the noise on the ward; (4) the lab says a patient's potassium result is dangerously high; (5) the director's LINE message asks for tomorrow's bed report.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Put these five tasks in order and explain your reasoning.
followUps: Which tasks can you safely delegate to someone else, and to whom?
How would you deal with two life-threatening problems at exactly the same time?
What if the child's mother called back saying the child now had a high fever and was very sleepy?
You are exhausted at 5 a.m. and worry you might make a mistake. What would you do?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You've ranked the director's message last. Your director decides your career. Isn't that naive?

keyPoints: Ranks the low blood sugar and high potassium first and explains both are immediately life-threatening, giving quick nurse instructions for one while going to the other
Uses delegation: nurses for immediate treatment steps, ward staff for the noise complaint
Gives clear safety-netting advice for the rash call and re-prioritises when new warning signs appear
Puts administrative tasks last and is willing to explain this to the director
Shows insight into fatigue and patient safety, e.g. calling the on-call senior or using checklists
warningSigns: Prioritises the director's message or the noise complaint over unstable patients
Tries to do everything personally with no delegation or communication
Thinks admitting tiredness or asking for help is a sign of weakness

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a young doctor at a community hospital in Ayutthaya during a severe flood. The roads to the provincial hospital are closed for at least 24 hours. Electricity is unstable and the generator has fuel for about 12 hours. You have: a woman in early labour with a previous caesarean, an elderly man who needs dialysis tomorrow, a child with high fever, and twenty people sheltering in the hospital lobby.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What are your priorities, and what is your plan for the next 24 hours?
followUps: Who would you contact first outside the hospital, and why?
The generator can only power either the operating theatre or the ward fridges with vaccines and insulin. Which do you choose?
What if the woman in labour now develops complications and a boat transfer would take three hours in the dark?
How would you keep the twenty people in the lobby calm and safe while you deal with patients?
interviewer.pressureProbe: There's no right answer here and someone may die because of your choice. How will you live with that?

keyPoints: Quickly identifies the highest-risk patient (labour after previous caesarean) and plans early for transfer or emergency surgery support
Contacts the provincial hospital, emergency services, military or local authorities for boats or helicopters and for fuel
Makes a reasoned decision about the generator, naming the trade-offs and looking for alternatives (ice boxes, moving insulin)
Uses non-medical resources: village health volunteers, local leaders, family members to support the shelter
Accepts uncertainty honestly and talks about documenting decisions and debriefing afterwards
warningSigns: Has no plan to seek outside help and tries to solve everything internally
Ignores the people sheltering in the lobby or the long-term needs of the dialysis patient
Panics, or claims they would definitely save everyone

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a final-year medical student on a hospital ward. Khun Fah, 34, had a breast biopsy last week. You saw on the computer that the report has just arrived and looks worrying, but the senior doctor has not yet reviewed it and will see Khun Fah tomorrow morning. Khun Fah stops you in the corridor and asks about her results. You have about five minutes.

interviewer.openingQuestion: The interviewer will play Khun Fah. Please begin when you are ready.
followUps: Why did you choose not to tell her what you saw on the screen?
How did you know whether she understood and felt supported?
What if she had said, 'I'm a nurse myself. Just show me the screen'?
What would you report to the senior doctor afterwards?
interviewer.pressureProbe: She has a right to know her own results. Isn't hiding them paternalistic?

actor.role: Khun Fah, 34, an office worker and mother of a five-year-old, waiting for breast biopsy results
actor.brief: You have barely slept for a week. You saw the student look at a screen and then look away, so you suspect bad news. You want an answer now because you have to arrange childcare if you need surgery; your hidden fear is leaving your daughter without a mother.
lines: Excuse me, you're on Dr Somchai's team, aren't you? Have my biopsy results come back? Please, just tell me.
I saw your face when you looked at the computer. It's bad, isn't it?
I have a five-year-old daughter. I need to know whether to plan for an operation.
actor.howToReact: If the candidate uses jargon, says 'I can't tell you' and walks off, or gives false reassurance, become more upset and press harder ('So it IS cancer!'). If they acknowledge your fear, are honest about their role and offer concrete help, such as asking the doctor to see you today, calm down and thank them.

keyPoints: Introduces themselves honestly as a student and explains that results must be reviewed and explained by the responsible doctor
Does not lie (e.g. 'I haven't seen anything') but also does not reveal or hint at unconfirmed findings
Acknowledges her anxiety, asks what she is most worried about, and offers support such as arranging an earlier appointment
Takes practical action: informs the senior doctor of her distress and asks whether the meeting can happen sooner
Checks for support at home and gives clear information about when and how she will get results
warningSigns: Tells her the result looks like cancer, or shows her the screen
Gives false reassurance such as 'I'm sure it's nothing'
Ends the conversation quickly to escape the discomfort

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a junior doctor in an outpatient clinic. Mr Prasert, 50, has a mild stomach upset. You have examined him, he is well hydrated, and he only needs medicine and rest at home. However, he insists on being admitted for two nights because his private insurance pays only for in-patient care, and he has already paid high premiums for years.

interviewer.openingQuestion: The interviewer will play Mr Prasert. Please begin when you are ready.
followUps: Why can't you simply admit him? Who would be harmed?
How did you show him that you understood his frustration?
What if he threatened to complain about you on Facebook and to the hospital director?
Your senior later says, 'Just admit him, it keeps customers happy.' What would you do?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Private hospitals are businesses. If you refuse, he'll go next door and they'll admit him. What have you achieved?

actor.role: Mr Prasert, 50, owner of a small printing business in Nonthaburi
actor.brief: You feel unwell and are annoyed that you have paid insurance premiums for ten years without using them. You believe 'everyone does this' and that the doctor is being difficult. Your hidden concern is money: business has been slow and you cannot afford two days off without compensation.
lines: Doctor, I need to be admitted. My insurance only pays if I stay in hospital.
I've paid premiums for ten years! My friend was admitted for exactly the same thing last month.
If I go home, I lose two days of work and get nothing. Do you understand how hard business is right now?
actor.howToReact: If the candidate lectures you about fraud, uses insurance or legal jargon, or seems to accuse you of lying, raise your voice and threaten to complain. If they recognise your financial worries, explain the reasons kindly and offer practical alternatives, become calmer and more reasonable.

keyPoints: Explains clearly and calmly that admission must be based on medical need, not on insurance rules
Mentions that unnecessary admission is insurance fraud, wastes beds and exposes him to hospital infection risks
Acknowledges his frustration about paying premiums and offers practical help, such as a clear medical certificate or advice on contacting his insurer
Gives safety-net advice about warning signs that would require him to return
Stays professional if threatened and would discuss the senior's instruction respectfully but firmly
warningSigns: Agrees to admit him to avoid conflict
Lectures him or accuses him of being dishonest
Uses technical language about policy without empathy

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are an intern at a community hospital in Chiang Rai. Grandma Boonmee, 79, has visited the hospital six times this month with mild dizziness. Each time, tests are normal and she is sent home. She lives alone; her daughter Nok works in Bangkok. Today Nok has phoned the hospital angry, and you have been asked to speak to her on the phone.

interviewer.openingQuestion: The interviewer will play Nok, Grandma Boonmee's daughter. Please begin when you are ready.
followUps: What do you think is really going on with Grandma Boonmee?
What support could the hospital or the community offer an elderly person living alone?
What if Nok asked you to admit her mother 'until I can come home at New Year'?
How does Thailand's ageing society affect hospitals like this one?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You're not a social worker. Your job is to treat disease. Why are you wasting time on loneliness?

actor.role: Nok, 45, Grandma Boonmee's daughter, an accountant in Bangkok
actor.brief: You are angry because your mother called you crying, saying the hospital 'keeps throwing her out'. You don't fully know she has had six normal visits. Your hidden concern is guilt: you moved to Bangkok for work and feel you have abandoned her.
lines: This is the sixth time you've sent my mother home! What kind of hospital are you running?
She's 79 and dizzy. Do you wait until she falls and breaks her hip?
I can't just leave my job and go back to Chiang Rai. What am I supposed to do?
actor.howToReact: If the candidate is defensive, quotes test numbers or rushes you, become angrier and say you will complain to the provincial health office. If they listen, acknowledge your worry and guilt, and offer a realistic plan for your mother, slowly calm down and start to talk about how lonely she has been.

keyPoints: Lets Nok express her anger, then acknowledges both her worry and her guilt at being far away
Explains the test results in plain language without dismissing the symptoms
Raises gently that loneliness, low mood or medication issues may be contributing, and asks about her mother's daily life
Suggests concrete community solutions: village health volunteers, home visits, elderly clubs, regular phone calls, a follow-up appointment
Explains clearly but kindly why long-term admission without medical need is not appropriate
warningSigns: Tells Nok her mother is 'wasting the hospital's time'
Becomes defensive about the hospital's decisions
Promises admission or further tests just to end the conflict

interviewee.doorPrompt: A health news website published the table below under the headline: 'Antibiotic resistance is out of control in Hospital D – avoid it!' You have one minute to study the table before discussing it with the interviewer.

data.caption: E. coli samples resistant to a common antibiotic, four hospitals, 2025
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Hospital D tested only 45 samples; as a referral centre it receives patients who have already failed treatment elsewhere. Testing methods were not standardised between hospitals.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What can and can't we conclude from this data?
followUps: Why might Hospital D show a higher percentage than the others?
What extra information would you need before deciding whether Hospital D is really worse?
If you were the director of Hospital D, how would you respond to the headline?
What can ordinary people in Thailand do to reduce antibiotic resistance?
interviewer.pressureProbe: 38 percent is nearly double the others. Surely the numbers speak for themselves?

keyPoints: Notices Hospital D's very small sample size (45 vs hundreds) and explains why percentages from small samples are unreliable
Recognises that a referral centre treats sicker, previously treated patients, so higher resistance may reflect patient mix, not poor practice
Asks about testing methods, time period and how samples were selected
Calls the headline misleading and suggests a fairer conclusion
Links AMR to Thai realities such as antibiotics bought without prescription and misuse for colds
warningSigns: Accepts the headline and says people should avoid Hospital D
Only reads numbers aloud without interpreting them
Ignores the note completely

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a junior doctor. A pharmaceutical representative gives you a brochure for 'Cardiolex', a new cholesterol drug, and invites you to a sponsored conference in Tokyo. The brochure includes the table below. Cardiolex costs about ten times more than the generic drug currently used in your hospital under the Universal Coverage Scheme.

data.caption: Cardiolex vs generic statin: 12-month results
rows: Patients who stopped due to side effects
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Study funded and analysed by the manufacturer of Cardiolex. Only 12 months long; patients were selected from private hospitals in Bangkok.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Based on this information, would you start prescribing Cardiolex? Why or why not?
followUps: Which parts of this study make you most cautious?
What does 'heart attacks reduced by 33%' actually mean in numbers of patients?
Should young doctors accept sponsored trips from drug companies? Where would you draw the line?
What if a senior consultant you admire strongly recommends Cardiolex?
interviewer.pressureProbe: If it helps even one patient, isn't cost irrelevant? You're putting money above lives.

keyPoints: Identifies the conflict of interest: manufacturer funding and analysis, and the sponsored trip
Notes small numbers of heart attacks (2 vs 3), so the '33% reduction' is a relative figure based on one patient
Points out higher side-effect discontinuation and short study length
Considers cost-effectiveness for a public system: money spent here cannot be spent on other patients
Would look for independent evidence and national guidelines before changing practice
warningSigns: Accepts the brochure's conclusions because the LDL fall is larger
Sees no problem with accepting the Tokyo trip
Says cost should never matter in medicine without considering the wider health system

interviewee.doorPrompt: A popular TikTok account with 800,000 followers posts this video caption: 'My uncle refused chemo and used cannabis oil from a shop in Bangkok instead. Six months later his tumour is GONE! Doctors don't want you to know this. Thousands of comments say the same thing!' Your grandmother, who has just been diagnosed with cancer, has sent you this video on LINE and asks whether she should stop her treatment.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you evaluate this claim, and what would you say to your grandmother?
followUps: Why is 'thousands of comments say the same thing' not good evidence?
What kind of evidence would convince you that cannabis oil can treat cancer?
Medical cannabis is legal for some uses in Thailand. What is the difference between those uses and this claim?
What if your grandmother said, 'I don't trust doctors, they just want my money'?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Doctors have been wrong before. Maybe this uncle found something big pharma is hiding. Can you prove he's wrong?

keyPoints: Identifies that a single anecdote cannot show cause and effect; we don't know the diagnosis, other treatments or follow-up
Mentions selection bias: people whose cannabis treatment failed do not post videos
Describes what proper evidence looks like (controlled trials, peer review, large samples)
Distinguishes approved medical uses (e.g. symptom relief, nausea) from claims of curing cancer
Responds to the grandmother with respect and empathy, encourages her to discuss it with her oncologist rather than stopping treatment alone
warningSigns: Says the claim might be true so the grandmother could try stopping chemo
Mocks the grandmother or dismisses her fears
Argues that cannabis has no medical use at all

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are in a group of four preparing a science fair project on PM2.5 in Bangkok schools. The deadline is in one week. One member, Ton, has not attended the last three meetings, has not done his section, and replies to the LINE group only with stickers. The other two members want to tell the teacher and remove Ton's name from the project.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do in this situation, and tell me about a real time you worked with someone who was not contributing.
followUps: What might be happening in Ton's life that you don't know about?
At what point, if any, would you go to the teacher?
Tell me about a real time you worked in a team where someone was not contributing. What did you do?
Looking back, what would you do differently, and how would this experience help you on a hospital ward team?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You're being too soft. In a hospital, a team member who doesn't do their job could kill someone. Shouldn't you just report him immediately?

keyPoints: Suggests speaking to Ton privately and kindly first, to find out the reason before judging
Considers possible causes such as family problems, illness, mental health or confusion about the task
Balances fairness to the other members with support for Ton, e.g. redistributing tasks, setting clear mini-deadlines
Gives a real STAR example with a specific action they personally took and an honest result
Links the lesson to clinical teamwork, safety and escalating concerns appropriately
warningSigns: Wants to remove Ton immediately without talking to him
Does all the work themselves silently and resents it
Cannot give a real example, or the example makes them the hero with no reflection

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a second-year medical student on a hospital visit with a small group. That evening you see that Mint, a classmate and close friend, has posted a TikTok video from the ward. It shows an elderly patient's face in the background and a caption joking about 'my first real patient lol'. The video already has 5,000 views.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do, and why? Then tell me about a real time you had to challenge a friend about something they did wrong.
followUps: Why is this a problem even if Mint meant no harm?
Mint says, 'Everyone posts stuff like this, chill.' What do you reply?
What if Mint deleted the video but you knew it had been screenshotted and shared?
Tell me about a time you had to challenge a friend or peer about something they did wrong. How did it go?
interviewer.pressureProbe: If you report your best friend, you'll lose her. Is a TikTok video really worth that?

keyPoints: Recognises the breach of patient confidentiality and dignity, and the damage to trust in doctors
Acts quickly: contacts Mint directly and asks her to remove the video immediately
Understands that if harm has spread, it may need to be reported to a tutor so the patient can be protected and informed
Shows loyalty in a mature way: supporting Mint to take responsibility rather than hiding it
Gives a real personal example of challenging a peer, with reflection on what they learned
warningSigns: Ignores it because Mint is a friend
Publicly shames Mint online or in the class LINE group
Says patient confidentiality only matters if the patient finds out

interviewee.doorPrompt: This is a reflective station with a demanding examiner. Doctors make mistakes, and how they respond to them affects patient safety. The examiner will ask you about a real mistake or failure in your own life, and may push you hard on the details. Think of a genuine example where you were at least partly responsible, not a situation where someone else was to blame.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Tell me about a significant mistake you made, and what you did about it.
followUps: What exactly was your part in it? Be specific.
How did you feel at the time, and how did you deal with those feelings?
What have you changed since then? Give me evidence that you really changed.
Imagine you are a doctor and you gave a patient the wrong dose of medicine. Nobody noticed. What would you do?
interviewer.pressureProbe: That doesn't sound like a real mistake. It sounds like a disguised strength. Do you have a real one?

keyPoints: Chooses a genuine, meaningful mistake and takes clear personal responsibility
Uses a clear STAR structure with honest emotions and specific actions taken to repair the situation
Shows concrete learning and evidence of changed behaviour over time
For the dose scenario, says they would check the patient, inform the senior doctor, tell the patient honestly and report it through the proper system
Stays composed and reflective when challenged
warningSigns: Gives a 'fake' weakness such as 'I work too hard' or 'I'm a perfectionist'
Blames others or circumstances for the mistake
Would hide the medication error because nobody noticed

vocabulary.def: tooth decay caused by bacteria that turn sugar into acid
vocabulary.example: Dental caries is still one of the most common diseases among Thai preschool children.

vocabulary.def: infection and inflammation of the gums and the bone that supports the teeth
vocabulary.example: Untreated periodontal disease is a major cause of tooth loss in older adults.

vocabulary.def: a protective coating painted on teeth to strengthen enamel and prevent decay
vocabulary.example: Applying fluoride varnish twice a year is a cheap way to protect young children's teeth.

vocabulary.def: a thin plastic coating placed in the grooves of back teeth to stop food and bacteria collecting
vocabulary.example: School programmes in Thailand place fissure sealants on children's first permanent molars.

vocabulary.def: a procedure that removes infected nerve tissue from inside a tooth to save it
vocabulary.example: Many patients are frightened of root canal treatment, but it usually feels like a normal filling.

vocabulary.def: the branch of dentistry that corrects the position of teeth and jaws, for example with braces
vocabulary.example: Orthodontics is popular in Bangkok, but braces should be fitted only by trained dentists.

vocabulary.def: the hard, protective outer layer of a tooth
vocabulary.example: Overusing strong whitening products can make enamel sensitive.

vocabulary.def: fear or stress about visiting the dentist, which can make people avoid treatment
vocabulary.example: Dental anxiety often begins with a painful experience in childhood.

vocabulary.def: a trained oral health worker who provides basic dental care and prevention, often at sub-district health centres in Thailand
vocabulary.example: In rural areas, dental therapists do much of the preventive work in schools.

vocabulary.def: giving more treatment than a patient actually needs
vocabulary.example: Replacing healthy fillings just to increase income is overtreatment.

vocabulary.def: skill and precision in using your hands
vocabulary.example: Dentistry demands excellent manual dexterity because you work in a very small space.

vocabulary.def: help a person feel relaxed and less worried
vocabulary.example: A good dentist puts nervous patients at ease before picking up any instrument.

vocabulary.def: find a sensible middle position between two competing needs
vocabulary.example: Dentists must strike a balance between a patient's cosmetic wishes and long-term oral health.

vocabulary.def: it is better to stop a problem from happening than to fix it later
vocabulary.example: In children's oral health, prevention is better than cure, and much cheaper too.

vocabulary.def: a situation where personal gain could influence a professional decision
vocabulary.example: Earning commission on every veneer sold creates a clear conflict of interest.

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are applying to a six-year Doctor of Dental Surgery programme. Some people say dentistry is 'medicine for the mouth'; others say it is closer to a craft or an art. Many applicants who choose dentistry also had good enough grades for medicine. The interviewer wants to understand why you have chosen dentistry and what you know about the profession.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Why do you want to become a dentist rather than a doctor?
followUps: What personal qualities and skills does a dentist need that a doctor might not?
How have you tested whether you have the manual dexterity for this work?
What did you see or learn when exploring dentistry that you did not expect?
How is oral health connected to a person's general health? Give an example.
interviewer.pressureProbe: Dentists earn more and work shorter hours than doctors. Isn't that the real reason?

keyPoints: Gives a specific reason for dentistry: combining health care with precise practical work, long-term relationships with patients, visible results
Describes real exploration such as observing at a dental clinic, a dental camp, or talking to dental students
Shows evidence of dexterity (e.g. drawing, music, model-making, sewing) and reflects on its relevance
Links oral health to general health, such as diabetes and gum disease, or pain affecting children's school performance
Answers the money question honestly without making income the main motive
warningSigns: Suggests dentistry is an 'easier' or second-choice version of medicine
Only mentions money, comfortable hours or family business
Has no idea what a dentist does beyond fillings and cleaning

interviewee.doorPrompt: In Bangkok, many private dental clinics advertise on Instagram and TikTok with 'Hollywood smile' veneers, whitening packages and celebrity patients. Meanwhile, in many provinces, children still have high rates of tooth decay and some adults lose most of their teeth before old age. Dentists in Thailand may work in government hospitals, health centres, universities or private clinics.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Is a dentist mainly a health professional or a provider of beauty services? What do you think?
followUps: What is the role of a dentist working in a government community hospital compared with a private clinic in Siam?
Is there anything wrong with dentists earning most of their income from cosmetic treatments?
Which area of dentistry interests you most, and why?
If you were offered a well-paid job in a cosmetic clinic or a lower-paid job in a rural hospital, how would you decide?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Thailand has enough dentists in Bangkok doing veneers. Why should the government invest in training one more?

keyPoints: Argues that dentistry is fundamentally health care, while accepting that appearance affects confidence and quality of life
Shows awareness of inequality between Bangkok and rural areas, and of public dental services and prevention programmes
Recognises ethical limits of cosmetic work, such as harming healthy teeth or overtreatment
Names a specific area of interest (paediatric dentistry, public health dentistry, oral surgery, orthodontics) with a sensible reason
Explains a career decision process that weighs personal and public responsibilities
warningSigns: Sees dentistry purely as a beauty business
Is dismissive of rural or public service work
Cannot name any part of dentistry beyond cosmetic treatments

interviewee.doorPrompt: This is a pressure station. The examiner will challenge your motivation directly and may suggest that you are not suitable for dentistry. Your task is to stay calm, listen to the challenge, and respond with honest, specific evidence from your own life. You will not be judged on agreeing or disagreeing with the examiner, but on how clearly and maturely you reason.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Convince me in two minutes that you will still enjoy dentistry after twenty years of looking into people's mouths.
followUps: Dentistry can be repetitive and physically tiring. Back and neck pain are common. How will you cope?
Many dentists say the most stressful part is not the teeth but the patients. Why might that be?
What will you do if you discover in third year that you are not good at practical work?
Where do you see yourself in fifteen years, and how might technology such as 3D printing and AI change your work?
interviewer.pressureProbe: I'm still not convinced. Honestly, I think you'd be happier in another field. Change my mind.

keyPoints: Stays calm, polite and confident without becoming defensive
Gives concrete evidence of sustained interest, such as repeated clinic observation or volunteering, not just a single visit
Shows realistic awareness of the physical, emotional and business pressures of the job
Responds to the 'not good at practical work' question with a growth mindset and specific strategies
Mentions how digital dentistry (scanners, CAD/CAM, 3D printing, AI imaging) will change the profession
warningSigns: Becomes upset or argues aggressively with the examiner
Repeats the same general phrase ('I love helping people') with no new evidence
Says they would simply quit if they found the work difficult

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a newly qualified dentist in a private clinic in Thonglor. Mint, a 20-year-old beauty influencer with 300,000 followers, wants 'the whitest teeth possible' before a brand event in five days. Her teeth already show some sensitivity and thin enamel. She asks for three strong whitening sessions this week and offers to promote the clinic for free. Your clinic manager is very excited about the publicity.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you respond to Mint's request?
followUps: What are the risks of what she is asking for?
How would you explain your recommendation to the clinic manager, who wants the publicity?
What if Mint said, 'It's my body and my money. I accept the risks'?
Is it ever acceptable for a dentist to treat someone in exchange for social media promotion?
interviewer.pressureProbe: If you say no, she'll go to the clinic across the road and they will do it anyway. So isn't it safer if you do it?

keyPoints: Puts the patient's oral health first and explains the risks of over-whitening on thin enamel (sensitivity, damage) clearly
Offers a safe alternative: a professional assessment, a gentler plan, realistic expectations about shade and timing
Respects Mint's autonomy but explains that a dentist should not provide treatment likely to cause harm
Identifies the conflict of interest created by free promotion and the clinic's commercial pressure
Is willing to stand firm with the manager while staying professional and suggesting ethical ways to market the clinic
warningSigns: Agrees to all three sessions because of the publicity
Dismisses Mint's wishes or lectures her about vanity
Says 'someone else would do it anyway' justifies doing it

interviewee.doorPrompt: You have just started working at a busy private dental chain in Bangkok. The owner holds a meeting and says each dentist must reach a monthly 'treatment value' target.
