He suggests recommending replacement of all old silver fillings with white ones and advising crowns 'whenever possible'. Your first patient, Mr Ton, 42, has several old fillings that are in good condition.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you recommend to Mr Ton, and how would you handle the owner's instructions?
followUps: Are there any situations where replacing old fillings would be appropriate?
How would you explain your treatment plan honestly if Mr Ton asked, 'Should I change them to white ones?'
What if you discovered other dentists in the chain were regularly overtreating patients?
You need this job to repay a loan. How does that affect your decision, if at all?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Every private business has targets. Isn't refusing just being unrealistic about the real world?

keyPoints: Recommends treatment based only on clinical need, explaining that replacing healthy fillings removes healthy tooth structure
Gives balanced information so Mr Ton can make an informed choice, including legitimate reasons for replacement
Recognises overtreatment as an ethical breach that harms patients and trust in the profession
Considers practical steps: discussing concerns with the owner, documentation, seeking advice from a senior or the Dental Council
Is honest about personal pressures but keeps patient welfare as the deciding factor
warningSigns: Follows the owner's instructions to meet targets
Says the patient will not know the difference anyway
Ignores colleagues' overtreatment because it does not affect them

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a junior dentist at a provincial hospital. Dr Somsak, 61, a senior dentist you admire and who trained you, has recently developed a visible tremor in his hands. You have noticed that several of his recent fillings have needed to be redone, and a patient complained of a cut on her lip. Dr Somsak jokes that it is 'just too much coffee' and plans to work for four more years.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What, if anything, would you do?
followUps: Whose interests do you need to consider here?
How would you start a conversation with Dr Somsak about this?
What if Dr Somsak became angry and told you to mind your own business?
What if the head of department is Dr Somsak's close friend and seems to ignore the problem?
interviewer.pressureProbe: He trained you and he has served this province for 30 years. Isn't reporting him a betrayal?

keyPoints: Recognises a potential patient-safety issue that cannot simply be ignored out of respect or loyalty
Plans a private, respectful conversation first, expressing concern for Dr Somsak's health rather than accusing him
Suggests supportive solutions such as a medical check-up, a change of duties (teaching, prevention, consultations), or reduced clinical load
Knows when and how to escalate if risk continues: department head, hospital director, professional body
Balances compassion for the senior colleague with the duty to protect patients
warningSigns: Ignores it because he is senior or a mentor
Goes straight to social media or tells patients
Speaks about the colleague with disrespect or assumes he is careless

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are the only dentist on a one-day mobile dental unit visiting a primary school in Sakon Nakhon. There are about 200 children, two dental assistants, one portable chair, and limited materials. Teachers tell you some children have toothache, many have never seen a dentist, and the school canteen sells sweet drinks every day. The bus leaves at 4 p.m.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you plan the day to help as many children as possible?
followUps: Which children would you treat first, and why?
What could the dental assistants and teachers do without you?
What if a child came in with a swollen face and fever at 3:45 p.m.?
How would you make sure this one day has a lasting effect after you leave?
interviewer.pressureProbe: One day per year achieves nothing. Isn't this just a photo opportunity for the university?

keyPoints: Starts with a quick screening of all children to identify those with pain, swelling or infection
Prioritises urgent cases (pain, abscess, swelling), then high-value prevention such as fluoride varnish and sealants
Uses teamwork and delegation: assistants and teachers run toothbrushing education and screening lists
Handles the late emergency safely, including referral to the local hospital and informing parents
Plans for sustainability: teacher training, daily school toothbrushing, talking to the school about sweet drinks, follow-up with local dental therapists
warningSigns: Treats children in arrival order regardless of need
Spends the whole day on a few complex treatments and ignores prevention
Has no plan for follow-up or referral

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are the dentist in charge at a small private clinic. At 9 a.m. the autoclave (sterilising machine) breaks down. You have enough sterile instruments for about three patients. Booked today: a patient with a painful swollen jaw, a whitening session, a child's routine check-up, an elderly man whose denture is loose, and a patient who flew in from Phuket for a crown fitting. More patients are waiting.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do, and in what order?
followUps: Why can't you just clean the instruments well with disinfectant and continue as normal?
How would you communicate with the patients you have to reschedule?
What if the patient from Phuket became angry and demanded to be seen first?
What would you change at the clinic so this problem does less damage in future?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Your owner says, 'Cancelling patients loses money. Use the instruments twice.' What do you do?

keyPoints: Refuses to compromise infection control and explains the risk of cross-infection (e.g. hepatitis B, HIV)
Prioritises the swollen jaw as potentially serious infection, then cases that can be done with few or no sterile instruments
Considers that the crown fitting may be possible and the patient travelled far, while the whitening and routine check can be rescheduled
Takes practical steps: contacting the repair company, borrowing sterilisation from a nearby clinic, single-use instruments
Communicates honestly and apologetically with patients and plans for backup equipment in future
warningSigns: Agrees to reuse unsterilised instruments
Treats patients purely by how much they pay
Does not explain the reason for delays to patients

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a young dentist advising your provincial health office. There is a budget of two million baht for oral health next year, enough for only ONE programme: (1) fluoride varnish for all preschool children; (2) free dentures for 400 elderly people who have lost most of their teeth; or (3) a campaign to remove sugary drinks from schools and teach healthy snacking. You must recommend one.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Which programme would you recommend, and how did you decide?
followUps: What information would you want before making the final decision?
Who will be disappointed by your choice, and what would you say to them?
What if a local politician strongly supported the denture programme because elderly voters are important?
Could you combine elements of the programmes in a creative way within the same budget?
interviewer.pressureProbe: An elderly person without teeth cannot eat properly today. You're choosing children who might get decay in the future over people suffering now. How is that fair?

keyPoints: Sets out clear decision criteria: number of people helped, severity of need, long-term impact, cost-effectiveness, equity
Discusses the strengths and weaknesses of each option rather than dismissing any
Asks for data: current decay rates, number of elderly without teeth, existing programmes, what other funding exists
Makes a reasoned recommendation and acknowledges the people it does not help
Shows awareness of Thailand's ageing society and children's sugar consumption
warningSigns: Chooses based only on personal feelings with no criteria
Refuses to choose
Is influenced by political pressure rather than evidence

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a final-year dental student. Your patient, Khun Ploy, 28, has not visited a dentist for ten years because of a painful experience as a child. She came today only because a back tooth is aching badly. The examination and X-ray show that she needs root canal treatment. She is sitting in the chair looking very tense.

interviewer.openingQuestion: The interviewer will play Khun Ploy. Please explain what she needs and help her decide what to do.
followUps: What did you do to reduce her anxiety?
How did you check that she understood the procedure?
What if she said, 'Just pull the tooth out, I don't care'?
How could dental clinics in Thailand make visits less frightening for children, so they don't grow up like Ploy?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You spent most of the time on feelings. Patients come for treatment, not therapy. Wasn't that inefficient?

actor.role: Khun Ploy, 28, a hotel receptionist in Bangkok
actor.brief: You are terrified. As a child, a dentist held you down and it hurt a lot. You only came because the pain kept you awake for three nights. You don't know what a root canal is but have heard it is extremely painful; your hidden fear is losing control and not being able to make the dentist stop.
lines: Is it bad? Please don't tell me I need a drill. I really, really hate this.
My friend said root canal is the most painful thing in the world.
What if it hurts and you don't stop?
actor.howToReact: If the candidate uses jargon, talks too fast, or picks up an instrument before explaining, become more anxious and try to get out of the chair. If they speak slowly, acknowledge your fear and give you control (a hand signal to stop, explaining each step), gradually relax and ask sensible questions.

keyPoints: Acknowledges her fear without judging her for avoiding the dentist
Explains root canal treatment in simple language, avoiding frightening words and jargon
Offers control: a stop signal, explaining each step, local anaesthetic, breaks, shorter appointments
Explains the consequences of extraction vs saving the tooth so she can make an informed choice
Respects her final decision while making sure it is informed
warningSigns: Tells her she should have come earlier, making her feel guilty
Uses technical terms like 'pulpectomy' or 'periapical lesion' without explanation
Pressures her to start treatment immediately without consent

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a junior dentist at a government hospital. Khun Nok has brought her four-year-old son, Peem, who has severe decay in most of his front teeth. Peem still drinks sweetened milk from a bottle at night, and his grandmother gives him sweets after kindergarten every day. Several teeth need treatment under general anaesthetic. Khun Nok is not aware of how serious it is.

interviewer.openingQuestion: The interviewer will play Khun Nok. Please explain the situation and what needs to happen next.
followUps: How did you avoid making Khun Nok feel blamed?
What practical changes did you suggest, and how realistic are they for this family?
What if Khun Nok said, 'They're only baby teeth, they will fall out anyway'?
Why do you think childhood tooth decay remains so common in Thailand?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Isn't this parental neglect? Shouldn't you be firmer with this mother?

actor.role: Khun Nok, 31, a factory worker and single mother; her mother helps look after Peem
actor.brief: You thought Peem's brown teeth were normal for small children. You work long shifts and the night bottle helps him sleep. Your hidden worry is cost and time off work, and you feel guilty when people suggest you are a bad mother.
lines: Are his teeth very bad? He doesn't complain much.
But they're only baby teeth. Won't new ones grow?
My mother looks after him when I'm at work. I can't control what she gives him.
actor.howToReact: If the candidate seems to blame you or uses words like 'neglect', become defensive and say you'll just bring him back when the teeth fall out. If they reassure you that many parents don't know, explain clearly and give realistic steps, become cooperative and ask how to talk to your mother.

keyPoints: Delivers the news clearly and honestly but without blame, recognising that many parents are not told about sugar and night bottles
Explains why baby teeth matter: pain, infection, eating, speech, school, and the health of adult teeth
Gives specific, realistic advice: water instead of sweet milk at night, limiting sweets to mealtimes, fluoride toothpaste, adult brushing
Considers the grandmother's role and suggests involving her respectfully
Checks understanding and arranges follow-up and preventive care
warningSigns: Blames or shames the mother or grandmother
Agrees that baby teeth do not matter
Overloads the parent with technical information

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a dentist at a private clinic. Mr Somchai, 55, lost a back tooth last year. Your colleague quoted him 60,000 baht for an implant. He has come back angry because a friend told him the government hospital is much cheaper, and he feels the clinic is 'ripping him off'. You have been asked to talk to him.

interviewer.openingQuestion: The interviewer will play Mr Somchai. Please begin when you are ready.
followUps: How did you explain the cost without sounding defensive or like a salesperson?
What alternatives to an implant did you mention, and why?
What if he asked you directly, 'Would you choose an implant if you were me?'
Is it fair that good dental care in Thailand often depends on what patients can afford?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Private dentistry is expensive because dentists want big houses and nice cars. Isn't he right?

actor.role: Mr Somchai, 55, a taxi driver in Bangkok
actor.brief: You feel cheated and embarrassed. Your friend paid much less at a government hospital. You don't know there are other options. Your hidden concern is that you are still paying your daughter's university fees and cannot afford 60,000 baht, but you are too proud to say so.
lines: Sixty thousand baht for one tooth? My friend paid a fraction of that. Are you cheating me?
You private clinics are all the same. It's all about money.
So what am I supposed to do, just chew on one side forever?
actor.howToReact: If the candidate argues, sounds like a salesperson or uses technical terms such as 'osseointegration', become angrier and threaten to post a bad review. If they listen, acknowledge the cost problem and honestly explain cheaper alternatives, calm down and admit that money is difficult for you right now.

keyPoints: Listens first and acknowledges his frustration about cost without arguing
Explains clearly what the price includes (materials, surgery, crown, follow-up) and why prices differ between sectors, including waiting times
Presents all options honestly: implant, bridge, removable denture, or leaving the gap if appropriate, with pros and cons
Is willing to recommend a cheaper or public option if it suits him, putting his interests above the clinic's income
Discusses the fairness question thoughtfully, mentioning public coverage and access gaps
warningSigns: Becomes defensive and insists the price is fair without explaining
Pushes the implant as the only option
Criticises the government hospital or his friend

interviewee.doorPrompt: A health organisation has published the table below with the claim: 'Sugary drinks are the main cause of tooth decay in Thai children. Banning them in schools will solve the problem.' You have one minute to study the information before discussing it.

data.caption: 12-year-old children: sugary drink intake and tooth decay, by region
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Drink intake was reported by children in a one-day questionnaire. The survey did not record toothbrushing, fluoride use or family income.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Does this data support the organisation's claim? Explain your reasoning.
followUps: What other factors could explain the differences between the regions?
Is the correlation between sugary drinks and decay still useful, even if it doesn't prove cause?
What kind of study would give stronger evidence?
If you were advising the Ministry of Education, would you support a ban? Why?
interviewer.pressureProbe: The pattern is obvious: more sugar, more decay. Why are you making this complicated?

keyPoints: Notes the correlation but explains it does not prove sugary drinks are the 'main' cause
Identifies confounding factors, especially access to dentists, income, fluoride toothpaste and brushing habits
Points out limitations: self-reported one-day data, regional averages hide individual differences
Suggests better evidence such as following children over time or comparing schools before and after a policy
Concludes carefully: reducing sugar is sensible, but 'will solve the problem' is overstated
warningSigns: Accepts the claim completely without discussing other factors
Ignores the 'dentists per 10,000' column
Rejects any link between sugar and decay

interviewee.doorPrompt: An advert on BTS station screens says: 'SparkWhite toothpaste: 5 shades whiter in 7 days! 9 out of 10 dentists recommend SparkWhite.' A friend asks if she should switch toothpaste. The company website shows the table below.

data.caption: SparkWhite company study results
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Study carried out by the manufacturer; dentists surveyed were paid consultants for the company; shade measured from photographs taken by staff.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What do you make of this advertisement and its evidence?
followUps: What does '9 out of 10 dentists recommend' actually tell us?
Why might the results in the company's own study be better than in real life?
Are there any possible risks of using strong whitening toothpaste every day?
What advice would you give your friend?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Lots of people buy it and they look whiter in photos. Isn't public satisfaction evidence enough?

keyPoints: Points out the very small and biased sample: only 20 dentists, who were paid consultants
Notes that there is no control group and that shade was judged from staff photos, which can be manipulated by lighting
Identifies that 30% of users reported sensitivity, which the advert ignores
Explains that abrasive whitening toothpaste may damage enamel over time
Gives balanced advice: see a dentist, use fluoride toothpaste, manage expectations
warningSigns: Accepts '9 out of 10 dentists' as strong evidence
Fails to notice the funding and payment conflict
Ignores the sensitivity figure

interviewee.doorPrompt: A Facebook page called 'Natural Thai Health' shares a post with 40,000 likes: 'Fluoride is a poison! It damages children's brains. In countries that stopped using fluoride, children are smarter. Use our herbal toothpaste with no chemicals instead.' Your aunt, who has two young children, sends it to the family LINE group and asks what you think, since you want to be a dentist.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you evaluate this post, and how would you reply in the family LINE group?
followUps: Is there any truth hidden in the post? What does the research say about fluoride amounts?
Who benefits if people believe this post?
What sources would you trust to check the claim, and why?
What if your aunt replied, 'You're just a student, you're brainwashed by the dental industry'?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You can't prove fluoride is 100% safe for every child. So isn't it better to be careful and avoid it?

keyPoints: Recognises the post is selling a product, which creates a conflict of interest
Explains that the dose matters: very high fluoride can cause problems, but normal toothpaste amounts are safe and prevent decay
Notes the claim about 'smarter children' mixes correlation with causation and gives no source
Names reliable sources such as the Ministry of Public Health, the WHO, Dental Association guidance, peer-reviewed research
Replies respectfully and simply, without embarrassing the aunt in front of the family, and suggests age-appropriate toothpaste amounts
warningSigns: Agrees the herbal toothpaste is safer because it is 'natural'
Mocks the aunt publicly in the group
Overclaims that fluoride is completely risk-free at any amount

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are volunteering with a team of six students at a weekend dental camp in a temple in Suphan Buri. Two team members, Fah and Krit, are arguing loudly about how to organise the patient queue. Elderly patients are waiting in the heat and some are starting to leave. The teacher in charge is busy treating patients.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do right now and after the camp? Then tell me about a real time you helped people in a team who disagreed.
followUps: How would you decide whose idea to follow, Fah's or Krit's?
What if both of them were angry at you for getting involved?
Tell me about a time you helped resolve a disagreement in a team. What did you do and what happened?
What did that experience teach you about yourself as a team member?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You're not the leader. Isn't it arrogant to step in?

keyPoints: Prioritises the patients first: suggests a quick, temporary queue solution so people are not left waiting
Moves the argument away from the patients and listens to both sides calmly
Focuses on the shared goal and a fair way to decide, such as trying one system and reviewing it later
Gives a real STAR example with their own specific actions and the result
Shows reflection about their own communication style and what they would improve
warningSigns: Takes sides immediately or ignores the conflict
Focuses only on who was right, not on the patients
Cannot provide a genuine personal example

interviewee.doorPrompt: In first-year dental school, students practise on plastic teeth before treating real patients. Imagine you have failed your tooth-carving practical test twice, while most of your friends have passed. The instructor says your work is 'not precise enough'. You are starting to wonder whether you are suited to dentistry.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you respond to this situation, and tell me about a real time you failed at something and had to try again.
followUps: What specific steps would you take to improve?
Who would you ask for help, and how would you ask?
Tell me about a real time when you struggled to learn a practical or physical skill. What did you do?
How do you know when to keep trying and when to change direction?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Maybe the instructor is right and your hands just aren't good enough. Why not accept it?

keyPoints: Responds with resilience rather than giving up or blaming the instructor
Describes specific improvement strategies: extra lab practice, asking for detailed feedback, watching skilled seniors, breaking the skill into steps
Seeks help appropriately from instructors, peers or tutors
Gives a real personal example of learning a hands-on skill (music, art, sport, cooking) with honest reflection
Shows mature thinking about persistence and self-awareness
warningSigns: Blames the instructor or the test as unfair
Says they would quit immediately
Gives an example where they succeeded without any difficulty

interviewee.doorPrompt: This station uses a strict examiner. Imagine you are a dental student treating a patient. Your supervisor looks at your work and says loudly, in front of the patient and other students, 'This is careless. Do it again.' You believe the supervisor misunderstood what you were doing. The examiner will then ask about your own experiences of feedback.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you react at that moment and afterwards? Then tell me about a real time you were criticised in front of others.
followUps: How do you think the patient felt watching this?
How would you raise your disagreement with the supervisor, if at all?
Tell me about the most difficult feedback you have ever received. How did you respond?
Have you ever given difficult feedback to someone else? How did you do it?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You seem to think you're always right. How do you know the supervisor wasn't simply correct?

keyPoints: Stays calm in front of the patient, follows the supervisor's instruction for patient safety and reassures the patient
Speaks to the supervisor privately and respectfully afterwards, asking for clarification rather than arguing
Is genuinely open to the possibility that they were wrong
Gives a real example of difficult feedback with honest emotions and clear learning
Shows they know how to give feedback kindly and constructively
warningSigns: Argues with the supervisor in front of the patient
Says they have never received negative feedback
Shows resentment or wants to complain formally as a first step

vocabulary.def: a disease that can spread between animals and humans
vocabulary.example: Rabies and bird flu are zoonoses, so vets play a key role in protecting public health.

vocabulary.def: a deadly viral disease spread mainly through the bites of infected animals, especially dogs
vocabulary.example: Once symptoms of rabies appear, it is almost always fatal, so vaccination is essential.

vocabulary.def: vaccines and treatment given after a possible exposure, such as an animal bite, to prevent infection
vocabulary.example: Anyone bitten by a street dog should go to hospital for post-exposure prophylaxis.

vocabulary.def: ending an animal's life painlessly to stop suffering
vocabulary.example: Euthanasia may be the kindest option when an animal's pain cannot be controlled.

vocabulary.def: an operation that stops an animal from being able to reproduce
vocabulary.example: Neutering street dogs helps reduce their numbers humanely over time.

vocabulary.def: measures that prevent diseases from entering or spreading on farms and in animal populations
vocabulary.example: Good biosecurity on pig farms helped limit the spread of African swine fever.

vocabulary.def: the time that must pass after an animal receives a drug before its meat, milk or eggs are safe to eat
vocabulary.example: Selling pigs before the withdrawal period ends can leave antibiotic residues in pork.

vocabulary.def: farm animals such as cattle, pigs and chickens kept for food or other products
vocabulary.example: Many vets in Thailand work with livestock rather than pets.

vocabulary.def: an unusual pet that is not a dog or cat, such as a reptile, bird or small wild mammal
vocabulary.example: Exotic pets bought online often suffer because owners do not understand their needs.

vocabulary.def: a widely used animal-welfare framework: freedom from hunger, discomfort, pain or disease, fear, and freedom to express normal behaviour
vocabulary.example: Keeping a parrot alone in a tiny cage fails several of the Five Freedoms.

vocabulary.def: an approach recognising that human, animal and environmental health are closely connected
vocabulary.example: Controlling bird flu is a One Health issue involving vets, doctors and environmental agencies.

vocabulary.def: how comfortable, healthy and able to enjoy life someone is
vocabulary.example: When we discuss euthanasia, the animal's quality of life must come first.

vocabulary.def: emotional exhaustion from repeatedly caring for those who are suffering
vocabulary.example: Vets are at high risk of compassion fatigue, so peer support matters.

vocabulary.def: find it hard to choose between two things you care about
vocabulary.example: Vets are often torn between an animal's welfare and the owner's financial limits.

vocabulary.def: a professional responsibility that goes beyond the individual client to protect society
vocabulary.example: A vet who suspects bird flu has a duty to the public to report it, even if the farmer objects.

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are applying to a six-year Doctor of Veterinary Medicine programme. Vets diagnose and treat patients who cannot describe their symptoms, and they must also communicate with owners, farmers and government officials. The interviewer wants to know why you have chosen veterinary science and what you have done to understand the realities of the job.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Why do you want to become a vet rather than a doctor who treats people?
followUps: What experience have you had working with animals other than your own pets?
Vets often say the hardest part of the job is the people, not the animals. What do you think they mean?
What was the most difficult or unpleasant thing you saw while exploring this career?
How do vets help protect human health as well as animal health?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Liking animals is not a career plan. Lots of people like dogs. What makes you suitable to be a vet?

keyPoints: Gives a specific reason for veterinary science beyond 'I love animals', such as interest in comparative medicine, problem-solving without verbal history, or public health
Describes real experience: clinic observation, a shelter, a farm, a zoo or wildlife project, with reflection
Shows awareness of difficult realities: euthanasia, bites and scratches, owners who cannot pay, emotional stress
Recognises the importance of communication with owners and farmers
Mentions zoonoses, food safety or One Health
warningSigns: Says they prefer animals because they 'don't like people'
Has no experience with animals beyond owning a pet
Sees vet science as an easier alternative to medicine

interviewee.doorPrompt: Many people think vets only work in pet clinics. In Thailand, vets also work on pig, poultry and dairy farms, in food-safety inspection, at the Department of Livestock Development, with elephants and wildlife, in pharmaceutical companies and in research on diseases such as rabies and bird flu. Thailand is also a major exporter of chicken and seafood.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What do you know about the different roles vets play in Thailand, and which area interests you most?
followUps: Why is veterinary work important for Thailand's economy and food exports?
What might a typical day look like for a vet working with dairy cows in Saraburi?
Are there any areas of veterinary work you would NOT want to do? Why?
Where do you see yourself working in ten years?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You've only talked about pets. Thailand has thousands of small-animal vets in Bangkok but too few on farms. Why should we train another pet vet?

keyPoints: Names several real career paths with accurate examples, not just companion-animal practice
Links vet work to food safety, export standards and disease control, e.g. bird flu or African swine fever
Describes realistic farm-vet work: herd health, vaccination programmes, early starts, travel, working with farmers
Is honest about preferences while remaining open to other areas
Gives a reasoned long-term plan
warningSigns: Believes vets only treat dogs and cats
Is dismissive of farm or food-safety work as 'dirty' or 'boring'
Cannot explain any public role for vets

interviewee.doorPrompt: This is a pressure station. The examiner will challenge whether you can cope with the hardest parts of veterinary work, including euthanasia, slaughterhouse inspection and difficult owners. Answer honestly. The examiner is not looking for someone without emotions, but for someone who has thought seriously about these challenges and has strategies to cope.

interviewer.openingQuestion: As a vet, you may have to put healthy animals to sleep or inspect animals at a slaughterhouse. Could you really do that?
followUps: How would you feel after euthanising an animal you had treated for years?
Vets have one of the highest rates of work stress of any profession. Why do you think that is?
What would you do if you realised a career in clinics was making you very unhappy?
How do you personally deal with stress now? Give an example.
interviewer.pressureProbe: Honestly, you seem too soft for this job. Prove me wrong.

keyPoints: Gives an honest, reflective answer that acknowledges emotions rather than claiming to feel nothing
Explains the purpose of difficult tasks: relieving suffering, protecting food safety and public health
Shows awareness of compassion fatigue and burnout in the profession
Describes realistic coping strategies: talking to colleagues, debriefing, exercise, hobbies, professional support
Stays calm and constructive when challenged
warningSigns: Says they would refuse ever to perform euthanasia
Claims they would feel nothing at all
Becomes upset or defensive under pressure

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a junior vet at a private clinic in Bangkok. Ton, a 19-year-old delivery rider, brings in his dog, which has just been hit by a car and has a broken leg. Surgery will cost about 25,000 baht. Ton has only 2,000 baht. The clinic owner's policy is 'no payment, no surgery', but the dog is in pain.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do?
followUps: What is your responsibility to the dog, to Ton and to the clinic?
What options could you offer Ton within his budget?
What if your boss said, 'If we treat everyone for free, we'll close in a month'?
Would you consider paying for the surgery yourself? Why or why not?
interviewer.pressureProbe: If a person can't afford a pet, perhaps they shouldn't have one. Why is this your problem?

keyPoints: Prioritises immediate pain relief and stabilisation regardless of the payment issue
Lays out options honestly: cheaper treatment such as a splint or amputation, payment plans, charities, university vet hospitals, crowdfunding
Respects the clinic's business needs while advocating for the animal
Discusses euthanasia sensitively as a possible option if treatment is truly impossible and suffering cannot be relieved
Recognises the risks of paying personally (setting a precedent, boundaries) while showing compassion
warningSigns: Sends Ton away with no pain relief or options
Ignores the clinic's legitimate financial concerns completely
Judges or lectures Ton about being poor

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a vet at a small clinic in Nonthaburi. Mrs Wanpen, 50, brings in her healthy eight-year-old Thai Bangkaew dog, Lucky. She is moving to a condominium that does not allow dogs and asks you to put Lucky to sleep. She says, 'Nobody will adopt an old dog, and I don't want him to suffer at a shelter or on the street.'

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you respond to her request?
followUps: Is it ever ethical to euthanise a healthy animal? Why or why not?
What alternatives would you explore with Mrs Wanpen?
What if she said she would simply release Lucky near a temple if you refused?
Should Thailand have stronger laws about pet ownership and abandonment?
interviewer.pressureProbe: The owner has the legal right to decide. Who are you to refuse?

keyPoints: Recognises the welfare conflict: Lucky is healthy and has good quality of life
Explores Mrs Wanpen's reasons with empathy and treats her concern for Lucky as genuine
Suggests realistic alternatives: rehoming through networks, breed groups, foundations, social media, relatives, foster care
Takes the abandonment threat seriously, explaining the risks to the dog and the community (traffic, rabies, conflict)
Knows a vet may decline a procedure they find unethical but should still help the client find a humane solution
warningSigns: Agrees immediately to euthanise the healthy dog
Insults or shames Mrs Wanpen
Ignores the risk that the dog will be abandoned

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a new vet at a clinic that treats exotic pets. A wealthy client brings in a sick baby slow loris she bought online as a pet. Slow lorises are protected wild animals in Thailand and cannot legally be kept as pets. She asks you to treat it, offers to pay double, and says, 'Please keep this between us. Many people own them.' The animal is weak and dehydrated.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do?
followUps: What are your duties to the animal, the client, the law and wildlife conservation?
Does client confidentiality apply in this situation?
What if your clinic director said reporting her would lose the clinic many rich clients?
What would you say to the client directly?
interviewer.pressureProbe: If you report her, the next person with a sick loris won't bring it to a vet at all. Aren't you making things worse for animals?

keyPoints: Gives emergency care to the animal first, without accepting extra payment as a condition
Explains that confidentiality does not cover illegal wildlife trade and that vets have a legal and public duty
Considers the right authority (Department of National Parks, Wildlife and Plant Conservation) and rescue centres where the animal can be cared for properly
Explains welfare issues honestly to the client: wild animals suffer in homes, illegal trade harms populations, zoonotic risk
Engages seriously with the 'hidden harm' argument and suggests wider solutions such as education
warningSigns: Accepts the double payment and keeps quiet
Refuses to treat the sick animal at all
Treats confidentiality as absolute even when the law is broken

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a veterinary student volunteering with the district office in Bangkok. A brown street dog that lives in a soi has just bitten a nine-year-old girl on the leg and, earlier, a delivery rider. The dog has not been vaccinated as far as anyone knows. Residents are gathering, angry and frightened; one man is holding a stick. You are the first person from the district to arrive.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do, step by step?
followUps: What advice would you give the girl's parents and the rider immediately?
What should happen to the dog, and why is it important not to kill it straight away?
What if the dog ran away before it could be caught?
In the long term, how should Bangkok manage street dogs and rabies?
interviewer.pressureProbe: The residents want every street dog in the soi removed today. Why not do what the public wants?

keyPoints: Prioritises human safety: wash the wounds immediately with soap and water for at least 15 minutes and go to hospital for rabies PEP
Calms the crowd and prevents violence towards the dog
Explains that the dog should be safely caught and observed for about 10 days, or tested if it dies, which helps decide treatment
Contacts the right people: district livestock/vet officials, health centre, dog-catching team
Proposes humane long-term solutions: mass vaccination, sterilisation, community education, responsible ownership
warningSigns: Focuses on catching the dog before helping the bitten people
Supports beating or killing the dog immediately
Says rabies PEP is unnecessary if the wound is small

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are the only vet on duty at a 24-hour animal hospital at 10 p.m. Waiting are: a large dog with a swollen stomach trying to vomit; a male cat straining in the litter box but producing no urine; a puppy due for vaccination; a rabbit that has not eaten for one day; and an owner who wants to discuss her dog's skin allergy. You have one nurse.

interviewer.openingQuestion: In what order would you see these patients, and why?
followUps: Why are the dog and the cat potentially so serious?
What could the nurse do while you are busy?
The puppy's owner is shouting that they have been waiting the longest. How would you handle it?
What if both the dog and the cat needed surgery immediately and you could only do one?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You've put the rabbit third. Most people think rabbits are less important than dogs. Are you just following that bias?

keyPoints: Identifies the dog with a swollen stomach (possible gastric dilatation-volvulus) and the blocked cat as life-threatening emergencies
Recognises a rabbit that stops eating can deteriorate quickly and should be seen soon
Delegates: the nurse takes vital signs, starts fluids under instruction, and communicates with waiting owners
Communicates honestly with waiting owners about triage and offers rebooking for non-urgent cases
Considers calling a backup vet or referral hospital if two surgeries are needed at once
warningSigns: Sees patients in arrival order
Treats exotic animals as automatically low priority
Does not communicate with waiting owners

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a young government vet in a rural district in Suphan Buri. A villager reports that 30 of his 50 backyard chickens died in two days. Neighbours keep chickens and fighting cocks, children play with the birds, and the village market is tomorrow. The farmer begs you not to report anything because he fears his birds will be destroyed and he will lose his income.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do first, and what is your plan for the next 48 hours?
followUps: Why is this a public health concern and not just an animal problem?
How would you protect yourself and others when visiting the farm?
The farmer offers you money to 'just write that it was heat stress'. What do you do?
How would you communicate with the village without causing panic?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You don't even know it's bird flu yet. Destroying a poor family's livelihood on a guess is cruel. Why not wait for more evidence?

keyPoints: Recognises sudden mass bird deaths as a possible avian influenza alert requiring urgent reporting to the livestock authority
Uses protective equipment and biosecurity: gloves, masks, disinfection, no movement of birds or carcasses
Arranges sampling and testing, and restricts movement of birds including to the market, until results are known
Works with the public health office to monitor people with contact, especially children
Shows compassion for the farmer, mentions compensation schemes, and refuses the bribe firmly
warningSigns: Agrees not to report because of the farmer's situation
Visits without any protective measures
Causes panic or ignores the human health risk

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a vet at a small-animal clinic. Mrs Ratana, 58, owns Bua, a 14-year-old dog. Tests show Bua has advanced cancer that has spread. She is in pain despite medication and has stopped eating. You believe euthanasia is now the kindest option. Mrs Ratana's husband died last year, and Bua was his dog.

interviewer.openingQuestion: The interviewer will play Mrs Ratana. Please explain the results and discuss what happens next.
followUps: How did you prepare her before giving the news?
How did you describe euthanasia, and why did you use those words?
What if she asked you, 'What would you do if Bua were your dog?'
What if she refused and wanted to continue treatment at any cost?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You recommended ending a life. Aren't vets supposed to save animals?

actor.role: Mrs Ratana, 58, a retired teacher and owner of Bua, a 14-year-old dog
actor.brief: You know Bua is old and ill but hope the tests will show something treatable. Bua belonged to your husband, who died last year, and losing her feels like losing him again. Your hidden fear is that agreeing to euthanasia means you are giving up on her and betraying him.
lines: So, doctor, the tests are back? She'll be OK with some medicine, won't she?
She was my husband's dog. She's all I have left of him.
If I say yes... does that mean I didn't love her enough?
actor.howToReact: If the candidate rushes, uses technical terms like 'metastasis', or pushes you to decide quickly, become tearful and angry and say you will find another vet. If they slow down, acknowledge your grief and reassure you that this choice is an act of love, become calmer and ask what the process involves.

keyPoints: Prepares her with a warning shot and checks what she already understands before giving the news
Explains the cancer and Bua's quality of life in clear, gentle language without jargon
Acknowledges her grief and the link to her late husband, allowing silence and emotion
Explains euthanasia honestly and kindly (peaceful, painless, she can be present) and gives her time to decide
Respects her decision while advocating for Bua's welfare, e.g. stronger pain relief if she needs more time
warningSigns: Rushes or uses euphemisms that confuse her (e.g. never clearly saying the dog will die)
Pressures her to decide immediately
Ignores her emotional reaction and focuses only on medical facts

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a veterinary student helping the district's free rabies vaccination and sterilisation project. Aunt Somsri, 65, feeds about 15 street dogs near a temple in Thonburi. Neighbours have complained after a dog chased a child. Your job is to persuade Aunt Somsri to help you catch the dogs this weekend so they can be vaccinated and sterilised, then returned.

interviewer.openingQuestion: The interviewer will play Aunt Somsri. Please begin when you are ready.
followUps: What did you learn about Aunt Somsri's worries, and how did you address them?
How did you explain why sterilisation helps the dogs and the community?
What if she agreed to vaccination but refused sterilisation because it is 'against nature'?
How would you build trust with other dog feeders in the area?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You only had five minutes and she still isn't sure. Wouldn't it be easier to catch the dogs without her permission?

actor.role: Aunt Somsri, 65, a retired market seller who feeds dogs at the temple every day
actor.brief: You love these dogs and feeding them is part of your merit-making. You have heard that dogs taken by officials sometimes never come back, and you suspect this is a trick. You are hurt by the neighbours' complaints; your hidden fear is losing the dogs, who are your main companions.
lines: Who sent you? Did the neighbours complain again? These dogs never hurt anyone.
Last time the officials took dogs from the market, they never came back.
Cutting them is not natural. Why can't you just leave them alone?
actor.howToReact: If the candidate lectures you, mentions the law or seems to side with the neighbours, become suspicious and refuse to help. If they praise your care, listen to your fears and promise the dogs will be returned with you present, gradually agree to help with vaccination first.

keyPoints: Shows respect for Aunt Somsri's care for the dogs and recognises her as a partner, not a problem
Discovers and answers her hidden fear that the dogs will be taken away or harmed
Explains simply how vaccination protects both dogs and people from rabies, and how sterilisation reduces fights, puppies and complaints
Offers practical reassurance: dogs returned to the same place, she can be present, follow-up care
Handles cultural or religious concerns respectfully and looks for compromise
warningSigns: Threatens her with complaints or the law as a first step
Lectures her about rabies statistics without listening
Dismisses her beliefs about nature or merit-making

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a junior vet at a busy clinic. This morning your senior colleague performed a routine dental cleaning under anaesthetic on Mr Krit's five-year-old cat, Mochi. Mochi did not recover from anaesthesia and died despite resuscitation. Your colleague has had to go to another emergency. Mr Krit has just arrived to collect Mochi, and you must speak to him.

interviewer.openingQuestion: The interviewer will play Mr Krit. Please begin when you are ready.
followUps: How did you deliver the news, and why did you choose those words?
What should you say, and not say, about what went wrong when you weren't in the operating room?
What if Mr Krit demanded a full refund and threatened to post the story on Facebook?
What should the clinic do after this event?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You're protecting your colleague. Admit it, the clinic made a mistake.

actor.role: Mr Krit, 32, a software engineer who lives alone with his cat, Mochi
actor.brief: You expected to pick up Mochi and take her home. You were told it was a 'simple, routine' procedure. When you hear the news you will be shocked, then angry; your hidden feeling is guilt, because you were the one who agreed to the procedure.
lines: Hi, I'm here to pick up Mochi. Is she awake yet?
What? She was perfectly healthy this morning! You said it was routine!
It's my fault. I didn't have to do the cleaning. I should have said no.
actor.howToReact: If the candidate is vague, uses medical jargon, or seems to defend the clinic, become angry and demand to speak to the owner, threatening to post online. If they are honest, sit with your grief, and explain clearly what will happen next, become quieter and start asking about seeing Mochi and what caused it.

keyPoints: Takes Mr Krit to a private space and delivers the news clearly, using the word 'died'
Expresses genuine sympathy and gives him time to react
Is honest about what is known and unknown, does not speculate or blame the colleague, and does not cover up
Explains the next steps: a meeting with the surgeon, option of a post-mortem, clinic review, how to complain formally
Stays calm and empathetic if threatened, understanding anger as part of grief
warningSigns: Avoids saying the cat died or delays the news
Blames the colleague or the anaesthetic before facts are known
Becomes defensive or argues about the threat to post online

interviewee.doorPrompt: A national newspaper prints this table with the headline: 'Province C is Thailand's rabies hotspot. Tourists should avoid it!' You are asked to comment on the data as a future vet. You have one minute to study it.

data.caption: Animal rabies results and dog vaccination coverage, four provinces, 2025
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Province C has a new laboratory and an active surveillance programme that encourages reporting. Vaccination coverage is estimated from district reports, not checked in the field.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What can we conclude from this data, and is the headline fair?
followUps: Why might Province C report more positive cases than the others?
What does it suggest that Province A tested so few samples?
What extra data would help you decide which province really has the highest risk?
If you were advising the Department of Livestock Development, what would you recommend?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Province C has twelve times more cases than Province A. Surely that settles it?

keyPoints: Calculates positivity rates: Province C 4% vs Province D about 12% and Province A 10%
Explains that more testing in Province C finds more cases; low testing elsewhere may hide the true problem
Notes that vaccination coverage is estimated, not verified, and links low coverage with higher positivity
Calls the headline misleading and unfair to Province C, which may be doing the best surveillance
Recommends better surveillance in low-testing provinces and targeted vaccination
warningSigns: Accepts the headline based on raw case numbers
Does not consider the number of samples tested
Ignores the note about surveillance and estimates

interviewee.doorPrompt: A consumer group posts this on social media: 'Fresh-market pork is dangerous! Buy only supermarket pork to protect your family.' They include the table below. Your family buys meat at the local fresh market, and your mother asks if she should change.

data.caption: Antibiotic residues above safe limits in pork samples, Bangkok, 2025
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Fresh-market samples were collected from three markets on one day; supermarket samples were collected over six months by a supermarket chain's own testing team.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What does this data really tell us, and what would you advise your mother?
followUps: What is an antibiotic residue, and why does it matter for human health?
Why might the comparison between markets and supermarkets be unfair?
What could explain residues in meat, and who is responsible for preventing them?
What should the government do based on this kind of finding?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Even 8% is too high. Why take any risk at all? Your mother should just switch.

keyPoints: Explains residues come from drugs given to pigs without respecting the withdrawal period, linking to antimicrobial resistance
Identifies very different and small sample sizes (25 and 10 vs 200) and different sampling periods
Notes the conflict of interest: supermarket samples were tested by the supermarket itself
Concludes that the data cannot prove market pork is more dangerous, though residues anywhere are a concern
Gives balanced advice and suggests system-level solutions: farm monitoring, vet prescription control, independent testing
warningSigns: Accepts the claim and tells the mother to switch immediately
Ignores who carried out the testing
Does not understand what an antibiotic residue is or why it matters

interviewee.doorPrompt: A popular pet influencer posts: 'I surveyed 500 dog owners in our Raw Feeding Thailand Facebook group. 92% say their dogs are healthier and happier since switching to raw meat. Raw-fed dogs live longer! Kibble is killing your dog.' The post links to a shop selling raw pet food. A friend who has just adopted a puppy asks you if she should feed raw meat.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you evaluate this claim, and what would you tell your friend?
followUps: What is wrong with surveying members of this Facebook group?
The post says 'healthier and happier'. How could you measure that properly?
Are there any health risks of raw feeding for dogs and for the people in the home?
What kind of study would give reliable evidence about diet and life expectancy in dogs?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Dogs' wild ancestors ate raw meat for thousands of years. Isn't that evidence enough?

keyPoints: Identifies selection bias: members of a raw-feeding group already believe in raw feeding
Notes that owner opinion is subjective, and the survey did not measure lifespan at all
Points out the conflict of interest (linked shop) and the unsupported claim that kibble is 'killing' dogs
Mentions zoonotic risks such as Salmonella from raw meat and nutritional imbalance in puppies
Advises the friend to discuss diet with a vet and choose a complete, balanced diet
warningSigns: Accepts '92%' as strong evidence
Ignores the risk to people in the household
Dismisses all raw feeding without explaining why the evidence is weak

interviewee.doorPrompt: You and five friends started a school volunteer project at a dog shelter in Pathum Thani, visiting every Saturday. After two months, only you and one other person still go. The others say they are busy with tutoring, but they still post photos from the first visits on Instagram as 'volunteering'. The shelter is counting on your group.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do about this situation, and tell me about a real time a team project lost its commitment.
followUps: How would you approach the friends who have stopped coming?
Is it dishonest for them to post the old photos? Would you say anything?
Tell me about a real time you led or kept a team going when motivation was low.
What did you learn from that about leadership and commitment?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Maybe your friends are right. Their exams are more important than a shelter. Why should they come?

keyPoints: Talks to the team openly and without blame, asking about their real constraints
Suggests realistic solutions: a rota, fewer visits, recruiting new volunteers, being honest with the shelter
Addresses the social-media issue tactfully, linking it to honesty and integrity
Gives a real STAR example with personal actions and an honest result
Reflects on reliability and commitment as essential qualities for a vet
warningSigns: Publicly shames the friends
Gives up on the project without telling the shelter
Cannot give a real example of teamwork or leadership

interviewee.doorPrompt: Imagine you are doing a summer internship at an animal hospital. During one difficult week, three animals you helped care for die, including a puppy you had grown attached to. You find it hard to sleep, and you begin to wonder whether you can handle this career. Vets regularly face loss and emotional strain.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you cope with this situation, and tell me about a real time you coped with a sad or stressful experience.
followUps: Who would you talk to, and what would you say?
How can you care about animals deeply without being overwhelmed by sadness?
Tell me about a real time you faced a sad or stressful experience. How did you cope?
How would you support a classmate who was struggling in the same way?
interviewer.pressureProbe: If one bad week makes you doubt your career, how will you survive forty years of it?

keyPoints: Accepts that grief is normal and shows healthy coping, not hiding or ignoring feelings
Seeks support from supervisors, colleagues, friends or family, and knows when to seek professional help
Describes healthy strategies: rest, exercise, reflection, focusing on the animals that were helped
Gives a genuine personal example with honest reflection
Shows care for peers and awareness of compassion fatigue in the profession
warningSigns: Says they would keep everything to themselves and 'just be strong'
Claims they have never felt stressed or sad
Has no strategies for coping

interviewee.doorPrompt: This station has a demanding examiner. Imagine you led a team of students organising a free rabies vaccination day in a village. Because of your planning mistake, the vaccines arrived late and half the dog owners went home. The village head is disappointed. The examiner will ask about this situation and about a real time when something you led went wrong.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do now, and what would you say to the village head? Then tell me about a real time your plan or mistake let other people down.
followUps: How would you take responsibility without just apologising?
How would you rebuild trust with the villagers who went home?
Tell me about a real time something you were responsible for went wrong. What happened?
What specifically have you done differently since then?
interviewer.pressureProbe: It sounds like you're blaming the delivery company, not yourself. Whose fault was it really?

keyPoints: Takes clear ownership of the planning mistake without blaming others
Gives a specific recovery plan: a new date, home visits, contacting owners through the village head or LINE groups
Communicates honestly and respectfully with the village head
Gives a real personal example with specific lessons and changed behaviour
Stays calm and reflective under challenge
warningSigns: Blames team members or the supplier
Gives up on the villagers who left
Offers a fake failure that is really a success

vocabulary.def: a licensed professional who assesses and treats mental health problems using psychological methods, not medication
vocabulary.example: In Thailand, a clinical psychologist often works in a hospital alongside psychiatrists.

vocabulary.def: a medical doctor who specialises in mental health and can prescribe medication
vocabulary.example: If a client needs medication, the psychologist may refer them to a psychiatrist.

vocabulary.def: keeping what a client says private, except in specific situations such as serious risk of harm
vocabulary.example: At the first session, the counsellor explains the limits of confidentiality.

vocabulary.def: sending someone to another professional or service that can give them the help they need
vocabulary.example: A peer supporter's most important skill is knowing when to make a referral.

vocabulary.def: negative attitudes and shame attached to something, such as mental illness, which can stop people seeking help
vocabulary.example: Stigma means some Thai families hide a relative's depression instead of seeking treatment.

vocabulary.def: a talking therapy that helps people change unhelpful thoughts and behaviours
vocabulary.example: CBT has strong evidence for treating anxiety and depression.

vocabulary.def: information people give about themselves, for example in a questionnaire, which may not be fully accurate
vocabulary.example: Self-report surveys about screen time often underestimate how long teens actually spend online.

vocabulary.def: participants in a study who do not receive the treatment, used for comparison
vocabulary.example: Without a control group, we cannot tell if the app or simply time made people feel better.

vocabulary.def: knowledge and understanding that helps people recognise, manage and seek help for mental health problems
vocabulary.example: Improving mental health literacy among parents could reduce stigma in Thai families.

vocabulary.def: basic, practical support given to people in distress to help them feel safe and connected to further help
vocabulary.example: Volunteers were trained in psychological first aid after the floods.

vocabulary.def: not criticising or showing disapproval of someone's feelings or choices
vocabulary.example: A non-judgemental response makes it easier for a teenager to open up.

vocabulary.def: listening with full attention, reflecting back what you hear and asking open questions
vocabulary.example: Active listening is more helpful than giving advice too quickly.

vocabulary.def: direct someone to services or people who can help them
vocabulary.example: As a peer listener, I would signpost her to the school counsellor and the 1323 hotline.

vocabulary.def: decide clearly what you can and cannot do for others, to protect yourself and them
vocabulary.example: Supporting a friend is kind, but you also need to set healthy boundaries.

vocabulary.def: two things happening together does not prove that one causes the other
vocabulary.example: Teens who use TikTok more may be more anxious, but correlation does not imply causation.

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are applying to a four-year psychology programme. Many people in Thailand are unsure of the difference between a psychologist, a psychiatrist and a counsellor, and some believe psychology is only about 'reading minds' or giving advice. The interviewer wants to understand why you have chosen psychology and what you know about the field.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Why do you want to study psychology, and what do you think a psychologist actually does?
followUps: What is the difference between a clinical psychologist and a psychiatrist?
Apart from clinical work, what other careers can psychology graduates have in Thailand?
What have you read or done to explore psychology outside the classroom?
Which area of psychology interests you most, and why?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You could just become a psychiatrist through medicine and earn more. Why choose psychology?

keyPoints: Explains accurately that psychiatrists are medical doctors who can prescribe, while psychologists use assessment, therapy and research
Knows psychology is a science based on research and statistics, not just giving advice
Names several career paths: clinical, counselling, educational, industrial-organisational/HR, UX research, research and policy
Refers to specific exploration such as books, online courses, a psychology club, volunteering or talking to professionals
Gives a genuine reason for preferring psychology over medicine (e.g. interest in behaviour, research, therapy rather than medication)
warningSigns: Thinks psychologists can read minds or 'tell if someone is lying'
Confuses psychologists and psychiatrists completely
Only motivation is wanting to understand their own problems or 'fix' friends

interviewee.doorPrompt: A relative tells you at a family dinner: 'Psychology is just common sense. Why spend four years studying something everyone already knows? Study engineering or business instead.' Psychology degrees include statistics, research methods, biology of the brain and experiments, as well as topics such as development, memory and social behaviour.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you respond to your relative, and why is psychology worth studying at university?
followUps: Can you give an example of a psychology finding that goes against 'common sense'?
Why do psychology students need to study statistics and research methods?
How could psychology help with a real problem in Thailand, such as road safety, scam calls or exam stress?
What do you think will be the most difficult part of a psychology degree for you?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Your examples sound interesting, but they're from Western studies. Do they even apply to Thai people?

keyPoints: Explains that psychology tests ideas scientifically and that intuition is often wrong
Gives a specific example such as the bystander effect, false memories, or confirmation bias
Understands why statistics matter (to separate real effects from chance)
Applies psychology to a Thai issue with a concrete idea, e.g. how scammers exploit fear and authority
Discusses cultural differences and the need for research with Thai populations
warningSigns: Cannot give any example beyond 'understanding people'
Seems surprised or unhappy that psychology includes statistics
Becomes rude or dismissive towards the relative

interviewee.doorPrompt: This is a pressure station. The examiner will challenge your decision to study psychology and your understanding of the job market in Thailand. Some psychology graduates work in hospitals or schools, but many work in HR, marketing, research or technology, and clinical roles often require further study and a licence. Stay calm and give honest, specific answers.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Many psychology graduates in Thailand don't work as psychologists. Why should you take a place on this programme?
followUps: What steps would you need to take to become a licensed clinical psychologist?
If you couldn't get a clinical job, what would you do with your degree?
AI chatbots can now give 'therapy' at any time for free. Will psychologists still be needed in 2040?
Where do you see yourself in ten years, realistically?
interviewer.pressureProbe: I think you've chosen psychology because it sounds interesting, not because you have a plan. Am I wrong?

keyPoints: Stays composed and answers directly instead of repeating general statements
Shows realistic knowledge of training routes: further study, supervised practice, licensing
Sees transferable skills (research, data analysis, understanding behaviour, communication) as valuable in many jobs
Argues thoughtfully about AI: useful for access and support, but limits in risk assessment, empathy, accountability and complex cases
Gives a realistic, flexible career plan
warningSigns: Has no idea about training or job routes
Becomes defensive or gives up when challenged
Claims AI will replace psychologists entirely, or dismisses AI completely

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a trained peer listener at your school. Fah, an M3 student, comes to talk to you. She says she has been feeling hopeless for weeks, is not sleeping, and has had thoughts that she 'doesn't want to be here anymore'. She asks you to promise not to tell anyone, especially her parents or teachers, because she is afraid they will be angry and ashamed.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do, and why?
followUps: Why can't you keep this promise, even though she asked you to?
How would you explain to Fah that you need to involve someone else, without losing her trust?
Who exactly would you tell, and what would you say?
What if Fah became angry and said she would never talk to you again?
interviewer.pressureProbe: If you break her trust, she may never ask anyone for help again. Isn't keeping her secret the safer choice?

keyPoints: Takes her words seriously and responds calmly, warmly and without judgement
Explains honestly that they cannot promise secrecy when her safety is at risk, and explains why
Encourages and supports Fah to speak to the school counsellor or a trusted adult, offering to go with her
Knows to inform the designated trained adult promptly and, if there is immediate danger, to get urgent help (e.g. emergency services, the 1323 mental health hotline)
Recognises the limits of a peer listener's role and looks after their own wellbeing too
warningSigns: Promises to keep the secret
Tries to handle the situation alone as her 'counsellor'
Responds with shock, blame or by telling her to 'think positive'

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are helping a university lecturer run an anonymous online survey about stress among M5 and M6 students at a large Bangkok school. Students were told their answers would be confidential. The school director now asks you for the names of the 20 students with the highest stress scores, saying, 'We need to help them before the TCAS exams.' The survey system does record student email addresses.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you respond to the director's request?
followUps: Why does it matter that students were promised confidentiality?
How could the school help stressed students without breaking that promise?
What if one student's answers suggested they were at serious risk of harm?
Who should make the final decision, you, the lecturer or the director?
interviewer.pressureProbe: The director has good intentions and these students might need help. Isn't protecting their data more important to you than their wellbeing?

keyPoints: Recognises the conflict between the director's good intentions and the research promise of confidentiality and informed consent
Does not hand over names and refers the request to the lead researcher and ethics committee
Suggests alternatives: sharing overall results, offering all students support, advertising counselling, a follow-up opt-in survey
Understands that a pre-agreed risk protocol, explained in the consent form, is the proper way to handle serious risk
Points out that breaking trust could make students less honest in future surveys
warningSigns: Hands over the names because the director is senior
Sees no ethical problem with identifying students
Ignores the possibility that a student is at serious risk

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a newly qualified psychologist at a private counselling centre. Your client is Krit, 17, who is struggling with anxiety and conflict at home. His parents, who pay for the sessions, are close friends of your mother. They call you and ask, 'What has Krit been saying about us? As his parents we have a right to know.' Krit has asked you not to share details.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do in this situation?
followUps: Does it make a difference that Krit is 17 and not 12? Or that his parents are paying?
How does the friendship between his parents and your mother complicate things?
What if Krit told you something that suggested he or someone else was in serious danger?
How could you involve the parents in a way that helps Krit?
interviewer.pressureProbe: In Thai culture, children should respect their parents. Aren't you being too Western by refusing them?

keyPoints: Maintains Krit's confidentiality while explaining the limits that apply (serious risk of harm)
Responds to the parents respectfully, acknowledging their worry and explaining confidentiality in a warm, clear way
Identifies the dual relationship problem and considers whether to refer Krit to another psychologist
Suggests involving the parents with Krit's agreement, e.g. a family session or general parenting guidance
Engages thoughtfully with cultural expectations without abandoning professional ethics
warningSigns: Tells the parents what Krit has said
Rejects the parents rudely or treats their concern as unimportant
Does not see any problem with treating a family friend's son

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a psychology intern helping the only counsellor at a secondary school in Nonthaburi. It is two weeks before final exams and the counsellor is off sick for three days. There are 30 student referrals waiting. They include exam anxiety, friendship conflicts, a student whose teacher reports serious concern about her safety, a student who has missed ten days of school, and several parents asking for meetings.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you prioritise these referrals over the next three days?
followUps: Which case would you act on first, and what exactly would you do?
What is within your role as an intern, and what is not?
How could you support many students with exam anxiety at once?
What if a parent arrived demanding to see someone immediately about a friendship problem?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You're only an intern. Wouldn't it be safer to do nothing until the counsellor comes back?

keyPoints: Immediately escalates the safety concern to a senior staff member or designated safeguarding lead rather than handling it alone
Uses a clear triage system: risk to safety first, then attendance and serious distress, then less urgent issues
Recognises the limits of the intern role and seeks supervision, e.g. contacting the counsellor by phone or the school director
Suggests efficient support such as group workshops on exam stress, information sheets and contacting families of absent students
Communicates with waiting students and parents clearly and kindly about timelines
warningSigns: Treats all referrals as equal and sees them in order
Attempts to counsel the student at risk alone without informing anyone
Does nothing because they are 'just an intern'

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are on the student council and have been asked to plan a Mental Health Awareness Week at your school. You have 5,000 baht, two weeks to prepare, and five volunteers. A recent class survey suggests many students feel stressed but would be embarrassed to visit the counsellor. Some teachers think the event is 'a waste of study time'.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you prioritise, and how would you plan the week?
followUps: How would you reduce stigma so that students actually take part?
How would you persuade the sceptical teachers?
What if a student shared something serious during one of your activities?
How would you know whether the week had made any difference?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Awareness weeks are just posters and selfies. Nothing really changes. Why bother?

keyPoints: Sets clear goals, such as reducing stigma and increasing awareness of the counsellor, and plans activities around them
Uses the budget and volunteers realistically: low-cost activities such as anonymous question boxes, talks, LINE/Instagram content, short wellbeing sessions
Plans a safety procedure so any serious disclosure goes straight to the counsellor
Addresses teachers' concerns with evidence that wellbeing supports learning and by keeping activities short
Suggests measuring impact with a simple before-and-after survey or counsellor visit numbers
warningSigns: Spends the whole budget on one big event with no clear goal
Has no plan for handling serious disclosures
Dismisses the teachers' views instead of engaging with them

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a third-year psychology student running your own research project on social media use and sleep among 300 M4 students. Three weeks before your deadline, you discover that 140 parents have not returned consent forms, one school has withdrawn, and your online questionnaire had an error so that one key question was skipped. Your supervisor is at a conference abroad for two weeks.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do, and in what order?
followUps: Could you use data from students whose parents did not return consent forms? Why or why not?
How would you contact your supervisor, and what would you ask?
What if a classmate suggested 'filling in' the missing answers based on similar students?
If you had to ask for a deadline extension, how would you justify it?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Everyone is under pressure. Isn't it more realistic to just use the data you have and not mention the problems?

keyPoints: Refuses to use data from participants without valid consent
Contacts the supervisor by email straight away with a clear summary and options, and seeks help from another academic if needed
Considers realistic options: a smaller sample, extending recruitment, reporting the missing question as a limitation, requesting an extension
Firmly rejects inventing or filling in data as research misconduct
Plans better for the future, e.g. piloting questionnaires and starting consent earlier
warningSigns: Uses data without consent or hides the problems
Agrees to fill in missing answers
Gives up on the project without seeking help

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a psychology intern at a school counselling centre. The counsellor has recommended that Ploy, 16, see a doctor because of signs of depression: she has lost interest in everything, her grades have dropped, and she often cries in class. Ploy agreed to talk to her parents. Her mother, Khun Malee, has come to the centre and wants to speak to you.

interviewer.openingQuestion: The interviewer will play Khun Malee. Please explain why the school is concerned and what support Ploy needs.
followUps: How did you respond when she said, 'Our family doesn't have mental illness'?
Which words did you avoid, and why?
What if she said she would take Ploy to a temple instead of a doctor?
Why do you think stigma about mental health is still strong in many Thai families?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You're a student. Who are you to tell a mother what is wrong with her own daughter?

actor.role: Khun Malee, 47, Ploy's mother, who runs a family restaurant in Bangkok
actor.brief: You love your daughter but feel shocked and embarrassed. You think Ploy is just tired or lazy because of her phone, and you worry relatives will gossip if she sees a 'mental doctor'. Your hidden fear is that it is somehow your fault because you work long hours.
lines: Why did the school call me? Ploy is fine. She's just a bit tired from studying.
Our family doesn't have mental illness. If people find out, they will talk.
Is this because I'm always at the restaurant? Is it my fault?
actor.howToReact: If the candidate uses words like 'mental disorder' or 'psychiatric', blames the family, or argues about your beliefs, become defensive and say you will handle it yourselves. If they reassure you that depression is common and treatable, that it is not your fault and that you can help Ploy, soften and ask what you should do next.

keyPoints: Listens first and acknowledges the mother's love, worry and fear of judgement
Explains depression in simple, non-stigmatising language, as a common and treatable health problem, not weakness or a family failing
Avoids labels like 'crazy' or overly technical diagnoses and describes the specific changes observed
Respects cultural and religious practices and suggests they can complement, not replace, professional help
Agrees on a concrete next step and offers ongoing support from the school
warningSigns: Argues with or dismisses the mother's beliefs
Uses heavy clinical jargon or gives a firm diagnosis
Shares details Ploy said privately without permission

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a psychology student volunteering at a youth centre. Mr Ton is the father of Mint, 14. Mint's grades have dropped, she uses TikTok until 3 a.m., and she recently became very upset after classmates made fun of her in a group chat. Mr Ton has decided to take her phone away 'until she finishes M3' and wants your support.

interviewer.openingQuestion: The interviewer will play Mr Ton. Please discuss the situation with him.
followUps: What are the risks of a complete phone ban for Mint?
What alternative plan did you suggest, and why is it more likely to work?
How would you suggest he talk to Mint about the group-chat incident?
What if he said, 'When I was young, we had no phones and we were fine'?
interviewer.pressureProbe: He's her father. Isn't it his decision? Why are you interfering?

actor.role: Mr Ton, 45, a government officer and single father of Mint, 14
