actor.brief: You are frustrated and worried. You feel that the phone has 'stolen' your daughter and you don't understand TikTok. Your hidden concern is that you don't know how to talk to her since her mother moved away, and the phone feels like the only thing you can control.
lines: She's always on that phone. I've had enough. I'm taking it away until she finishes M3.
Those apps are poison. Everyone says social media makes kids depressed.
She doesn't talk to me anymore. I don't know what else to do.
actor.howToReact: If the candidate disagrees with you directly or lectures you about 'digital natives', become stubborn and say young people don't understand responsibility. If they respect your role as a father, recognise your worry and offer practical steps you can manage, open up about how hard it is to talk to your daughter.

keyPoints: Acknowledges his concern and agrees that sleep and online safety are real issues
Explains gently that a total ban may lead to secrecy, isolation from friends and damaged trust
Suggests a balanced plan: phone out of the bedroom at night, agreed screen-time limits, involving Mint in setting rules
Raises the cyberbullying incident as something Mint needs support with, and suggests involving the school
Encourages open, calm communication and modelling healthy phone use by parents too
warningSigns: Tells him he is wrong or a bad parent
Supports a total ban without discussing the emotional issues
Ignores the bullying incident

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a peer mentor in M6. Nok, an M6 student, has just received her mock A-Level results, which are much lower than she needs for her chosen faculty. She is crying in the corridor and very angry with herself. Her parents have spent a great deal on tutoring, and she says she cannot face them. You have a few minutes before the next class.

interviewer.openingQuestion: The interviewer will play Nok. Please begin when you are ready.
followUps: How did you decide when to listen and when to suggest practical steps?
How did you check whether she was safe and had support?
What if she said, 'Everyone else is doing better, I'm just stupid'?
Why is exam stress such a big issue for Thai students?
interviewer.pressureProbe: She needs facts, not hugs. Wouldn't it be better to tell her clearly that she must study harder?

actor.role: Nok, 17, an M6 student hoping to study pharmacy
actor.brief: You have studied hard and feel humiliated. Your parents have paid for expensive weekend tutoring and you feel you have let them down. Your hidden fear is that you are not clever enough and that your parents will be disappointed in you forever.
lines: Leave me alone. I failed. Everything I did this year was for nothing.
My parents spent so much money on tutoring. How can I tell them?
Everyone else is doing fine. Maybe I'm just stupid.
actor.howToReact: If the candidate tells you to stop crying, gives quick advice or compares you to others, turn away and refuse to talk. If they sit with you, listen and acknowledge how much effort you made, calm down and start to discuss what to do next and how to talk to your parents.

keyPoints: Stays calm, gives her space to express feelings and uses active listening before giving advice
Validates her disappointment while gently challenging all-or-nothing thinking ('one mock exam is not the final result')
Helps her think of practical next steps: talking to a teacher, analysing mistakes, a revision plan, alternative pathways and TCAS rounds
Explores how to talk to her parents and offers support with that
Checks in on her wellbeing and signposts her to the school counsellor if her distress continues
warningSigns: Says 'Don't cry, it's only a mock' or minimises her feelings
Compares her negatively with other students
Gives a long lecture on study techniques while she is upset

interviewee.doorPrompt: A news website publishes the table below with the headline: 'Science proves TikTok makes Thai teens anxious. Ban it for under-18s!' The data comes from an online survey of secondary school students. You have one minute to read it.

data.caption: Daily social media use and anxiety scores, Thai secondary students
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Students volunteered after seeing a link on Instagram. Anxiety was measured with a 5-question online quiz, not a validated clinical scale. Data collected during exam season.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Does this data prove the headline? What can we conclude?
followUps: Could the relationship work in the opposite direction?
What other factors might explain why heavy users report more anxiety?
What are the limitations of how this data was collected?
What kind of study would give stronger evidence about cause and effect?
interviewer.pressureProbe: The pattern rises perfectly with every hour. What more proof do you want?

keyPoints: States clearly that this shows a correlation, not proof that TikTok causes anxiety
Considers reverse causation: anxious teens may use social media more to cope or escape
Names confounding factors: sleep, exam stress, family problems, loneliness, cyberbullying
Identifies limitations: volunteer sample recruited on Instagram, self-reported hours, non-validated quiz, exam season, small top group
Suggests better studies (following students over time, experiments reducing use) and a balanced policy view
warningSigns: Agrees the data proves social media causes anxiety
Ignores how participants were recruited
Dismisses any possible link between social media and mental health

interviewee.doorPrompt: A Thai start-up launches 'JaiDee AI', a chatbot that offers 24-hour 'therapy' in Thai for 99 baht a month. Its advert says: 'Clinically proven: as effective as a human psychologist!' The company's website shows the study results below. Your school is considering buying it for all students.

data.caption: JaiDee AI study: 4-week results
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Study designed and funded by the company. Participants were university students in Bangkok who chose which group to join. Stress measured only at the end of week 4.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Based on this evidence, would you recommend the school adopts JaiDee AI? Why or why not?
followUps: What does the high drop-out rate suggest?
What are the possible benefits of an AI chatbot for Thai teenagers?
What risks are there, especially for a student in crisis?
What safeguards would you require before a school uses an AI mental health tool?
interviewer.pressureProbe: There are not enough psychologists in Thailand. Isn't an imperfect AI better than no help at all?

keyPoints: Notes that only 84 of 200 (42%) completed, so results describe the people who stayed, probably those it worked for
Identifies the lack of a control group, self-selection into groups, short duration and company funding
Recognises that 'as effective as a psychologist' is not supported by this design or this sample
Weighs real benefits (access, cost, anonymity, reducing stigma) against risks (missing crisis signs, privacy of data, wrong advice)
Recommends safeguards: independent evaluation, clear crisis referral to humans/hotlines, data protection, use alongside counsellors
warningSigns: Accepts the company's claim at face value
Ignores data privacy and crisis-safety issues
Rejects any role for technology without considering access problems

interviewee.doorPrompt: A viral TikTok video says: 'Take this 10-question quiz to find out if you have ADHD or depression! Over 2 million people have taken it, and 70% found out they have ADHD. If you scored high, you're not lazy, you have a disorder!' Several of your classmates are now telling everyone they 'have ADHD'. A friend asks you, as someone who wants to study psychology, what you think.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you evaluate this video and its claims?
followUps: Why might 70% of people who took the quiz score high?
What is the difference between a screening quiz and a professional diagnosis?
Can videos like this ever be helpful? How?
What would you say to a friend who is convinced from the quiz that they have ADHD?
interviewer.pressureProbe: If the quiz helps people feel understood, why does it matter if the science isn't perfect?

keyPoints: Explains that a self-selected online sample is biased: people who suspect they have ADHD are more likely to take it
Notes that the quiz is not validated, and many symptoms (poor focus, tiredness) are common in stressed teenagers
Distinguishes screening from a full assessment by a qualified professional
Recognises benefits (awareness, reduced stigma) and harms (misdiagnosis, missed real problems, labelling, self-medication)
Responds kindly to the friend, encouraging professional assessment rather than dismissing their experience
warningSigns: Treats the quiz result as a diagnosis
Mocks classmates or claims ADHD is 'not real'
Fails to mention seeing a qualified professional

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are in a group of five doing a school research project on sleep and screen use. One member, Nat, is very confident and keeps rewriting everyone's sections without asking, saying, 'Mine is better.' Two quieter members have stopped contributing ideas. The presentation is in ten days and Nat is doing a lot of good work.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do in this situation, and tell me about a real time one person dominated a group you were in.
followUps: How would you speak to Nat without making him defensive?
How could you help the quieter members to contribute?
Tell me about a real time you worked with someone whose style was very different from yours.
What did that experience teach you about group dynamics?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Nat is producing the best work. Maybe the team should just let him lead. Why change anything?

keyPoints: Acknowledges Nat's strengths while recognising the impact on the team
Suggests a private, respectful conversation using specific examples and 'I' statements
Proposes structural fixes: clear roles, agreed process for editing, everyone presenting their own section
Gives a genuine STAR example with personal actions and reflection
Links the example to psychological ideas such as group roles or motivation, without showing off
warningSigns: Complains about Nat to the teacher immediately without talking to him
Lets the problem continue to avoid conflict
Cannot give a real example

interviewee.doorPrompt: Your close friend Beam has been going through a difficult time since his parents separated. For the past month he has messaged you late every night to talk, sometimes for two hours. You want to support him, but you are exhausted, your own grades are falling, and you feel you don't know how to help him properly.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do? Then tell me about a real time you supported a friend and had to look after yourself too.
followUps: How can you keep supporting Beam while also looking after yourself?
How would you suggest professional support without making him feel rejected?
Tell me about a real time you supported someone through a difficult period. What did you learn?
Why is setting boundaries important for people who work in psychology?
interviewer.pressureProbe: A real friend would always be there. Aren't you being selfish?

keyPoints: Recognises that their own wellbeing matters and that burnout would not help Beam
Suggests honest, kind boundaries (e.g. agreed times to talk) explained with care
Encourages Beam to use other support: family, other friends, the school counsellor, and keeps checking how he is
Gives a genuine personal example with honest reflection about what worked and what didn't
Links this to professional boundaries and supervision in psychology
warningSigns: Cuts contact suddenly with no explanation
Continues sacrificing their own health without seeking any other help
Sees themselves as Beam's therapist

interviewee.doorPrompt: This station has a demanding examiner. Psychologists must recognise their own biases and be willing to change their opinions when given evidence. The examiner will ask you about a time you misjudged someone or held a belief that turned out to be wrong, and will push for honest detail. Choose a real example.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Tell me about a time you were wrong about a person or an idea. What changed your mind?
followUps: What do you think caused your original judgement?
How did you feel when you realised you were wrong?
What do you do now to check your assumptions about people?
Can you name a bias that a psychologist might have about clients from different backgrounds in Thailand?
interviewer.pressureProbe: That example is quite safe. Everyone misjudges someone at school. Do you have something more honest?

keyPoints: Gives a genuine, specific example with clear personal responsibility
Identifies the reasons for the misjudgement, such as first impressions, stereotypes or limited information
Shows real change in behaviour, not just a statement of learning
Names a relevant bias (e.g. confirmation bias, stereotypes about rural, LGBTQ+ or older clients) and how to reduce it
Remains reflective and open under challenge
warningSigns: Claims they are never wrong or never biased
Gives an example where the other person was really at fault
Becomes defensive when pushed for more detail

vocabulary.def: any person or group affected by a business decision, such as staff, customers, suppliers, owners or the community
vocabulary.example: Before closing the branch, the manager listed every stakeholder who would be affected.

vocabulary.def: the percentage of revenue that is left as profit after costs are paid
vocabulary.example: Delivery-app commission cut the stall's profit margin from 30% to 12%.

vocabulary.def: the movement of money into and out of a business over a period of time
vocabulary.example: The shop was profitable on paper but failed because of poor cash flow.

vocabulary.def: the specific group of customers a business aims to sell to
vocabulary.example: Their target market is office workers near BTS stations who want a quick lunch.

vocabulary.def: a company's commitment to act ethically and contribute to society and the environment, not only to make profit
vocabulary.example: Planting mangroves was part of the hotel's CSR programme.

vocabulary.def: all the steps and businesses involved in producing and delivering a product to the customer
vocabulary.example: The floods in Ayutthaya disrupted the supply chain for car parts.

vocabulary.def: how much profit is gained compared with the money spent
vocabulary.example: The TikTok campaign looked popular, but its return on investment was very low.

vocabulary.def: the ability of a business to grow without costs rising at the same rate
vocabulary.example: A cooking-class business has limited scalability because the owner can only teach so many people.

vocabulary.def: to change a business's strategy or product significantly after the original plan does not work
vocabulary.example: The startup pivoted from selling tutoring to selling exam-prep videos.

vocabulary.def: small and medium-sized enterprise; a business with a limited number of staff and turnover
vocabulary.example: SMEs make up the vast majority of businesses in Thailand.

vocabulary.def: to consider carefully what you gain and what you lose with each option
vocabulary.example: I would weigh up the trade-offs between short-term savings and long-term reputation.

vocabulary.def: the ability of something to continue successfully over many years
vocabulary.example: Cutting staff training might save money now, but it threatens the company's long-term sustainability.

vocabulary.def: to accept full responsibility for a task, decision or mistake
vocabulary.example: As team leader, I took ownership of the missed deadline instead of blaming others.

vocabulary.def: a risk taken after carefully thinking about the possible results
vocabulary.example: Opening a second branch was a calculated risk based on six months of sales data.

vocabulary.def: to be expected to explain and accept the consequences of your actions or decisions
vocabulary.example: Managers should be held accountable for misleading advertising, not just the intern who posted it.

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are applying to an international BBA programme at a leading Thai university. Business is one of the most competitive programmes, and many applicants say it 'keeps their options open'. The interviewer wants to understand what genuinely draws you to business and management, what you have done to explore it, and how realistic your picture of a manager's working life in Thailand is.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Why do you want to study business, and what do you think a manager actually does on a normal working day?
followUps: What have you done outside the classroom to explore business, for example a project, a competition, a family business or a part-time job?
What do you think is the least glamorous part of a manager's job, and how would you cope with it?
Name a Thai company you admire. What is one decision it made that you would question?
What if you discovered in your second year that you dislike managing people? What would you do with your degree then?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Lots of applicants say business 'keeps their options open'. Isn't that just a polite way of saying you don't know what you want?

keyPoints: Gives a specific, personal trigger for their interest (e.g. a school market-day stall, helping in a relative's shop) and what it taught them
Describes realistic daily work: meetings, handling staff problems, making decisions with incomplete information, meeting targets
Analyses a real Thai company decision critically instead of only praising the company
Connects specific programme features (case studies, internships, exchange, electives) to their own goals
Admits what they do not yet know and explains how they will find out
warningSigns: Motivation is only money, status or 'becoming a CEO' with no idea of the path
Cannot name any real exploration or experience of business
Describes business as 'easy' or 'just common sense'

interviewee.doorPrompt: Thailand's economy is changing fast: an ageing workforce, a growing digital economy, tourism recovering after COVID-19, and strong competition from Vietnam and other ASEAN neighbours. The interviewer is interested in your long-term vision and whether you understand the forces that will shape business careers in Thailand over the next decade.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Where do you see yourself ten years after graduating, and how will a business degree help you get there?
followUps: Which trend in the Thai economy do you think will affect your career most, and why?
What if AI can do most entry-level analysis jobs by the time you graduate? How would that change your plan?
Would you rather work for a large Thai conglomerate, a multinational or a startup? What are the downsides of your choice?
What skills do you think a business degree cannot teach you, and how will you develop them?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Ten-year plans almost never work out. Why should we take yours seriously?

keyPoints: Names a specific sector or role and gives realistic steps (graduate programme, experience, further study) rather than jumping straight to 'owner' or 'CEO'
Shows awareness of at least one concrete Thai trend, such as the ageing society, digital payments, or tourism dependence
Considers the downsides of their chosen path, e.g. long hours in consulting or instability in startups
Shows flexibility: explains what they would do if their plan changes
Recognises skills learned outside lectures, such as negotiation, resilience or leading people older than themselves
warningSigns: No plan beyond 'being successful' or 'being rich'
Ignores economic or technological change entirely
Rigid answer that cannot adapt when the interviewer changes the condition

interviewee.doorPrompt: This is a pressure station. The examiner is deliberately stern and may interrupt you. Business programmes receive thousands of applicants with similar grades and similar answers. Some applicants have already started small online shops or won national business competitions. You must explain what makes you a strong choice, and you may be challenged about whether this choice is really yours or your family's.

interviewer.openingQuestion: We have thousands of applicants with good grades. Why should we choose you rather than someone who has already started a real business?
followUps: Is studying business your decision or your family's? How do you know?
Tell me one thing about yourself that I would not learn from your portfolio.
What if you are rejected today? What would you do next year?
You said you are good at leadership. Prove it with one example, in one minute.
interviewer.pressureProbe: Everything you've said so far sounds rehearsed. Tell me something you genuinely haven't prepared.

keyPoints: Stays calm and polite under interruption, and does not become defensive
Gives concrete evidence (a project, a result, a lesson) rather than adjectives like 'hard-working' or 'passionate'
Answers the family-expectation question honestly, acknowledging influence while showing personal ownership of the decision
Turns the comparison into a strength, e.g. what university can give them that a person running a shop already does not need
Has a mature 'plan B' that shows resilience rather than panic
warningSigns: Becomes flustered, argumentative or visibly upset
Criticises other applicants to make themselves look better
Says they are only applying because their parents want them to, with no personal reason

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a summer intern in the marketing team of a Thai skincare brand. Your manager asks you to brief five TikTok influencers for a new serum campaign. She tells you to ask them NOT to label their posts as advertising, and to say the serum 'brightens skin in 7 days'. You know this claim has not been tested. The campaign launches next week and your internship report depends on her evaluation.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do, and why?
followUps: Who are all the stakeholders here, and who could be harmed?
What if your manager says 'Every brand does this; if we don't, we'll lose to competitors'?
What if one of the influencers has many teenage followers who trust her completely?
Suppose you raise your concern and she gives you a poor evaluation. Was it still the right decision?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You're an intern. Isn't it arrogant to think you know better than an experienced marketing manager?

keyPoints: Identifies two separate problems: hiding paid promotion from consumers and making an unproven product claim
Considers consumers, especially young followers, the influencers' credibility, the brand's long-term reputation and legal risk
Chooses a respectful, staged approach: asks questions first, suggests honest alternatives (e.g. 'results may vary', clear #ad labelling), escalates only if needed
Recognises the power imbalance and their own self-interest, but does not let the evaluation decide the ethics
Points out that being caught misleading customers can destroy trust far faster than honest marketing builds it
warningSigns: Simply follows the instruction because 'the manager is responsible, not me'
Immediately posts about the company on social media or quits without trying to talk first
Does not notice that the 7-day claim is a separate problem from the hidden sponsorship

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are an assistant manager at a small family-owned resort in Krabi. The resort advertises itself as '100% plastic-free', and many guests book for this reason. Costs have risen sharply and the owner, Khun Prasert, asks you to quietly switch back to plastic water bottles in the rooms while keeping the 'plastic-free' message on the website. He says that if the resort loses money, staff jobs will be cut.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you respond to Khun Prasert?
followUps: Is it ever acceptable for a business to break a sustainability promise to protect jobs?
What alternatives could reduce costs without misleading guests?
What if a guest notices the plastic bottles and posts a photo on Google Reviews?
What if Khun Prasert is a close family friend who gave you this job?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Staff need salaries to feed their families. Aren't you putting a marketing slogan above real people's lives?

keyPoints: Separates the business decision (whether to use plastic) from the honesty issue (keeping the claim while breaking it)
Takes the owner's financial pressure and staff jobs seriously rather than dismissing them
Suggests realistic alternatives, e.g. refill stations, honest updated wording, cost savings elsewhere, explaining the change to guests
Considers reputational risk: a 'greenwashing' review could cost more bookings than the bottles save
Shows how they would raise the issue respectfully with an older owner in a Thai workplace
warningSigns: Agrees to mislead guests because 'nobody will notice'
Treats the issue as purely black and white and ignores the threat to staff jobs
Has no practical alternative to offer the owner

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are an HR intern at a large company in Bangkok. While preparing documents, you see a confidential list of 40 employees who will be laid off next month. Your best friend's father, Mr Somchai, is on the list. Your friend tells you excitedly that her father is about to sign a 30-year mortgage for a new condo this Friday. You signed a confidentiality agreement when you started.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What do you do?
followUps: What duty do you owe to the company, and what duty do you owe to your friend?
What if you could hint without actually breaking the agreement, for example saying 'maybe wait before signing anything big'? Is that different?
What if the list is still a draft and Mr Somchai might not be laid off after all?
If your friend later finds out you knew and said nothing, how would you explain yourself?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Be honest: if this were your own father, would you really keep quiet? If not, isn't your answer hypocritical?

keyPoints: Recognises the genuine conflict between confidentiality, loyalty to a friend and preventing serious financial harm
Considers why confidentiality matters here: fairness to all 40 employees, possible panic, the list may change
Explores legitimate routes, e.g. asking HR whether affected staff can be told earlier, or whether timing can be reconsidered
Treats 'hinting' honestly as a form of disclosure rather than a clever loophole
Accepts that every option has a cost and explains which cost they would accept and why
warningSigns: Immediately tells the friend everything without considering the other 39 employees or the agreement
Says the friend's problem is 'not my business' with no empathy
Refuses to commit to any decision

interviewee.doorPrompt: Aunt Somsri sells khao man gai from a stall near an MRT station. Since office workers began ordering through delivery apps, her sales have fallen by about 30%. She has 20,000 baht in savings, no social media accounts and is not confident with smartphones. She asks you to help her during your four-week school holiday. You cannot do everything at once.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do first, and how would you plan the four weeks?
followUps: How would you find out WHY sales have fallen before spending any money?
Delivery apps take around 30% commission. How would you decide whether joining one is worth it?
What if Aunt Somsri refuses to use a smartphone at all after your holiday ends?
How would you measure whether your plan has worked after four weeks?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You're 17 and have never run a business. Why should Aunt Somsri trust your plan with her savings?

keyPoints: Starts with diagnosis (talking to customers, observing lunchtime traffic, checking competitors) before spending money
Calculates or reasons about app commission against her profit margin rather than assuming digital is always better
Prioritises low-cost, low-risk steps first, e.g. a LINE Official Account, a pre-order system, a Google Maps listing
Designs a plan she can maintain alone after the holiday, respecting her skills and preferences
Sets simple measures of success, such as daily orders, new versus returning customers, profit per day
warningSigns: Spends most of her savings immediately on ads or equipment
Builds a complicated system that only the candidate can operate
Ignores what Aunt Somsri actually wants

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are the assistant manager of a 20-room guesthouse in Chiang Mai. It is March, PM2.5 haze is severe, and 40% of April bookings have been cancelled. You have 12 staff, enough cash to pay everyone for about two months, and three angry online reviews about the air quality. The owner is abroad and has asked you to send a plan within one week.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What are your priorities this week, and in what order?
followUps: Would you cut staff hours, cut salaries or keep everyone on full pay? Justify your choice.
How would you respond to the negative reviews about air quality, which you cannot control?
What new customer groups could you target during smoke season?
What if the haze lasts much longer than expected and cash runs out in five weeks instead of eight?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Haze comes back every year. Isn't this a long-term strategic failure rather than a short-term crisis?

keyPoints: Protects cash flow first: checks exact cash position, delays non-essential spending, talks to suppliers
Considers staff fairly and transparently, e.g. discussing options with them rather than announcing cuts suddenly
Responds to reviews honestly and practically (air purifiers, flexible rebooking) rather than defensively
Thinks about new segments or offers, such as domestic tourists, long-stay remote workers, or rebooking incentives for the cool season
Distinguishes between immediate actions and a long-term plan for the annual haze season
warningSigns: Fires staff immediately without considering alternatives
Deletes or argues with negative reviews
Produces a list of ideas with no order or reasoning

interviewee.doorPrompt: You and your friend Krit launched a student app that matches M4–M6 students with university tutors. You raised 300,000 baht from family and friends. Six months later, 60,000 baht is left, monthly users have stopped growing at around 400, and few users pay. Krit wants to spend all the remaining money on a TikTok ad campaign. Your university entrance exams are in two months.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do, and how would you decide?
followUps: What information would you want to see before deciding whether to pivot, continue or shut down?
How would you handle the disagreement with Krit?
What do you owe the family and friends who invested?
What if a large tutoring company offers to buy your user list for 50,000 baht? Would you accept?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Most founders who quit say they 'learned a lot'. Isn't that just an excuse for failure?

keyPoints: Asks for meaningful data: retention, why users do not pay, cost per new user, what the 400 users actually value
Rejects spending everything on one untested campaign, e.g. suggests a small test budget first
Balances the business against their own priorities and wellbeing during exam season
Takes responsibility to investors through honest communication, not only through returning money
Spots the data-privacy and trust problem in selling the user list
warningSigns: Makes a decision based only on emotion or optimism with no evidence
Ignores the investors or the co-founder relationship
Agrees to sell user data without thinking about users' consent

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a junior purchasing officer at a Bangkok café chain. For eight years, the chain has bought coffee beans from Mr Wichai, who runs a small family farm in Chiang Rai. Head office has decided to buy most beans from a cheaper importer, so orders from Mr Wichai will fall by 60% from next month. Your manager has asked you to tell him in person today.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Please go in and speak to Mr Wichai.
followUps: How did you decide what to say first?
What could you honestly offer Mr Wichai, and what should you not promise?
What if he asks you directly whether the decision is final?
How would you report this conversation back to your manager?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You kept saying 'I understand'. Do you really think you understand what losing 60% of your income feels like?

actor.role: Mr Wichai, 55, owner of a small family coffee farm in Chiang Rai and supplier to the chain for eight years
actor.brief: You are proud of your beans and see the café chain as a partner, almost like family. You do not know about the decision yet. Your hidden concern: you recently took a 400,000-baht bank loan for new drying equipment because the chain's manager hinted orders would grow.
lines: Ah, good to see you! Have you tried the new honey-process beans I sent last week?
Sixty percent? After eight years? Did I do something wrong? Was the quality bad?
Your manager told me last year that orders would grow. I borrowed money because of that. What am I supposed to tell the bank?
actor.howToReact: If the candidate uses business jargon ('cost optimisation', 'strategic sourcing') or rushes, become hurt and say 'So I'm just a number to you now?'. If they ignore your feelings, go quiet and cold. If they acknowledge the relationship, apologise sincerely and ask about your situation, calm down and begin asking what can realistically be done.

keyPoints: Delivers the news clearly and early instead of hiding it behind small talk
Acknowledges the eight-year relationship and Mr Wichai's emotions before moving to solutions
Listens and discovers his hidden concern (the equipment loan) by asking open questions
Offers only realistic support, such as notice time, introductions to other buyers, or passing his concerns to head office, without false promises
Remains respectful to an older person, using appropriate politeness
warningSigns: Blames head office in a way that sounds like 'it's not my problem'
Promises to reverse the decision or keep orders unchanged
Talks mostly about the company's costs and ignores his feelings

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are the shift manager at a busy bubble-tea shop in Siam Square. A customer, Fah, comes to the counter angry. Her online order of 15 drinks arrived 90 minutes late and several drinks had melted. She is holding up her phone and appears to be filming. The shop was short of two staff today. You need to handle the situation.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Please speak to the customer.
followUps: Why did you choose to apologise or not apologise in the way you did?
What would you offer her, and how did you decide what was fair?
What if she posts the video anyway and it gets 200,000 views? What would you do next?
What would you change in the shop so this does not happen again?
interviewer.pressureProbe: The delay was partly the delivery rider's fault. Why should your shop take the blame?

actor.role: Fah, 24, an office worker who ordered 15 drinks online
actor.brief: You are embarrassed and angry. The drinks were for your mother's 60th birthday lunch with relatives, and you had to serve nothing. You want an apology and for someone to take responsibility, more than you want money.
lines: Are you the manager? Look at this. Ninety minutes late and everything melted. I'm recording this.
Don't tell me you were busy. That's not my problem. I paid for these.
It was my mother's sixtieth birthday. Everyone was waiting. Do you know how embarrassing that was?
actor.howToReact: If the candidate makes excuses or blames the rider, raise your voice and say you will post the video now. If they offer something small too quickly, say 'You think a free drink fixes this?'. If they apologise sincerely and ask what happened, lower the phone, explain about your mother and accept a reasonable solution.

keyPoints: Stays calm and does not argue about the filming; focuses on the customer, not the camera
Apologises sincerely without making excuses about staff shortages first
Discovers what the order was for (her mother's party) and responds to that personal impact
Offers a concrete, proportionate remedy, such as a refund or remaking the order, and checks it is acceptable to her
Thinks beyond the moment: records the issue and suggests process changes, e.g. limiting large orders when short-staffed
warningSigns: Blames the rider, the app or the staff in front of the customer
Asks her to stop filming in a defensive or aggressive way
Offers a tiny gesture that does not match the problem

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are 25 and have just become operations manager at your family's distribution company. You want to replace the paper-based stock records with a simple barcode inventory system. Khun Nok, 50, has managed the warehouse for 20 years using her own notebooks. She is respected by the staff. You need her support or the new system will fail. You have asked to meet her.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Please speak to Khun Nok and try to get her support.
followUps: How did you show respect for her experience while still pushing for change?
What if she agrees in this meeting but then quietly keeps using her notebooks?
How would you involve the other warehouse staff?
If she still refuses after a fair trial, what would you do?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Honestly, aren't you only in this position because your parents own the company? Why should she listen to you?

actor.role: Khun Nok, 50, warehouse supervisor for 20 years
actor.brief: You knew the candidate as a child and are polite but sceptical. You think your system works perfectly and you have seen 'modern' ideas fail before. Hidden concern: you are not confident with technology and fear that if the system works, the company will not need you any more.
lines: Khun, it's nice to see you in the office now. So, what is this meeting about?
My notebooks have worked for twenty years. We've never lost a single delivery. Why change?
If a computer can do it, what will I do here? Will I still have a job?
actor.howToReact: If the candidate uses technical jargon or says 'my father agrees', become stiff and say 'Then why do you need my opinion?'. If they talk down to you, stop cooperating. If they ask about your experience and reassure you honestly about your role, become warmer and suggest a small trial.

keyPoints: Opens by asking about her process and listening, not by presenting the system
Explains the benefit in terms that matter to her (fewer counting errors, less overtime, easier stock checks) rather than technology jargon
Addresses her hidden fear of being replaced directly and honestly
Proposes involving her as a leader of the change, e.g. a pilot or training other staff
Handles the 'boss's kid' challenge calmly, acknowledging it without becoming defensive
warningSigns: Uses family authority: 'My father has already decided'
Dismisses her notebook system as old-fashioned or wrong
Makes promises about her job that they cannot keep

interviewee.doorPrompt: A management consultancy publishes a report with the headline: 'Thai family businesses that hire an outside professional CEO grow twice as fast.' It includes the table below. A friend whose family owns a large furniture company asks you whether her parents should hire an outsider instead of handing the business to her older brother.

data.caption: Thai family businesses after the founder steps back: performance over 10 years
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Published by a consultancy that sells CEO recruitment services. Only firms with annual revenue above 500 million baht were included. Firms that hired an outside CEO were, on average, about three times larger at the start of the period.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What does this data show, and does it support the headline?
followUps: Why might the 'outside CEO' group be different from the other groups before the new CEO even arrived?
What does the small number of firms in one group mean for how confident we can be?
Who published this report, and why does that matter?
What if your friend's brother has worked in the company for ten years? What would you advise, and what else would you need to know?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Twice the growth and higher survival. The numbers are clear. Why can't you just accept the conclusion?

keyPoints: Notes the 'twice as fast' claim compares 8% with 4% but depends on just 15 outside-CEO firms
Spots the possible selection effect: outside-CEO firms were already larger, so growth and survival may not be caused by the CEO
Identifies the consultancy's conflict of interest, since it sells CEO recruitment services
Points out missing information: profit, industry type, how 'growth' is measured, firms below 500 million baht
Turns the analysis into careful advice that depends on the brother's ability, not only on averages
warningSigns: Repeats the headline as proven fact
Says correlation proves an outside CEO causes growth
Gives advice to the friend without any reference to the data's limitations

interviewee.doorPrompt: A news website publishes the headline: 'Thai tourism fully recovered – back to pre-COVID levels!' A travel company plans to open five new hotels based on this story. You are shown the table below, which the article used. You are asked whether the headline is fair and what the company should consider.

data.caption: International visitors to Thailand and their spending
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Figures are rounded and simplified. 2026 values are a forecast by a tourism industry association. No breakdown by region, visitor nationality or length of stay is given.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Does this data support the headline 'Thai tourism fully recovered'?
followUps: Which number in the table do you think the headline writer focused on, and which did they ignore?
Why might total spending matter more to hotel owners than the number of arrivals?
What if most of the recovery is in Bangkok and Phuket, but not in smaller provinces?
What would you advise the travel company before it opens five new hotels?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Arrivals are almost back to 2019 levels. Isn't that what 'recovered' means? You're overcomplicating it.

keyPoints: Notices arrivals are close to 2019 but average spending per visitor and total revenue are still lower
Points out the data shows only national totals, not regional differences, hotel occupancy or profit
Questions what 'recovered' means and for whom: airlines, hotels, street vendors, workers
Notes that the 2026 figure is only a forecast
Gives balanced advice, e.g. research specific locations and target segments before expanding
warningSigns: Agrees with the headline after reading only one column
Ignores the forecast label on the 2026 row
Cannot turn the analysis into practical advice for the company

interviewee.doorPrompt: A popular Thai 'business coach' with two million followers posts on TikTok: '90% of startups fail. University business degrees are useless — I dropped out at 18 and made my first million by 22. My students who skip university earn 3x more than graduates! Join my 9,900-baht course today.' Your younger cousin shares the post in the family LINE group and says she will not go to university.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you evaluate the claims in this post?
followUps: Take the claim '3x more than graduates'. What information would you need to check it?
Is the claim '90% of startups fail' an argument for or against studying business?
What is survivorship bias, and how does it apply to this coach's own story?
How would you talk to your cousin about this without making her defensive?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You are applying to a business faculty, so of course you'll defend degrees. Isn't your view just as biased as his?

keyPoints: Identifies the conflict of interest: the coach profits from people believing the claim
Questions the '3x' statistic: who was measured, how many, compared over what period, self-reported or verified
Explains survivorship bias: we hear from the successful dropout, not the many who struggled
Notes the logical gap: a high startup failure rate does not prove degrees are useless
Acknowledges their own possible bias honestly and still reasons from evidence
warningSigns: Simply insults the coach without analysing the claims
Accepts that degrees are useless because of one success story
Becomes defensive when their own bias is questioned

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are in a team of four for a national business case competition. The final presentation is in five days. One member, Ton, has missed two meetings, has not done his market research section and replies to LINE messages with only a sticker. The others want to remove his name from the slides. Afterwards, the interviewer will ask about your own real experience of teamwork.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do about Ton, and can you tell me about a time you worked with someone who was not contributing?
followUps: What might be going on in Ton's life that you don't know about?
Is it fair to remove his name from the slides? Who should decide?
In your real example, what exactly did you do, and what was the result?
Looking back, what would you do differently?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Many people who complain about lazy teammates were actually poor leaders themselves. Could that have been true of you?

keyPoints: Talks to Ton privately and asks what is happening before judging him
Balances fairness to the hard-working members with understanding for Ton
Proposes a practical plan, e.g. reallocating tasks with clear deadlines, agreeing as a team how credit will be shared
Gives a real, specific example using a clear structure (situation, task, action, result)
Reflects honestly on their own role and what they learned
warningSigns: Immediately reports Ton or removes him without speaking to him
Describes doing all the work themselves as a success
Cannot give any real example, or blames others entirely

interviewee.doorPrompt: Business leaders often say they learned more from failure than success. Imagine you led a school club's charity fundraiser: you ordered 500 printed tote bags to sell, but only 120 were sold and the club lost 8,000 baht. The interviewer will ask how you would handle that, and then about a real time something you led or planned did not go well.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Tell me about a time something you were responsible for did not go as planned.
followUps: In the tote-bag situation, what would you say to the club members and to the teachers?
In your real example, how much of the failure was your responsibility?
What did you actually change afterwards? Give me evidence.
What if the same thing happened again at university with real money from a sponsor?
interviewer.pressureProbe: That sounds more like bad luck than failure. Can you tell me about a time it was clearly your fault?

keyPoints: Chooses a genuine failure with real consequences, not a disguised success
Takes ownership without excessive self-criticism or blaming others
Analyses causes specifically, e.g. no market testing, over-ordering, no pre-orders
Shows concrete change in later behaviour, with an example
For the hypothetical, communicates honestly with members and teachers and suggests ways to recover some of the loss
warningSigns: Says they have never really failed
Gives a 'failure' that is really a boast ('I worked too hard')
Blames teammates, teachers or bad luck for everything

interviewee.doorPrompt: This is a pressure station. Imagine that after a group project, three teammates give you anonymous feedback: 'Good ideas, but controlling. Doesn't let others make decisions. Rewrote our work without asking.' The examiner will push you on how you respond to criticism and will ask about real feedback you have received. Be honest; the examiner is looking for self-awareness, not perfection.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you react to that feedback, and tell me about a time you received criticism that was hard to hear.
followUps: Is there any truth in that feedback about you? Give an example.
How do you know when to lead and when to step back?
What if you believe your teammates' work really was poor quality?
In your real example, how did the other person know you had taken the feedback seriously?
interviewer.pressureProbe: I notice you've described your weaknesses as strengths. Tell me a weakness that is actually a weakness.

keyPoints: Responds with curiosity rather than defensiveness, e.g. would ask teammates for specific examples
Admits a real weakness and shows how they manage it
Distinguishes between high standards and controlling behaviour, e.g. giving feedback versus rewriting others' work
Gives a specific real example and a visible change they made
Stays composed under the examiner's challenge
warningSigns: Dismisses the feedback as jealousy or teammates being lazy
Gives a cliché weakness such as 'I'm a perfectionist' with no depth
Becomes irritated or silent under pressure

vocabulary.def: an independent check of an organisation's financial records to see whether they are accurate and fair
vocabulary.example: The external audit found that some sales had been recorded in the wrong year.

vocabulary.def: the principle that an auditor must be free from personal or financial ties that could affect their judgement about a client
vocabulary.example: Accepting a job offer from the client during the audit would threaten auditor independence.

vocabulary.def: formal reports showing a company's financial performance and position, such as the income statement and balance sheet
vocabulary.example: Banks study a company's financial statements before approving a loan.

vocabulary.def: the rules about when a sale can be recorded as income
vocabulary.example: Recording January's sales in December breaks the rules of revenue recognition.

vocabulary.def: procedures a business uses to protect its money and make sure records are accurate, such as needing two people to approve payments
vocabulary.example: With proper internal controls, one person could not transfer 480,000 baht alone.

vocabulary.def: how large or important an error must be before it could change the decisions of people using the accounts
vocabulary.example: A 500-baht mistake is usually below materiality, but a 2-million-baht one is not.

vocabulary.def: an amount that can legally be subtracted from income before tax is calculated
vocabulary.example: She did not know that her shop rent was a tax deduction.

vocabulary.def: a tax added to the price of goods and services at each stage of production and sale
vocabulary.example: Once her sales passed 1.8 million baht a year, she had to register for VAT.

vocabulary.def: secretly stealing money that you have been trusted to look after, especially by an employer
vocabulary.example: The missing club funds turned out to be a recording error, not embezzlement.

vocabulary.def: how easily a business can pay its short-term debts with available cash
vocabulary.example: The company was profitable but had a liquidity problem when customers paid late.

vocabulary.def: an attitude of questioning evidence carefully rather than accepting it at face value
vocabulary.example: Professional scepticism means checking the 'consultant' invoice, even if the manager is friendly.

vocabulary.def: a situation where personal interests could influence someone's professional judgement
vocabulary.example: Auditing your uncle's company would be a clear conflict of interest.

vocabulary.def: to do something less carefully or properly than you should, usually to save time or money
vocabulary.example: Under deadline pressure, it is tempting to cut corners on checking receipts.

vocabulary.def: to keep high standards of honesty, even when it is difficult
vocabulary.example: Accountants must uphold integrity even when a client threatens to move to another firm.

vocabulary.def: the confidence that society has in a profession or institution to act honestly
vocabulary.example: One accounting scandal can damage public trust in the whole stock market.

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are applying to a Faculty of Commerce and Accountancy in Bangkok. Many teenagers see accounting as 'boring number-crunching', and some people believe AI will soon do most bookkeeping. The interviewer wants to know why you have chosen this field, what you understand about an accountant's working life in Thailand, and what you have done to explore it.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Why do you want to study accounting, and what do you think accountants actually spend their days doing?
followUps: What have you done to find out what accountants really do, for example talking to someone in the profession, an internship or a project?
Audit firms have a very busy period every year with long working hours. How do you feel about that?
Which area interests you most: audit, tax, corporate finance or something else? Why?
What if, after your first year, you find you prefer finance or data analysis to accounting? Would you regret this choice?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You say you like numbers. So do mathematicians and engineers. What is it about ACCOUNTING specifically?

keyPoints: Shows that accounting is about judgement and communication, not only calculation (e.g. explaining results, advising clients, assessing risk)
Knows realistic facts about the career path, such as becoming a licensed CPA, busy seasons, starting in junior roles
Gives a concrete example of exploration (talking to an auditor, helping with a family shop's records, a finance competition)
Distinguishes between different branches of the profession and gives a reason for their preference
Acknowledges the downsides honestly but explains why they still want this path
warningSigns: Says they chose accounting because it is 'safe' or their parents told them to, with no personal reason
Believes accounting is just maths and needs no people skills
No awareness of how the profession is changing

interviewee.doorPrompt: When a large company hides losses or inflates its profits, thousands of ordinary investors, employees and pension funds can lose money. Accountants and auditors are meant to protect the public from this. The interviewer wants to know whether you understand the role of accounting in society, and where you see yourself in the profession in the future.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How do accountants contribute to society, beyond helping companies count their money?
followUps: Why do you think investors trust an audited set of accounts more than accounts prepared by the company itself?
Who is harmed when accountants fail to do their job properly? Give a concrete example.
Where do you see yourself ten years after graduating: in a large audit firm, a company's finance team, government or your own firm?
What if you discovered that your future employer had helped a client hide losses? Would you stay?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Auditors are paid by the companies they check. Isn't the whole system a bit of a joke?

keyPoints: Explains the link between reliable financial information and trust in markets, banks and taxes
Identifies specific people who can be harmed: small investors, employees, suppliers, the government's tax revenue
Shows understanding of independence and why it matters
Has a realistic career plan with stages, and a reason linked to values rather than only salary
Handles the 'auditors are paid by clients' challenge thoughtfully, e.g. mentioning regulation, professional standards and reputation
warningSigns: Sees accounting only as helping companies reduce tax
Cannot name anyone who is affected by inaccurate accounts
Agrees the system is pointless but still wants to join it, without resolving the contradiction

interviewee.doorPrompt: This is a pressure station with a stern examiner. AI software can already read receipts, record transactions, reconcile bank accounts and prepare simple tax returns. Some experts predict that most entry-level accounting jobs will disappear within ten years. The examiner will challenge whether studying accounting is a wise choice and whether you have really thought about your future.

interviewer.openingQuestion: AI can already do most bookkeeping. Why should we spend four years training you for a job that may not exist?
followUps: Which parts of an accountant's work do you think AI will NOT be able to do well? Why?
If junior tasks are automated, how will new accountants gain experience?
What skills will you develop at university to make sure you are not replaced?
What if you are wrong, and AI does replace most accountants? What is your plan B?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You haven't convinced me. Every applicant says 'AI can't replace human judgement'. What evidence do you actually have?

keyPoints: Stays calm and engages seriously with the threat rather than dismissing it
Distinguishes routine tasks (data entry, reconciliation) from judgement-based work (estimates, fraud risk, advising clients, ethics)
Identifies a real problem, such as how juniors will learn if entry-level work disappears
Names specific skills they would build: data analytics, communication, understanding business, ethics
Gives a flexible plan B that uses transferable skills
warningSigns: Says AI will never affect accounting
Becomes defensive or gives up and agrees the degree is pointless
Repeats the same answer when pushed for evidence

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are an intern in the finance department of a medium-sized electronics distributor. It is 30 December. The company is 3% short of its annual sales target, which it promised its bank in a loan agreement. The finance manager, Khun Krit, asks you to record a large order that will be delivered on 10 January as December sales. He says, 'It's only ten days. We'll get there anyway.'

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do?
followUps: Why does it matter which year a sale is recorded in, if the money arrives anyway?
Who could be harmed by this, even if the order is delivered successfully?
What if Khun Krit tells you that if the target is missed, the bank may demand repayment and 50 staff could lose their jobs?
What if he says, 'I'll do it myself. Just don't mention it to anyone'?
interviewer.pressureProbe: It's ten days and you are an intern. Isn't refusing just naïve? Real business doesn't work like that.

keyPoints: Recognises that recording sales in the wrong period misleads the bank and other users of the accounts
Takes the jobs argument seriously but explains why misleading the bank could create bigger risks later
Asks questions respectfully and suggests honest alternatives, e.g. talking to the bank early about the shortfall
Knows when and how to escalate, e.g. to a more senior person or an ethics channel, if pressured
Recognises that staying silent when someone else does it is still a decision with consequences
warningSigns: Agrees because 'it's a small amount' or 'my manager is responsible'
Threatens to report Khun Krit immediately without trying to discuss
Does not understand why timing of revenue matters

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a junior auditor checking the accounts of a hotel group. The client's finance director, Khun Wanpen, has been very kind to you. Over lunch, she offers you a job at her company, at almost double your current salary, starting after the audit. That afternoon, you find a 2-million-baht payment to a 'consultant' with no contract or clear explanation. She signs all payments of this size.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you handle this situation?
followUps: Is accepting the job offer a problem in itself, even if you were completely honest in your work?
What would you do about the 2-million-baht payment?
What if your audit manager says, 'Don't worry about it, she's a good client'?
What if you really need the higher salary to support your family?
interviewer.pressureProbe: There's probably a simple explanation for the payment. Aren't you being paranoid about a kind person who just offered you a great job?

keyPoints: Recognises that the job offer creates a conflict of interest and must be disclosed to their own firm
Treats the payment with professional scepticism: asks for supporting documents and investigates without accusing
Understands that both issues are connected, since the offer may affect their objectivity about her payment
Escalates to a senior auditor if the explanation is unsatisfactory, even if the manager is reluctant
Acknowledges the personal financial temptation honestly
warningSigns: Accepts the job and ignores the payment
Accuses Khun Wanpen of fraud before gathering evidence
Does not see any conflict of interest in the job offer

interviewee.doorPrompt: This is a pressure station. Your mother runs a small online clothing shop. Most customers pay by bank transfer to her personal account. She asks you, as a future accounting student, to help with her tax return. She tells you to declare only the sales made through the shopping platform, not the personal transfers. 'Everyone does this. The big companies avoid millions. We're just trying to survive.'

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you say to your mother?
followUps: Is there a difference between legally reducing tax and hiding income?
Your mother says big companies avoid far more tax than she does. How would you respond?
What if the business really is struggling and paying the full tax would mean closing it?
What if she refuses to listen and files the return herself? Is that your problem any more?
interviewer.pressureProbe: She's your mother and she raised you. Would you really put the tax office before your own family?

keyPoints: Distinguishes between legal tax planning (deductions, correct expenses) and illegal non-declaration of income
Responds to her fear and financial stress with empathy rather than a lecture
Explains real risks to the family: bank records can be traced, penalties and interest, stress later
Offers practical help: claiming legitimate expenses, checking whether she qualifies for lower rates, getting advice from a professional
Holds a clear personal line about not signing or preparing a false return, while staying loyal and kind
warningSigns: Agrees to help hide income because 'it's family'
Is cold or judgemental and shows no understanding of her situation
Does not know that bank transfers can be traced or that tax law applies to small sellers

interviewee.doorPrompt: You work part-time as a bookkeeper for a small family trading company. At 1:30 pm you receive a LINE message that appears to be from the owner, Mr Somchai: 'Urgent. Transfer 480,000 baht to this new supplier account before 3 pm or we lose the deal. I'm on a flight, can't talk.' Staff salaries must also be paid today, and an auditor is waiting for documents.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do, and in what order?
followUps: What signs suggest this could be a scam?
How could you try to confirm the request if Mr Somchai is really on a flight?
What if the supplier then calls you, sounding angry and professional, saying the deal will be cancelled?
Afterwards, what internal controls would you suggest so this situation cannot happen again?
interviewer.pressureProbe: If this is real and you don't pay, the company loses its biggest deal and it's your fault. Are you willing to take that risk?

keyPoints: Prioritises not sending money until the request is verified through a separate, known channel
Recognises classic scam signals: urgency, new account, unable to talk, secrecy, LINE instead of normal process
Tries practical verification: calling the owner's family or another manager, checking the supplier's known contact details
Still handles the other tasks: pays salaries as planned, tells the auditor about any delay
Suggests concrete controls, e.g. two-person approval, call-back rule for new accounts, written payment policy
warningSigns: Transfers the money because the boss 'said so'
Ignores salaries and the auditor while dealing with the message
Cannot explain why the request looks suspicious

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are the new treasurer of your school's music club. Two days before the teachers check the club accounts, you discover that 6,500 baht from the concert ticket sales is missing. Several receipts are lost, and the previous treasurer, your friend Mint, kept the cash box at home for a week. The club president wants you to 'just make the numbers match'.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you deal with this in the next two days?
followUps: What would you check first before you talk to anyone?
How would you approach Mint without damaging your friendship?
What if you find that Mint borrowed the money for a family emergency and plans to pay it back?
What would you say to the teacher if you cannot find the money by the deadline?
interviewer.pressureProbe: It's only 6,500 baht and Mint is your friend. Why not just make the numbers match like the president said?

keyPoints: Starts with evidence: recounts cash, checks ticket numbers sold against money recorded, looks for bank deposits or recording errors
Considers innocent explanations (recording error, unrecorded expenses) before assuming theft
Talks to Mint privately and fairly, asking rather than accusing
Refuses to falsify the records and is honest with the teacher, explaining what is known and unknown
Proposes better controls for the future, such as receipts for every sale and two people counting cash
warningSigns: Changes the figures to hide the missing money
Publicly accuses Mint without evidence
Pays the money themselves secretly to make the problem disappear

interviewee.doorPrompt: This is a pressure station. You are a junior accountant. Today, you must submit the monthly VAT return before midnight or the company pays a penalty. The CFO wants a cash report for a board meeting at 4 pm. A key supplier threatens to stop deliveries unless an overdue invoice is paid today. At 11 am, the accounting system crashes, and IT says it may take three hours to fix.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What will you do first, and why?
followUps: What can you do while the system is down?
Who would you tell about the problem, and what exactly would you say?
What if the system is still down at 3 pm?
If you can only complete two of the three tasks, which one will you let fail, and how will you manage the consequences?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You've just listed everything you would do. In reality, you'd panic. Tell me honestly what you would do in the first five minutes.

keyPoints: Quickly assesses deadlines, consequences and who can help, rather than starting work randomly
Communicates early with the CFO and supplier, setting realistic expectations
Uses the downtime productively, e.g. gathering bank statements, preparing a manual cash estimate, checking VAT data from other sources
Makes a clear, reasoned choice about which task to protect, recognising that legal deadlines carry penalties
Stays composed under the examiner's pressure and admits limits honestly
warningSigns: Tries to do everything alone without telling anyone
Ignores the legal VAT deadline because the CFO is more senior
Freezes or cannot commit to any priority

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are volunteering at a free university tax clinic for small business owners. Mrs Ratana, who sells handmade bags at Chatuchak Market and on Instagram, arrives holding a letter from the Revenue Department asking her to explain her income. She has never filed a business tax return. You need to help her understand what the letter means and what she should do next.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Please speak to Mrs Ratana.
followUps: How did you check that she understood what you explained?
What did you choose NOT to explain today, and why?
What if she asks you to tell her the exact amount she will have to pay?
What if she says she wants to stop selling online so the tax office cannot find her?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You used the words 'it's simple' several times. Do you think it felt simple to her?

actor.role: Mrs Ratana, 58, sells handmade bags at Chatuchak Market and through Instagram
actor.brief: You are frightened and embarrassed. You did not know you had to file tax because you thought small sellers were exempt. Your hidden concern: you have saved 150,000 baht for your son's university fees and fear the government will take it all.
lines: Excuse me, can you help me? I got this letter. Am I in trouble? Will they put me in jail?
I'm not a big company. I just make bags. I didn't know I had to do anything.
I saved money for my son's university. Will they take that?
actor.howToReact: If the candidate uses technical words or speaks too fast, look confused and say 'I don't understand, I only finished Prathom 6'. If they seem impatient, start to cry or say you will just ignore the letter. If they slow down, reassure you and explain step by step, become calmer and ask practical questions.

keyPoints: Acknowledges her fear first and reassures her that a letter is a request for information, not an arrest
Explains clearly in plain language, avoiding terms like 'assessable income' without explanation
Discovers her hidden concern (her savings and her son's university fees) and responds to it
Gives a simple, concrete next step, e.g. gather sales records and receipts, book an appointment, respond before the deadline
Is honest about the limits of what a student volunteer can advise and refers her to a qualified professional
warningSigns: Uses technical tax vocabulary that confuses her
Promises she will not have to pay anything
Encourages her to hide income or ignore the letter

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a customer-service officer at a bank branch. Mr Prasert, a retired teacher, wants to withdraw his entire savings of 1.2 million baht in cash. He tells you a friend from a Facebook group has introduced him to an investment that pays 5% every month. You strongly suspect a scam. You cannot legally refuse to give him his own money.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Please speak to Mr Prasert.
followUps: How did you try to persuade him without making him feel foolish?
Why is 5% per month a warning sign? How would you explain this in simple numbers?
What if he insists and becomes angry? What can and can't you do?
What if he admits that he has already transferred 200,000 baht and been told to send more to 'unlock' his profits?
interviewer.pressureProbe: It's his money and he's an adult. Isn't it disrespectful for a young person to question an older customer's decision?

actor.role: Mr Prasert, 68, a retired schoolteacher who lives alone
actor.brief: You are proud and do not like being told what to do by young people. You trust your new online friend, who calls you every day. Hidden motivation: you want to make money quickly to help pay for your grandchildren's education and to feel useful again.
lines: I'd like to withdraw all my savings, please. In cash. Today.
My friend has shown me screenshots. People in the group are making a lot of money. Why are you asking so many questions?
I taught for thirty-five years. I'm not stupid. I want to do something for my grandchildren.
actor.howToReact: If the candidate lectures you or calls it a scam too directly, become offended and say 'Just give me my money'. If they rush or use financial jargon, become impatient. If they show respect, ask about your grandchildren and explain gently with examples, begin to hesitate and agree to wait a day.

keyPoints: Respects his autonomy and age while clearly expressing concern
Explains the risk with simple numbers, e.g. 5% a month is about 80% a year, far above any safe investment
Asks questions that help him notice the warning signs himself (pressure, secrecy, online-only contact)
Discovers his hidden motivation (loneliness and wanting to help his grandchildren) and responds with empathy
Suggests practical steps: waiting 24 hours, checking with family or the SEC's list of licensed firms, reporting if money has already been sent
warningSigns: Lectures him or calls him naïve
Refuses to give him his money or threatens him
Gives up quickly and processes the withdrawal without any attempt to help

interviewee.doorPrompt: This is a pressure station. You are a junior auditor. The audit of a family-owned furniture company has found that its inventory records are unreliable; stock worth around 8 million baht could not be verified. Your firm has decided it cannot give a 'clean' audit opinion. You have been sent to explain this to the managing director, Khun Nat, who needs the report for a bank loan next week.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Please explain the situation to Khun Nat.
followUps: How did you explain a qualified audit opinion to someone who is not an accountant?
What if Khun Nat offers to 'make it worth your while' if the report is clean?
What could the company realistically do now to improve the situation?
What if he threatens to change audit firms next year?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Your firm has charged him 300,000 baht and now you're ruining his loan. Wasn't it your job to help him?

actor.role: Khun Nat, 52, managing director of a family furniture company founded by his father
actor.brief: You are stressed and angry. You believe your stock is fine and the auditors are being 'too strict'. You need the bank loan to pay for a new factory machine. Hidden concern: your father, the founder, does not yet know about the loan and you are afraid of looking like a failure.
lines: So, the report is ready? Good. The bank needs it by Monday.
Unreliable? My warehouse manager has worked here for twenty years. You young auditors just tick boxes.
Listen. Help me this time and I'll make sure your firm keeps our business for many years. We understand each other?
actor.howToReact: If the candidate uses jargon ('qualified opinion', 'scope limitation') without explaining, demand 'Speak normally!'. If they hesitate or seem to negotiate, push harder with your offer. If they stay calm, show respect and explain what can be done, become quieter and ask what you should do next.

keyPoints: States the outcome clearly and early, with a brief reason, without hiding behind jargon
Stays calm and respectful while being firm that the opinion will not change without evidence
Explains what the opinion means for the bank and what evidence could resolve the problem in future, such as a proper stock count
Refuses any inducement immediately and professionally
Shows understanding of his stress and the consequences for his staff and business
warningSigns: Suggests the opinion might change if he is upset enough
Becomes defensive or argues personally with him
Cannot explain what the problem actually is in simple language

interviewee.doorPrompt: A software company publishes a report titled 'AI will replace 80% of accounting jobs by 2030'. It includes the survey results below. Your school's careers adviser shares it with M6 students and suggests they avoid accounting degrees. You are asked to evaluate whether the data supports the report's headline.

data.caption: Use of AI tools in accounting firms (survey of firm managers)
columns: Firms planning to use AI by 2028
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Survey conducted by a company that sells AI accounting software. Questionnaire sent to 400 large firms; 50 replied. No small or medium-sized firms were included.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Does this data support the claim that AI will replace 80% of accounting jobs by 2030?
followUps: What is the difference between automating a TASK and replacing a JOB?
Who produced this report, and how might that influence its conclusions?
The survey asked firms about their plans. Why might plans differ from what actually happens?
What if a second survey of small Thai accounting firms showed very different results? How would you decide which to trust?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Most firms are already using AI for data entry. Isn't it obvious the jobs are disappearing? Stop making excuses for your chosen career.

keyPoints: Points out the data shows automation of specific tasks, not loss of jobs; time saved can be used for other work
Notes the conflict of interest: an AI software company benefits from people believing AI is powerful
Identifies sampling problems: only 50 large firms, low response rate, not representative of small Thai firms
Notices that the '80%' headline figure does not appear anywhere in the table
Draws a balanced conclusion: routine roles will change, but the claim is not supported by this evidence
warningSigns: Accepts the 80% headline because it appears in a report
Rejects the data purely because they want to study accounting
Does not notice that the headline number is not in the data

interviewee.doorPrompt: A government press release states: 'Online scam losses fall sharply – our new anti-scam measures are working!' It is based on the table below. A journalist asks you, as a finance student volunteer at a consumer-protection group, to comment on whether the conclusion is justified.

data.caption: Reported online scam cases and losses, Thailand
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. From 2025, cases are counted only if reported through the new online portal; phone and police-station reports are no longer included. New anti-scam measures began in March 2025.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Do these figures show that the anti-scam measures are working?
followUps: What is the difference between the number of cases and the total amount lost? Which tells us more?
Why might the number of REPORTED cases be different from the real number of scams?
What if the method of counting cases changed in 2025? How would that affect your conclusion?
What other explanations could there be for the change in 2025, apart from the new measures?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Cases went down. Losses went down. What more evidence do you need?

keyPoints: Notices that while cases and total losses fell, average loss per case rose, so each victim may be losing more
Recognises underreporting: embarrassed or elderly victims may not report
Identifies the change in counting method as a major problem for comparison
Considers alternative explanations, e.g. scammers moving to new platforms, bank freezes, seasonal or economic factors
Concludes cautiously, e.g. 'possibly encouraging, but this data alone cannot prove the measures caused the fall'
warningSigns: Agrees with the press release without checking the average loss column
Ignores the change in counting method
Confuses correlation with causation

interviewee.doorPrompt: This is a pressure station. An investment app runs an advert on YouTube: 'Our Thai Growth Fund returned 42% last year! A bank deposit gives you only 1.5%. Why are you still saving like your grandparents? Invest from 100 baht today.' The small print shows the fund's five-year record below. Your older cousin, who has just started work, wants to put all her savings into it.

data.caption: Thai Growth Fund: annual returns
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Returns are shown before the fund's annual management fee of 2%. Data supplied by the fund company itself.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you tell your cousin about this advert and the data?
followUps: What is the average yearly return over the five years, roughly, and how does it compare with the headline?
Why did the advert choose to show last year's return?
Is comparing this fund with a bank deposit a fair comparison? Why or why not?
What if your cousin is 23 and does not need the money for 20 years? Does that change your advice?
