Considers power and long-term risk in the tour-company offer
warningSigns: Decides what the village should do without consultation
Sees tourism as only good or only bad
Speaks only to the headman

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are leading a student project on how elderly people in your Bangkok district cope with living alone. You have three weeks, four team members, no budget and a 10-page report to write. One teammate wants to survey 500 people online. Another wants to do just three long interviews.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you design the project in the time available?
followUps: What are the strengths and weaknesses of each teammate's idea?
How would you reach elderly people who do not use the internet?
What if an elderly person you interview seems unwell or in danger?
What if your results are much smaller or less interesting than you hoped?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Three interviews prove nothing and an online survey misses the people you care about. So isn't this project pointless?

keyPoints: Compares quantitative and qualitative approaches fairly
Recognises that an online survey would miss many elderly people
Suggests a realistic mixed design, e.g. a short paper survey through community centres plus several interviews
Plans for ethical responsibilities if someone is at risk (contacting family, health volunteers or local services)
Accepts and reports limitations honestly
warningSigns: Chooses an online-only survey without seeing the problem
Ignores participant welfare
Exaggerates small findings

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a volunteer at a cultural festival celebrating ethnic minority communities in a northern province. Two hours before the main show, a performer group threatens to leave because organisers changed their costumes without asking. A sponsor wants a 'more exotic' show, it is raining, and journalists are arriving.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do first, and how would you prioritise?
followUps: Why does the costume change matter so much to the performers?
How would you handle the sponsor's request?
What if the organisers say the performers must follow the sponsor's wishes or not be paid?
How would you prevent this problem at future festivals?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Without the sponsor, there is no festival. Shouldn't the performers just compromise?

keyPoints: Prioritises listening to the performers and stopping the costume change
Recognises cultural meaning and the right of communities to represent themselves
Explains to the sponsor why 'exotic' framing is harmful and suggests alternative ways to make the show attractive
Escalates appropriately to festival organisers while managing practical issues like rain and journalists
Proposes future co-design with communities
warningSigns: Sides with the sponsor without considering the performers
Ignores the cultural meaning of costumes
Has no practical plan for the next two hours

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are an intern at an international NGO in Bangkok. A new foreign colleague, Sam, is upset because Thai colleagues keep saying 'yes' in meetings but then do not follow his plans. He thinks they are lazy or dishonest. Your manager asks you to talk to him.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Please begin speaking with Sam.
followUps: How did you explain the cultural differences without stereotyping Thai people?
What might be the real reasons behind the Thai colleagues' behaviour?
What if Sam says, 'So Thai people can't be honest?'
What could both Sam and the Thai team change?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Isn't Sam right that saying 'yes' when you mean 'no' is unprofessional?

actor.role: Sam, 34, a project manager from Australia who has just started working in Bangkok
actor.brief: You are frustrated and confused. You think you have been clear and friendly. Your hidden concern is that your project is behind schedule and your boss abroad is blaming you.
lines: I don't get it. I ask the team if the plan works, everyone says yes, and then nothing happens.
Why don't they just tell me if they disagree? Is it laziness, or are they just not honest?
My boss back home thinks I can't manage people.
actor.howToReact: If the candidate lectures you or defends the team without understanding you, become defensive. If they listen and explain gently with examples, become curious and ask what you can do.

keyPoints: Acknowledges Sam's frustration before explaining
Explains possible reasons such as kreng jai, hierarchy, saving face or unclear plans, without overgeneralising
Avoids defending or blaming either side
Suggests practical strategies: one-to-one check-ins, asking open questions, written follow-ups
Encourages mutual understanding rather than one side changing completely
warningSigns: Agrees that the Thai colleagues are lazy
Uses stereotypes such as 'all Thai people are shy'
Becomes defensive and dismisses Sam's experience

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a university student starting a research project in a village. Uncle Somchai, a respected elder, approaches you. He is suspicious because previous researchers came, took photos and information, and never returned. He wants to know why the village should help you.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Please begin speaking with Uncle Somchai.
followUps: How did you build trust with Uncle Somchai?
What did you promise, and can you keep those promises?
What if he asks you to pay the village for participating?
How will you share your findings with the community?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You're a student. Can you really promise anything that will benefit his village?

actor.role: Uncle Somchai, 67, a respected village elder in a northern province
actor.brief: You are polite but suspicious. You have seen researchers come and go without sharing anything. Your hidden concern is that last time a photo of the village appeared in a tourism brochure without permission, and villagers felt used.
lines: Another student from Bangkok. What do you want from us this time?
The last group took many photos and asked many questions. We never saw them again.
Then we saw our village in a tourist brochure. Nobody asked us.
actor.howToReact: If the candidate gives a long academic explanation or makes big promises, cross your arms and say you will tell the villagers not to talk. If they listen, admit past problems and make realistic promises, become more open.

keyPoints: Listens to his past experiences and acknowledges that his concerns are fair
Explains the research honestly in simple language, including its limits
Makes only realistic promises (returning results, translated summaries, respecting withdrawal)
Discusses compensation honestly and suggests checking with the supervisor
Shows humility and respect for community decision-making
warningSigns: Promises benefits that cannot be guaranteed
Gets defensive about previous researchers
Pressures the elder to participate

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a guide on a community-based tourism trip in a Mon village. A tourist, Mr Lee, has walked into a sacred area that villagers asked visitors not to enter, and is now arguing with a villager. You must speak to Mr Lee calmly.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Please begin speaking with Mr Lee.
followUps: How did you protect the community's rules without humiliating the tourist?
How did you explain the cultural meaning?
What if Mr Lee says, 'I paid for this tour, I can go where I want'?
What should the tour organisers change to prevent this?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Tourists bring money to the village. Wouldn't it be better to let him look and keep him happy?

actor.role: Mr Lee, 45, a tourist on a paid community-tourism trip
actor.brief: You are annoyed and embarrassed. You did not understand the rule and think the area just looked interesting. Your hidden concern is that you feel publicly accused in front of your family, and you lose face.
lines: What's the problem? I just wanted to take some pictures.
Nobody told me clearly. There was no sign.
My family is watching. Do you have to make such a big deal about it?
actor.howToReact: If the candidate lectures you publicly, become more defensive and say you will complain about the tour. If they speak privately, explain respectfully and offer an alternative, calm down and agree to leave the area.

keyPoints: Calmly separates Mr Lee from the confrontation
Explains the meaning and rule clearly without blaming or lecturing
Respects the community's authority over its own sacred places
Offers a respectful alternative activity
Suggests better briefing before trips
warningSigns: Allows him to stay in the sacred area
Shouts at or humiliates the tourist
Takes the tourist's side against the villagers

interviewee.doorPrompt: A newspaper headline says: 'Thai youth no longer care about family values.' It is based on the survey below, and the article has been widely shared by parents on LINE. You are asked to interpret the data carefully and decide whether the headline is a fair summary.

data.caption: Survey: Family values of Thai university students
rows: Family is very important to me
I want to live near my parents after graduating
I would follow my parents' choice of career
I will financially support my parents in future
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Online survey of 410 students at two Bangkok universities. Statements were written by the newspaper.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What does this data show, and is the headline justified?
followUps: What is the difference between 'care about family' and 'live near family'?
What are the limitations of how the survey was carried out?
What other explanations could there be for these answers?
What if a similar survey in a rural province showed very different results?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Only 38% want to live near their parents. Doesn't that prove the headline?

keyPoints: Notes that most young people still say family is very important
Distinguishes values from behaviour or practical choices (jobs, housing, studies)
Identifies sample limitations: online, Bangkok universities, small size, wording of questions
Considers economic and social explanations such as urban jobs and changing family structures
Concludes that the headline is exaggerated and misleading
warningSigns: Accepts the headline
Uses only one row of the table
Ignores the sampling limitations

interviewee.doorPrompt: A tourism company claims: 'Tourism brings wealth to local communities.' It presents the data below from an island in southern Thailand where tourism has grown rapidly over the last ten years. You are asked to evaluate whether the data really supports the company's claim.

data.caption: Tourism and local economy on one island
rows: Average rent for a local house (baht/month)
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Data provided by a tourism company. Household income figures based on a survey of 60 households.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you interpret this data?
followUps: Who benefits most from the increase in tourism income?
What information is missing?
Why might the company present only total income?
What if you learned that many local families had sold their land to outside investors?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Total income tripled. Isn't that clear evidence that tourism is good for the island?

keyPoints: Notices the gap between total income growth and the small share kept by local families
Identifies rising living costs that may cancel out income gains
Notes the conflict of interest in a tourism company presenting the data
Asks for missing information: employment, land ownership, environmental impact, quality of jobs
Draws a nuanced conclusion: tourism creates wealth, but distribution is unequal
warningSigns: Accepts the claim because total income increased
Ignores the distribution of income
Rejects tourism completely without nuance

interviewee.doorPrompt: A viral TikTok video says: 'Gen Z in Thailand are lazy. They change jobs every year and don't want to work hard like their parents.' The video uses a chart showing that young workers change jobs more often than older workers. A teacher asks you to analyse the claim.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you evaluate this claim?
followUps: What different explanations could there be for young people changing jobs more often?
Is it fair to compare young workers today with older workers at the same age in the past?
What kind of research would better test this claim?
What if a survey shows that young people are working longer hours than older generations did?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Everyone knows young people are less patient. Why don't you just accept it?

keyPoints: Separates the data (job changes) from the interpretation ('lazy')
Suggests alternative explanations: gig economy, short contracts, low wages, career exploration
Recognises the need to compare people at the same life stage
Suggests better research: longitudinal studies, interviews about reasons
Avoids defending or attacking any generation emotionally
warningSigns: Accepts the stereotype
Responds only with emotion as a member of Gen Z
Cannot suggest any alternative explanation

interviewee.doorPrompt: Social scientists often work in diverse teams and with people who have very different backgrounds and beliefs. Imagine you are working on a school project with classmates from different regions or backgrounds, and you have different views about the topic.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Tell me about a time you worked with someone whose views or background were very different from yours.
followUps: What did you learn from that person?
Did any of your assumptions change?
What if you strongly disagreed with that person's values?
How would you build trust in a team where people do not know each other?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Most students mix only with people like themselves. Is your example really that different?

keyPoints: Gives a real, specific example with honest detail
Shows reflexivity: recognises their own assumptions
Describes respectful ways of dealing with disagreement
Shows genuine learning or change in perspective
Suggests realistic ways to build trust
warningSigns: Gives a superficial example
Shows no change in perspective
Speaks negatively about people from different backgrounds

interviewee.doorPrompt: Anthropologists often make mistakes when they enter a new culture: they misunderstand customs, offend people unintentionally or make wrong assumptions. Learning from these mistakes is essential. The interviewer wants to know how you respond when you get something wrong.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Tell me about a time you misunderstood a person or situation. What happened and what did you learn?
followUps: How did you realise you had misunderstood?
How did you repair the situation?
What would you do differently now?
What if you unintentionally offended someone in a community during fieldwork?
interviewer.pressureProbe: That sounds like a small misunderstanding. Have you ever really been wrong about something important?

keyPoints: Provides a real example and admits the mistake honestly
Explains the cause of the misunderstanding thoughtfully
Describes a respectful repair such as an apology or a conversation
Explains a lasting change in behaviour or thinking
Applies the lesson to fieldwork with humility
warningSigns: Blames the other person entirely
Cannot think of any example
Shows no learning

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are in a four-person team researching street vendors in Bangkok. Two team members do all the interviews in hot markets, while one member only edits slides from home and says interviewing is 'not her strength'. The final presentation is next week and tension is rising.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you handle this team situation, and tell me about a real time when the work in your team was unequal.
followUps: How would you start the conversation with the member working from home?
Is it fair for team members to contribute in different ways?
What if she says she has social anxiety and cannot do interviews?
Tell me about a real time when work in your team was unequal.
interviewer.pressureProbe: Isn't she just avoiding the hard work? Why not report her to the teacher?

keyPoints: Talks to her privately and without accusations
Recognises that different contributions can be fair if they are agreed and balanced
Responds sensitively to a possible personal difficulty and finds alternative tasks such as data analysis or transcription
Addresses the tension with the whole team openly
Links to a real experience with reflection
warningSigns: Reports her to the teacher without talking to her
Dismisses her personal difficulty
Cannot give any real example

vocabulary.def: Thailand's central university admission system, with rounds for portfolio, quota, admission scores and direct entry
vocabulary.example: I applied in the portfolio round of TCAS because it lets me show my projects.

vocabulary.def: a large division of a university that teaches a group of related subjects
vocabulary.example: The Faculty of Arts offers majors in languages, history and philosophy.

vocabulary.def: your main subject at university, and a second subject you study in less depth
vocabulary.example: She majored in economics with a minor in data science.

vocabulary.def: combining ideas and methods from two or more subjects
vocabulary.example: Climate change needs interdisciplinary solutions that combine science, economics and policy.

vocabulary.def: abilities such as communication, teamwork and problem-solving that are useful in many different jobs
vocabulary.example: Running the school radio club taught me transferable skills like planning and public speaking.

vocabulary.def: activities outside normal lessons, such as clubs, sport, volunteering or competitions
vocabulary.example: My extracurricular activities helped me discover that I enjoy organising events.

vocabulary.def: a collection of evidence of your achievements and work, used in university applications
vocabulary.example: Her portfolio included a research project on PM2.5 and certificates from science camps.

vocabulary.def: being honest in your studies: not cheating, copying or presenting others' work as your own
vocabulary.example: Submitting an essay written by AI as your own breaks academic integrity.

vocabulary.def: a year taken between school and university to work, travel, volunteer or explore interests
vocabulary.example: Gap years are still unusual in Thailand, but some students use them to gain experience.

vocabulary.def: a short period of work experience, often for students, to learn about a job or industry
vocabulary.example: A summer internship at a start-up showed me what working in tech is really like.

vocabulary.def: avoid making a final choice too early so that several possibilities remain
vocabulary.example: I chose a broad degree because I want to keep my options open.

vocabulary.def: focus on activities that use the things you are good at
vocabulary.example: I want a degree that plays to my strengths in maths and communication.

vocabulary.term: step out of my comfort zone
vocabulary.def: try something new or difficult that makes you feel slightly uncomfortable
vocabulary.example: Joining the debate team made me step out of my comfort zone.

vocabulary.def: decide after collecting and considering relevant information
vocabulary.example: I visited three open days so that I could make an informed decision.

vocabulary.def: a balanced view that considers many different angles
vocabulary.example: Talking to students from different faculties gave me a well-rounded perspective.

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are applying to university but have not yet fully decided which field you want to study. This is common: many students change their plans during their first year. The interviewer is not looking for a perfect answer, but wants to understand how you are making this decision, what interests you, and what you know about your own strengths.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How are you deciding what to study at university?
followUps: Which school subjects or activities have you enjoyed most, and what exactly did you enjoy about them?
What have you done to find out more about different degrees, such as open days, online courses or talking to students?
Who or what has influenced your thinking most so far: family, friends, teachers or social media? Is that influence helpful?
If you had to choose a faculty tomorrow, which would it be, and what would make you change your mind?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Isn't 'I'm still deciding' just a polite way of saying you haven't thought about it?

keyPoints: Describes an active, thoughtful decision process (researching programmes, open days, talking to students, trying courses or camps)
Connects specific interests and experiences to possible fields, with concrete examples
Reflects honestly on external influences such as family expectations, friends or job security
Is comfortable with some uncertainty while showing a sensible plan to narrow choices
Gives a reasoned answer when forced to choose, including what would change their mind
warningSigns: Says they will choose whatever their parents or friends choose
Has done nothing to explore options
Chooses based only on which faculty is 'famous' or easiest to get into

interviewee.doorPrompt: Universities want students who understand themselves. Some students are strong in numbers, others in languages, creativity, leadership, or working with people. Strengths are most convincing when they are supported by evidence from real experiences. The interviewer will ask you about your strengths and how they might guide your choice of degree and career.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What are your two greatest strengths, and how do you know?
followUps: Give me a specific example where one of these strengths made a real difference.
What is a weakness you are working on, and what are you doing about it?
Which university subjects or careers would play to these strengths?
How might your strengths be different from what your parents or teachers think they are?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Every candidate says 'teamwork and communication'. What makes your strengths different?

keyPoints: Names specific, genuine strengths rather than generic labels
Supports each strength with a concrete example and an outcome
Identifies a real weakness and describes active steps to improve it
Links strengths logically to possible fields of study
Shows self-awareness, including how others may see them differently
warningSigns: Lists strengths with no evidence
Gives a fake weakness such as 'I'm too hard-working'
Cannot connect strengths to any academic or career direction

interviewee.doorPrompt: This is a pressure station. The examiner will challenge you directly about being undecided and about your readiness for university life. Stay calm and polite, think before you answer, and use honest examples. The examiner wants to see how you respond to uncertainty and criticism, not whether you agree with them.

interviewer.openingQuestion: If you don't know what you want to study, why should a university give you a place instead of someone who does?
followUps: Wouldn't it be better to take a gap year and decide first? Why or why not?
Many students drop out or change faculty in first year. How will you avoid wasting your place?
With AI changing the job market, how can anyone choose a 'safe' degree?
What will you contribute to our university community, not just take from it?
interviewer.pressureProbe: I'm not convinced. It sounds like you're hoping university will decide for you.

keyPoints: Stays composed and responds to the challenge directly
Argues convincingly that curiosity, adaptability and broad skills are valuable, giving evidence
Weighs a gap year sensibly, noting its benefits and risks in the Thai context
Shows realistic thinking about AI and the job market: transferable skills, lifelong learning
Describes a concrete contribution (clubs, volunteering, peer support, specific skills)
warningSigns: Becomes defensive or upset
Agrees that they are not ready and gives up
Claims they could succeed in any subject without effort

interviewee.doorPrompt: Your close friend Mint is preparing her TCAS portfolio. She volunteered at a children's library for only one day, but the organiser, a family friend, has offered to sign a certificate saying she volunteered for 60 hours. Mint asks you, 'Everyone does this, right? It's not really lying, I did go there.' She also asks you to confirm the hours if anyone asks.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you say and do?
followUps: Who could be affected if Mint used this certificate?
What would you do if a teacher asked you directly whether Mint really volunteered for 60 hours?
What if Mint said your friendship would be over if you didn't support her?
Is this a problem with Mint, or with the admission system? Explain.
interviewer.pressureProbe: If 'everyone does it', then refusing just puts honest students at a disadvantage. Isn't that unfair?

keyPoints: Recognises the certificate is dishonest and could harm other applicants and Mint herself (if discovered)
Talks to Mint privately and kindly, understanding the pressure she feels
Offers constructive alternatives: describe the real experience honestly, volunteer more now, highlight other strengths
Refuses to lie for Mint while trying to keep the friendship
Discusses wider pressures in the admission system and portfolio culture thoughtfully
warningSigns: Agrees to support the false certificate
Reports Mint immediately without speaking to her first
Says honesty doesn't matter because 'everyone does it'

interviewee.doorPrompt: You have a part-time job at a new café near your school. Business is slow. The owner, Khun Nok, asks you and other staff to post five-star reviews on Google Maps and Wongnai using different accounts, and to report negative reviews from a competitor as 'spam'. She says, 'Small businesses must fight to survive. The big chains do worse things.' You need this job to pay for tutoring.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do?
followUps: Who is harmed by fake reviews? Think about customers, other businesses and online platforms.
How could you help the café attract customers honestly?
What if the owner said you would lose your job if you refused?
Is there any difference between writing a fake review and asking real happy customers to write one?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You need the money and it's only a few reviews. Isn't refusing a luxury you can't afford?

keyPoints: Identifies that fake reviews deceive customers and are unfair to competitors, and may break platform rules or consumer law
Shows understanding of the owner's real pressures as a small business (SME)
Suggests honest alternatives: asking real customers for reviews, social media content, promotions, partnerships with nearby schools
Considers their own position realistically and explains how they would refuse respectfully
Distinguishes clearly between encouraging genuine reviews and creating fake ones
warningSigns: Agrees because 'everyone does it online'
Ignores the owner's difficulties and responds with a lecture
Does not see any harm to customers

interviewee.doorPrompt: It is 10 p.m. the night before a major final exam. Someone posts what appear to be the real exam answers in your class LINE group of 40 students. Many have already seen them. Your best friend messages you: 'Don't tell anyone. If the teacher finds out, the whole class will have to retake the exam and everyone will hate whoever reported it.' You have not opened the file.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do, and why?
followUps: Does it matter that you haven't opened the file yourself?
Who are all the people affected by your decision?
What if you discovered that your best friend was the one who posted the answers?
If you reported it, how would you protect yourself from your classmates' anger?
interviewer.pressureProbe: If you report it, 39 people suffer and you lose your friends. If you don't, nobody really gets hurt. Isn't silence the logical choice?

keyPoints: Does not use the answers and recognises that a leaked exam is unfair to everyone, including future grades and university admissions
Considers all stakeholders: classmates, other classes, teachers, students who studied honestly
Thinks about practical ways to inform the teacher, such as speaking privately or anonymously before the exam
Handles the friend twist thoughtfully, balancing loyalty with fairness
Shows courage and reasoning under pressure, without self-righteousness
warningSigns: Opens and uses the answers
Stays silent mainly to protect their popularity
Announces the problem publicly to shame classmates

interviewee.doorPrompt: You have just moved from Khon Kaen to start university in Bangkok. This week: your dorm rent (6,000 baht) is due Friday but your allowance arrives Monday; a group report is due Thursday and one member is missing; your part-time café shift is Wednesday night; freshman welcome activities run every evening; and your roommate has a fever and asks you to buy medicine.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you prioritise this week, and what would you do first?
followUps: Which of these tasks could you negotiate, delay or ask others to help with?
How would you handle the rent problem without causing trouble?
What if the freshman activity leaders said attendance was 'compulsory' and seniors would be upset if you missed it?
What support services do universities usually offer new students, and when would you use them?
interviewer.pressureProbe: University is about freedom and new friends. Aren't you being too serious about all this?

keyPoints: Deals first with the roommate's health and checks whether the fever needs medical attention
Communicates early and honestly about the rent, e.g. contacting the dorm manager or parents
Plans the group report: contacts the missing member, divides tasks, informs the lecturer if needed
Balances social activities with responsibilities and feels able to say no politely to unreasonable demands
Mentions university support such as student affairs, health centre or advisers
warningSigns: Ignores the roommate's illness
Misses the shift or deadline without telling anyone
Feels they must attend every activity because seniors expect it

interviewee.doorPrompt: It is PM2.5 season in Chiang Mai and air quality has been unhealthy for two weeks. Your school club has raised 8,000 baht and has eight volunteers available on Saturday to help the local community. Ideas include: giving N95 masks to street vendors and motorbike taxi riders, making DIY air purifiers for a nearby kindergarten, or creating a TikTok campaign about how to read the air-quality index.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you decide what to do with the money and the volunteers?
followUps: Who is most at risk from PM2.5, and why?
What information would you need before deciding?
What if the club members disagreed strongly and wanted to split the money three ways?
How would you measure whether your project made any difference?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Masks and fans won't solve air pollution. Isn't this just a feel-good project?

keyPoints: Identifies vulnerable groups: young children, the elderly, outdoor workers, people with lung conditions
Compares options using clear criteria: number of people helped, level of risk, cost, lasting impact
Gathers information first (needs of vendors and the kindergarten, mask costs, how DIY purifiers work)
Manages disagreement in the club fairly, perhaps combining a direct-help option with low-cost awareness
Admits the project's limits and links it to wider causes (burning, traffic) and long-term solutions
warningSigns: Chooses based only on what would look best on social media
Has no criteria for deciding
Ignores the views of the people they want to help

interviewee.doorPrompt: Your parents own a small khao soi shop in Chiang Mai. This year, tourists are fewer because of PM2.5 and economic problems, the delivery app takes about 30% commission, and the landlord wants to raise the rent. Your parents have 20,000 baht for changes and ask you to help them decide what to do this weekend. Your exams start on Monday.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you advise your parents, and how would you decide?
followUps: What information would you collect first, and how?
Should the shop stay on the delivery app? What are the trade-offs?
What if your parents disagreed with each other about your plan?
How would you balance helping your family with preparing for your exams?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You're 18 and have never run a business. Why should your parents listen to you at all?

keyPoints: Starts by understanding the numbers: income, costs, which dishes and channels make a profit
Weighs specific options (adjusting prices on the app, direct LINE orders, targeting local office workers, negotiating rent, social media) with trade-offs
Recognises uncertainty and suggests small, low-cost trials before big changes
Respects parents' experience and decision-making authority while offering their skills (digital, data)
Plans time realistically around exams, e.g. a short session this weekend and follow-up after exams
warningSigns: Suggests spending all the money on one idea without testing it
Ignores their exam commitments completely or refuses to help at all
Dismisses parents' knowledge of their own business

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are visiting your grandmother, Aunt Somsri, 72. She is on the phone, very frightened. A man claiming to be a police officer has told her that her bank account is linked to money laundering and that she must transfer her savings to a 'safe account' today or be arrested. She is about to open her banking app. She trusts authority figures and is embarrassed easily.

interviewer.openingQuestion: The interviewer will play Aunt Somsri. Please begin when you are ready.
followUps: How did you stop the transfer without making her feel foolish?
What did you say to explain that it was a scam?
What practical steps would you take after the call?
Why do you think scam call centres are so successful in Thailand, especially with older people?
interviewer.pressureProbe: What if it really was the police? Aren't you taking a big risk by telling her to ignore them?

actor.role: Aunt Somsri, 72, a retired market trader living in Nonthaburi
actor.brief: You are terrified of being arrested and shamed in front of neighbours. The caller knew your name and ID number, so you believe him. Your hidden fear is that you have done something wrong without knowing it, and you are embarrassed to admit you don't understand banking apps.
lines: Shh! I'm talking to the police. They say my account is being used by criminals!
He knew my ID number. How could he know that if he's not real police?
If I don't transfer the money now, they'll come and arrest me. What will the neighbours think?
actor.howToReact: If the candidate panics, grabs the phone, or tells you that you are being silly, become defensive and insist on continuing the transfer. If they calmly ask you to hang up first, reassure you that you have done nothing wrong and explain how scammers get ID numbers, slowly agree to stop and call the bank.

keyPoints: Acts quickly but calmly to pause the transfer, e.g. asking her to hang up before doing anything
Explains clearly and kindly that real police never ask people to transfer money over the phone
Protects her dignity: reassures her that scammers trick many smart people
Suggests concrete steps: calling the bank, checking with the real police on 1441 or 191, reporting the number, enabling app security
Listens to her fear and stays with her until she feels safe
warningSigns: Grabs the phone or shouts at her
Says 'How could you believe that?', making her feel stupid
Gives no practical next steps

interviewee.doorPrompt: Your father, Mr Somchai, has always expected you to study accounting so that you can one day take over the family's successful hardware business in Rayong. After exploring different subjects this year, you are now interested in environmental science. You have decided to tell him tonight and hope to get his support.

interviewer.openingQuestion: The interviewer will play your father, Mr Somchai. Please begin the conversation.
followUps: How did you show respect for your father's hopes while explaining your own?
What compromise options, if any, did you suggest?
What if he said he would only pay for your studies if you chose accounting?
Is it ever right for children to follow their parents' career wishes rather than their own? When?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Your father built that business for you. Isn't it selfish to walk away from it?

actor.role: Mr Somchai, 52, owner of a hardware business in Rayong
actor.brief: You built the business over 25 years and always imagined your child taking over. You know little about environmental science and fear it has poor job prospects. Your hidden concern is that the business will close when you retire and that your life's work will disappear.
lines: Environmental science? What job will you get with that? Planting trees?
I worked every day for twenty-five years so you would have a future. This business is your future.
Who will look after the shop when I'm old?
actor.howToReact: If the candidate is dismissive of the business or argues that it is 'their life', raise your voice and refuse to discuss it further. If they show respect for your work, explain their interest with real evidence and suggest ways the business could still continue, become calmer and start asking real questions about the degree.

keyPoints: Opens respectfully, acknowledges his hard work and the meaning of the family business
Explains their interest with specific evidence (experiences, courses, research), not just feelings
Addresses his likely worries: job prospects, income, the future of the business
Explores creative compromises: a minor in business, environmental sustainability in the business, family succession plans
Listens genuinely and stays calm if he becomes upset, aiming for continued dialogue rather than winning
warningSigns: Becomes angry or dismissive of the family business
Gives in immediately without explaining their view
Has no evidence or reasons for the new interest

interviewee.doorPrompt: Your friend Fah is in her first year at university with you. She tells you she is going to drop out next week to sell skincare full-time on TikTok Shop, because she earned 40,000 baht last month. Her parents do not know and are paying her fees. She wants you to support her decision and help her tell her parents.

interviewer.openingQuestion: The interviewer will play Fah. Please begin when you are ready.
followUps: How did you respond without simply telling her she was wrong?
What questions did you ask to help her think about the risks?
What if she said, 'You're just jealous because I'm already making money'?
Is a university degree still necessary in the digital economy? What do you think?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Many successful entrepreneurs dropped out of university. Shouldn't you encourage her?

actor.role: Fah, 18, a first-year business student who sells skincare on TikTok Shop
actor.brief: You are excited and proud of your success and tired of boring lectures. You feel nobody takes your business seriously. Your hidden worry is that your sales dropped in the last two weeks and you are afraid the success won't last, but you don't want to admit it.
lines: I've decided! I'm quitting uni next week. I made forty thousand baht last month. That's more than my lecturer earns!
Why waste four years studying theory when I'm already doing it for real?
Will you come with me when I tell my parents? They'll freak out.
actor.howToReact: If the candidate criticises you, says online selling isn't real work, or lectures you, become defensive and say they are just jealous. If they show interest in your business and ask good questions, gradually admit that sales have dropped recently and that you are a bit scared.

keyPoints: Listens and shows genuine interest in her success before raising concerns
Asks open questions that help her think: is income stable, what are the costs, are there risks with the products, can she continue both
Explores middle options: taking a leave of absence, studying part-time, a business-related degree, testing for one more term
Encourages honesty with her parents and offers support, without taking over
Respects that it is ultimately her decision
warningSigns: Tells her she is foolish or that online selling is not a real job
Agrees to help hide the decision from her parents
Gives a long lecture instead of a conversation

interviewee.doorPrompt: A popular education page on Facebook posts the table below with the caption: 'Want to be rich? Study Engineering. Arts graduates earn the least!' Your younger cousin has seen it and says she will now choose engineering, even though she loves languages. You have one minute to study the table.

data.caption: Average first-job monthly salary by faculty, one Bangkok university, 2025 graduates
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Online survey six months after graduation; graduates who were still job-hunting or studying further were less likely to reply. Data from one university only; salaries are averages and do not show the range.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What can and can't we conclude from this data?
followUps: Why might the response rates matter?
What does a starting salary tell us, and what doesn't it tell us?
What other factors should your cousin consider when choosing a degree?
What extra data would you want before giving her advice?
interviewer.pressureProbe: The numbers are clear: engineering pays more. Isn't it irresponsible to tell her to follow her passion?

keyPoints: Notices very different response rates (Arts 15%, Science 26% vs Engineering 52%) and the resulting bias
Explains that averages hide the range, and that starting salary is not the same as lifetime earnings or satisfaction
Notes that data comes from one university and may not generalise
Gives balanced advice: consider interests, strengths, job demand, combining languages with other skills
Avoids both extremes: neither 'only money matters' nor 'money doesn't matter'
warningSigns: Accepts the post's conclusion without questioning the data
Ignores the response rates
Tells the cousin to ignore income completely

interviewee.doorPrompt: A technology company publishes the table below in a press release titled: 'Students who use our AI study assistant get higher grades.' Your school is deciding whether to pay for licences for all M4–M6 students. You have been asked to give a student opinion.

data.caption: GPA of students who did and did not use the AI study assistant
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Data from three private international schools in Bangkok. Students chose whether to use the AI. Study carried out by the company that sells the assistant.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Does this data show that the AI assistant improves grades?
followUps: What kind of students might choose to use an AI study assistant?
What other explanations could there be for the difference in GPA?
How would you design a fairer test of whether the AI helps?
Apart from grades, what other effects of AI study tools should the school consider?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Every year the gap is bigger. Surely that shows it works?

keyPoints: Identifies self-selection: motivated, higher-achieving or wealthier students may choose to use AI
Notes that AI users also study more hours, a confounding factor
Points out the funding conflict and that private international schools may not represent other schools
Suggests a fairer design, such as randomly assigning students or comparing the same students before and after
Raises other considerations: academic integrity, over-reliance, data privacy, equal access
warningSigns: Accepts the company's claim at face value
Ignores the study-hours column
Dismisses AI tools entirely without considering any benefits

interviewee.doorPrompt: A famous tutoring school in Siam Square advertises on a giant BTS billboard: '98% of our students got into their first-choice university! Join our 120,000-baht TCAS Super Course.' Your parents are considering paying for the course for your younger brother. The advert gives no further details.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you evaluate this advertisement before your parents spend the money?
followUps: What questions would you ask the tutoring school about the 98% figure?
How could a tutoring school make its results look better than they really are?
Even if the figure were true, would it prove the course caused the success?
What does Thailand's tutoring culture say about the education system and fairness?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Lots of successful students went to this school. Isn't it safer to pay than to risk it?

keyPoints: Asks what '98%' is based on: how many students, who was counted, who chose to report results
Notes possible tricks: counting only top students, accepting only high-ability students, students choosing 'safe' first choices
Explains that students who can afford expensive tutoring may succeed for other reasons (ability, motivation, family support)
Suggests alternatives: free online resources, school support, asking past students, trial classes
Discusses fairness and inequality in access to tutoring in a balanced way
warningSigns: Accepts the 98% figure as proof
Cannot identify any possible bias
Dismisses all tutoring as useless without reasoning

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are one of the leaders of your colour team for school Sports Day. Two weeks before the event, the cheerleading group and the parade group are arguing over the shared budget and practice space. Some members have stopped coming, and people are complaining about each other in the team LINE group. The teacher adviser says, 'Sort it out yourselves.'

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you handle this situation, and tell me about a real time you helped two groups who disagreed.
followUps: How would you decide how to divide the budget and the practice time fairly?
What would you do about the negative messages in the LINE group?
Tell me about a real time you were part of a team with conflict. What did you do?
What did you learn about yourself from that experience?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Sports Day is supposed to be fun. Isn't all this planning taking it too seriously?

keyPoints: Brings both groups together face-to-face rather than arguing online
Uses fair, transparent methods for budget and time, such as a shared timetable and agreed criteria
Addresses negativity in the group chat calmly and sets basic expectations
Gives a real STAR example with specific personal actions
Reflects honestly on their own role and what they would do differently
warningSigns: Takes one side because of friendships
Lets the conflict continue and hopes it resolves itself
Cannot provide a real personal example

interviewee.doorPrompt: Imagine you prepared for three months to be selected for a national English debate competition. You were confident, but the teacher chose another student instead, saying your arguments were 'strong but not well organised'. Everyone in your class knows you were not chosen. The examiner will then ask about a real experience of disappointment.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you react to this disappointment, and tell me about a real time you were not chosen for something you wanted.
followUps: What would you do with the teacher's feedback?
How would you treat the student who was chosen?
Tell me about a real time you failed or were disappointed. How did you respond?
How has that experience changed the way you approach challenges now?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Maybe the teacher just preferred the other student. Why should you accept the feedback?

keyPoints: Acknowledges disappointment honestly and shows healthy coping
Asks the teacher for specific feedback and makes a concrete plan to improve
Congratulates and supports the selected student
Gives a genuine STAR example of failure with clear learning
Shows resilience and growth over time
warningSigns: Blames the teacher or the other student
Says they have never failed at anything
Gives up the activity completely without reflection

interviewee.doorPrompt: This station has a demanding examiner. Imagine you are class president. You proposed using the class fund for a trip to help at a rural school, but the class voted for a party at a Bangkok restaurant instead. Some classmates now say you are 'too serious' to be president. The examiner will ask how you would respond and about your real experience of leadership.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do after the vote? Then tell me about a real time a group decided against your idea.
followUps: Should a leader always follow the majority? Why or why not?
Could you combine both ideas in some way?
Tell me about a real time you led others. What was your biggest leadership mistake?
How would your friends describe your leadership style, honestly?
interviewer.pressureProbe: It sounds like you wanted to impose your values on everyone. Isn't that bad leadership?

keyPoints: Accepts the democratic decision gracefully and organises the party well
Reflects on how the proposal was presented and whether classmates' views were heard
Suggests creative compromise or alternative ways to pursue the volunteering idea, e.g. a voluntary group trip
Gives a real leadership example including a genuine mistake and what they learned
Stays calm and self-aware when challenged about their style
warningSigns: Refuses to accept the vote or tries to overturn it
Criticises classmates as shallow
Cannot identify any weakness in their leadership

vocabulary.def: a broad university education across languages, history, philosophy, literature and social sciences, focused on thinking skills rather than one job
vocabulary.example: A liberal arts programme lets you take courses in both philosophy and economics.

vocabulary.def: an original document or object from the time being studied, such as a letter, diary, photo or official record
vocabulary.example: A king's letter from 1890 is a primary source; a textbook about it is not.

vocabulary.def: careful, detailed analysis of a short text, paying attention to word choice, structure and meaning
vocabulary.example: Close reading of the poem showed how the writer used silence to express grief.

vocabulary.def: combining ideas and methods from two or more academic subjects
vocabulary.example: Her interdisciplinary project used history and linguistics to study old shop signs in Yaowarat.

vocabulary.def: adapting a text, product or game so that it feels natural to people in another language and culture
vocabulary.example: Good localisation changed the jokes in the game so Thai players would actually laugh.

vocabulary.def: buildings, objects, traditions and knowledge passed down through generations that a community values
vocabulary.example: Old shophouses in Bangkok are part of the city's cultural heritage.

vocabulary.def: returning objects, especially museum artefacts, to the country or community they originally came from
vocabulary.example: The repatriation of the stone lintel was celebrated in Buriram.

vocabulary.def: the art of using language to persuade, or language designed to persuade rather than inform
vocabulary.example: The speech was full of emotional rhetoric but contained few facts.

vocabulary.def: the way a topic is talked or written about in a society, which shapes how people think about it
vocabulary.example: Media discourse about Gen Z often describes young people as lazy.

vocabulary.def: evaluating who created a source, when, why and for whom, to judge how reliable it is
vocabulary.example: Source criticism helped the students see that the diary was written to impress a future reader.

vocabulary.def: abilities such as writing, analysis and communication that are useful in many different jobs
vocabulary.example: A history degree builds transferable skills like researching and arguing clearly.

vocabulary.def: explain the background or situation that helps people understand something correctly
vocabulary.example: We need to put this old law into context before judging the people who wrote it.

vocabulary.def: an opinion that recognises small but important differences and avoids simple yes/no answers
vocabulary.example: She gave a nuanced view of AI translation, praising its speed but noting its cultural blind spots.

vocabulary.def: seriously consider different viewpoints, including ones you disagree with
vocabulary.example: Studying philosophy trains you to engage with multiple perspectives before deciding.

vocabulary.def: describes meaning, tone or humour that disappears when language is translated
vocabulary.example: The pun in the Thai title was completely lost in translation.

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are applying to a humanities programme, such as languages, history, philosophy or literature, at a leading Thai university. Your exam results are strong enough for medicine or engineering, and some relatives have asked why you are 'wasting' your grades. The interviewer wants to understand your motivation and how you made this decision.

interviewer.openingQuestion: With grades like yours, why have you chosen humanities instead of medicine or engineering?
followUps: Tell me about a specific book, class or experience that convinced you this is the right subject.
How did you discuss this decision with your family, and how did they react?
What do you think you will find hardest or least enjoyable in this programme?
What if, after your first year, you realise you miss science? What would you do?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Isn't it a bit of a waste for Thailand when a strong student chooses a subject with fewer clear jobs?

keyPoints: Presents humanities as a positive choice driven by genuine interest, not as an escape from science or maths
Gives a concrete source of motivation, e.g. a novel read in English, a history project, a debate competition, translating for a relative
Shows respect for the family's concerns while explaining their own reasoning calmly
Is realistic about challenges: heavy reading, long essays, competitive job market, less clear career ladder
Argues that society needs strong thinkers, communicators and cultural experts, not only doctors and engineers
warningSigns: Says they chose humanities because it is 'easier' or because they dislike maths
Speaks disrespectfully about their family or about science careers
Cannot name any specific course, text or experience connected to the subject

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are applying to an international or liberal arts programme, for example at Chula, Thammasat or Mahidol. People often ask humanities students, 'What job will you get with that?' The interviewer wants to know whether you understand this programme and have a realistic picture of possible careers in Thailand and abroad.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What do you know about our programme, and what kind of career do you imagine after it?
followUps: Why this programme specifically, rather than a similar one at another university?
Which skills from a humanities degree do employers in Thailand actually need?
What have you done so far to find out what humanities graduates really do?
What if your first job after graduating is not related to your degree at all? Would that mean the degree failed?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Graduates in many fields can write and think. What can you do that a business graduate cannot?

keyPoints: Refers to specific features of the programme, e.g. language requirements, majors or concentrations, exchange options, small seminar classes
Names realistic career paths: translation and localisation, diplomacy and international organisations, publishing, media, education, tourism and heritage, UX writing, policy research, HR
Explains transferable skills with an example: researching, writing clearly, analysing arguments, cross-cultural communication
Has explored careers actively, e.g. talked to a graduate, attended an open house, read alumni stories
Accepts that career paths may be non-linear and shows a plan to build practical skills alongside the degree
warningSigns: Only says 'I want to be a translator' with no understanding of the work or how AI is changing it
Knows nothing about the programme beyond its name or ranking
Claims a humanities degree guarantees a high salary or an easy job

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are applying to study languages, linguistics or translation. AI translation tools and chatbots can now translate, summarise and write in many languages within seconds. The interviewer is sceptical and will push you hard on whether your chosen field still has a future, and whether you have really thought about it.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Machine translation is free and instant. Why should anyone spend four years and a lot of money studying languages?
followUps: Give me one specific example where an AI translation would fail or cause harm.
How do you personally use AI tools, and how do you check their output?
What will a language graduate's job look like in ten years?
What if our faculty decided to replace half of its language courses with AI-assisted courses? Would you still apply?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Honestly, you sound like you are defending a dying profession because you like languages. Convince me you have thought about this seriously.

keyPoints: Takes AI seriously and admits it will replace some routine translation work, rather than dismissing it
Gives a concrete example of meaning lost in translation: humour, politeness levels, legal or medical risk, cultural references, Thai pronoun and particle choices
Describes new roles: post-editing, localisation, quality control, cross-cultural consulting, training and evaluating AI
Argues that studying a language also means studying culture, history and how people think, which goes beyond word-for-word transfer
Stays calm and reasoned under pressure, acknowledging the interviewer's point before answering
warningSigns: Insists AI will never be useful for translation
Becomes defensive, flustered or simply repeats 'I love languages'
Has no idea how professional translators currently work

interviewee.doorPrompt: You work part-time for a small translation agency in Bangkok. A client pays you to translate a Thai health-product brochure into English for export. While translating, you notice it claims the herbal drink 'cures diabetes and replaces medication'. Your job is only to translate, and the client wants it finished tomorrow.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do, and why?
followUps: Is a translator responsible for the content of a text, or only for the accuracy of the translation?
Who could be harmed if you translate the brochure exactly as written?
What if the client says, 'Just translate it. That's what I'm paying you for'?
What if your agency manager tells you to finish it quietly because this client brings in a lot of business?
interviewer.pressureProbe: If you refuse, someone else will translate it anyway. So what difference does your choice make?

keyPoints: Recognises the conflict between professional duty (faithful translation, client service) and preventing harm to readers
Identifies stakeholders: diabetic consumers abroad, the client, the agency, the translator's own reputation
Chooses a measured first step: raising the concern with the agency manager and the client, not secretly changing the text
Mentions that such health claims may break advertising or consumer laws in Thailand and the export country
Is willing to decline the work if the claim stays, while explaining this professionally
warningSigns: Secretly softens or rewrites the claim without telling anyone
Says 'It's not my problem; I'm just the translator'
Immediately posts about the client on social media

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a first-year literature student. Your close friend Mint asks you to read her essay before she submits it. It is far more polished than her usual writing, and she admits she generated most of it with an AI chatbot and 'just changed some words'. The course clearly bans undeclared AI writing. The essay counts for 30% of the grade.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you say to Mint, and what would you do next?
followUps: Is using AI to write an essay the same as copying from a classmate? Why or why not?
Should you report Mint to the lecturer if she refuses to change it?
What if Mint explains she has been caring for a sick parent and had no time to write?
What if you later discover that half the class did the same thing?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Everyone will use AI at work anyway. Aren't these university rules already out of date?

keyPoints: Talks to Mint privately first, honestly and without judgement, before considering any report
Explains why the rule matters in literature: the essay is meant to show her own reading, thinking and voice
Suggests practical alternatives: asking the lecturer for an extension, declaring AI use, rewriting with her own ideas
Responds to the personal hardship with compassion while still not helping her break the rule
Separates the question 'are the rules perfect?' from 'should we follow the current rules?'
warningSigns: Helps Mint edit the essay so the AI use is harder to detect
Reports Mint immediately without speaking to her
Says it doesn't matter because 'everyone does it'

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a junior curator at a private museum in Bangkok. A 900-year-old carved stone statue in the collection was bought from a dealer in the 1970s. A community from a neighbouring country has asked for it to be returned, saying it was taken from their temple without permission. The museum's founder says the purchase was legal, and the statue is the museum's most popular object.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Should the museum return the statue? Explain your reasoning.
followUps: What evidence would you want to see before making a decision?
Does it matter that the purchase was legal at the time?
What if returning it meant the museum loses its biggest sponsor and has to cut staff, including you?
Thailand has asked foreign museums to return Thai artefacts. Does that change how Thailand should act here?
interviewer.pressureProbe: If every museum returned every object with a complicated history, museums would be empty. Isn't that a ridiculous standard?

keyPoints: Distinguishes legal ownership from ethical ownership and explains why both matter
Proposes investigating provenance: dealer records, export documents, photos of the original temple, expert advice
Considers the community's spiritual and cultural connection, not only the object's artistic or financial value
Suggests middle options: joint research, a long-term loan, a replica, or a shared exhibition, while being honest about their limits
Recognises consistency: if Thailand values repatriation of its own artefacts, the same principle should apply
warningSigns: Says 'finders keepers' or that a legal purchase ends the discussion
Ignores the community's view entirely and focuses only on visitor numbers
Suggests hiding the statue or quietly ignoring the request

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a junior officer in a city heritage team. Construction of a new rail station has uncovered brick remains that may be part of a 200-year-old city wall. Work has stopped, the contractor says each day of delay costs millions of baht, local residents want the station opened, and a history group is already posting about it online. You have two weeks to give a recommendation.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What would you do first, and how would you plan the next two weeks?
followUps: Who would you consult, and in what order?
How would you decide whether the remains are important enough to change the station design?
What if the experts disagree about how old or valuable the wall is?
What if a newspaper reports that the heritage team is 'blocking progress'? How would you respond?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Thousands of commuters need this train. Why should a few old bricks matter more than their daily lives?

keyPoints: Prioritises protecting and recording the site immediately: photos, measurements, a fence, an archaeologist on site
Brings in experts quickly to assess age and significance using records, old maps and the bricks themselves
Identifies all stakeholders: commuters, contractor, residents, history groups, the city authority
Considers compromise options: redesigning one entrance, preserving part of the wall in the station, a display or glass floor
Plans clear, regular public communication to reduce rumours and conflict
warningSigns: Lets construction continue immediately without any assessment
Insists the whole project must stop permanently without considering costs to commuters
Ignores public communication until the end of the two weeks

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a student volunteer coordinator at a Bangkok international literature festival. In two hours, a famous Japanese author is due to speak to 300 people. Her flight is delayed by 90 minutes, the Thai-English interpreter has called in sick, and the books for the signing session are still at the warehouse. You have three volunteers and a phone.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What are your priorities, and what would you do in the next 30 minutes?
followUps: Which problem is the most urgent, and why that one?
How would you communicate with the audience who are already arriving?
What if the only person who can interpret is a volunteer whose English is good but not professional?
What if the author lands but says she is too tired to speak today?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You have chosen to focus on the interpreter. Surely the audience is the real priority, isn't it?

keyPoints: Sorts problems by urgency and impact: the interpreter is essential to the event; the books matter less
Delegates clearly to the three volunteers, e.g. one tracks the flight, one calls the warehouse, one contacts language departments or backup interpreters
Informs the festival director early rather than solving everything alone
Plans honest communication with the audience: a short announcement, a revised schedule, an alternative such as a moderated reading
Considers the quality risk of an untrained interpreter and suggests ways to reduce it, e.g. consecutive interpreting or the author's slides in Thai
warningSigns: Tries to fix every problem personally without delegating
Hides the delay from the audience until the last minute
Panics or gives no clear order of actions

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are an intern at a provincial office in a tourist area. A flood warning has just been issued: some low-lying areas must evacuate within three hours. Your manager asks you to make the warning understandable to foreign tourists and migrant workers within one hour. You speak Thai and English well. The community includes speakers of Burmese, Khmer, Chinese and Russian.

interviewer.openingQuestion: How would you get this warning to everyone who needs it in one hour?
followUps: Which groups would you focus on first, and why?
Would you use machine translation for the languages you do not speak? What are the risks?
Apart from words, how else could you make the message clear?
What if you later find that one translation contained an error that sent people to the wrong shelter?
interviewer.pressureProbe: You only have an hour. Why waste time checking translations? Isn't a rough translation better than nothing?

keyPoints: Starts by simplifying the Thai message: short sentences, key action, place, time, a map, an emergency number
Prioritises groups by risk and numbers, e.g. migrant workers in low-lying areas before tourists in high-floor hotels
Uses people as well as tools: employers, community leaders, hotel staff and bilingual workers to check and spread translations
Uses machine translation for speed but asks a native speaker to check the key information before sharing
Uses non-verbal methods such as icons, maps, loudspeakers and LINE or Facebook groups that each community already uses
warningSigns: Only produces an English version and assumes everyone will understand it
Spends the whole hour perfecting one translation
Shares unchecked machine translations of important details such as the shelter location

interviewee.doorPrompt: You have decided to apply for a philosophy major. Your mother, who runs a small business and paid for your tutoring for years, is worried. She has asked to talk with you tonight before you submit your application. You want to explain your choice honestly and keep a good relationship with her.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Please begin speaking with your mother.
followUps: How did you explain what philosophy is in simple, everyday language?
Which of your mother's worries do you think is the most reasonable?
What if she says she will only pay for university if you choose a 'safer' major?
What compromise, if any, would you be willing to accept?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Your mother is the one paying. Isn't it selfish to choose a subject she disagrees with?

actor.role: Khun Wanida, 49, the candidate's mother, who runs a small printing shop in Nonthaburi
actor.brief: You love your child and are proud of her grades, but you are scared. You did not go to university and think a degree should lead to a clear, stable job. Your hidden concern is that relatives and friends will think you failed to guide her, and that she will struggle financially like you did when you were young.
lines: Philosophy? What do you even do with that? Sit and think all day?
Your cousin is studying pharmacy. She will have a good job. What will you tell people you are?
I just don't want you to struggle like I did.
actor.howToReact: If the candidate uses difficult words, sounds impatient or says you don't understand, become more upset and repeat that you only want what is best. If the candidate listens, acknowledges your fear and gives concrete examples, soften and ask what her plan is after graduating.

keyPoints: Listens to and acknowledges the mother's worries before explaining, e.g. 'I understand you want me to be secure'
Explains philosophy in plain language with a relatable example, such as ethics in business or AI decision-making
Links philosophy to real skills and careers: law, policy, consulting, writing, teaching, tech ethics, further study
Shows evidence of planning: a minor, internships, language skills, a realistic first-job plan
Stays respectful and calm, and offers to keep talking rather than 'winning' the argument
warningSigns: Uses academic jargon such as 'epistemology' without explanation
Dismisses the mother's concerns as old-fashioned
Gives in immediately without explaining their own view

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a student volunteer guide at a historical park in central Thailand. A foreign visitor at the entrance is upset because Thai citizens pay 30 baht and foreigners pay 100 baht. He says this is unfair and discriminatory, and other visitors are starting to watch. Your supervisor asks you to talk to him.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Please begin speaking with the visitor.
followUps: How did you explain the reason for the two prices without sounding defensive?
Do you personally think dual pricing is fair? Why or why not?
What if he says he has lived and paid taxes in Thailand for five years?
What would you suggest the park could change to reduce complaints like this?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Charging people more because of their nationality is discrimination. How can you defend that?

actor.role: Daniel, 41, a visitor from Germany on his second trip to Thailand
actor.brief: You are hot, tired and feel singled out. You love Thai history and have read about this site. You do not know why the prices are different. Your hidden concern is that you feel like a 'walking wallet' after being overcharged by a taxi driver this morning.
lines: Excuse me, why is it more than three times the price for me? That's discrimination.
In my country, everyone pays the same price at a museum.
I've already been ripped off once today. I'm starting to feel like everyone sees me as a bank.
actor.howToReact: If the candidate is defensive, quotes rules or ignores your frustration, raise your voice slightly and say you will write a bad review. If they acknowledge your feelings and explain the reasons respectfully, calm down and ask what you should not miss inside.

keyPoints: Stays calm and acknowledges his feelings before explaining, e.g. 'I can see why that feels unfair'
Gives balanced reasons: Thai taxpayers already fund the site, keeping heritage affordable for local families, conservation costs
Avoids blaming the visitor or making generalisations about foreigners
Responds sensibly to the resident-taxpayer twist, e.g. checking whether a work permit or resident card gives the Thai price
Turns the conversation toward the value of the visit, e.g. what the fee pays for and what he can see
warningSigns: Tells him to pay or leave without explanation
Argues with him in front of other visitors
Makes promises they cannot keep, such as letting him in for free

interviewee.doorPrompt: You are a junior editor at a Thai publishing house. A new novel you helped edit is set in a southern fishing village. A teacher from a real village nearby has come to the office. She says the book shows her community as poor, dishonest and backward, and that students at her school are now being teased. Your manager is in a meeting and asks you to speak with her first.

interviewer.openingQuestion: Please begin speaking with the teacher.
followUps: How did you respond to her anger without immediately agreeing or defending the book?
Where is the line between artistic freedom and harming a real community?
What if she demands that the book be withdrawn from shops today?
What could the publisher and the author realistically do now?
interviewer.pressureProbe: It's fiction. If writers have to worry about offending everyone, aren't we just encouraging censorship?

actor.role: Khru Ari, 45, a secondary-school teacher from a fishing village in Trang
actor.brief: You are angry and hurt, and you travelled a long way to come here. You have read the whole book. Some descriptions closely match your village's real pier and morning market. Your hidden concern is that your students now feel ashamed of where they come from, and you feel powerless.
lines: Have you ever been to a village like mine? Because this book makes us look like thieves and fools.
My students are being laughed at. Some of them don't want to say where they're from anymore.
I want to know who is responsible, and what you are going to do about it.
actor.howToReact: If the candidate defends the book immediately, says it is 'just a story' or rushes you, become sharper and say you will contact the newspapers. If the candidate listens, asks about your students and is honest about what they can do, become calmer and say you want the community to be heard, not to destroy the book.

keyPoints: Listens carefully and asks questions to understand the specific harm, e.g. which passages and how students are being teased
Acknowledges her feelings without admitting legal fault or making promises beyond their role
Shows understanding of both sides: freedom of expression and responsibility when fiction resembles a real place
Suggests realistic actions: passing her concerns to the manager and author, an author's note, a meeting with the community, changes in a future edition
Offers clear next steps and a timeline so she does not leave feeling ignored
warningSigns: Dismisses her by saying 'it's only fiction' or 'you're too sensitive'
Promises to withdraw the book without authority to do so
Blames the author entirely to protect the publisher

interviewee.doorPrompt: A popular Facebook page shares the table below with the caption: 'Thai teenagers have stopped reading. Social media is destroying our culture.' Your school librarian wants to use it in an assembly. You are asked to interpret the data carefully and advise whether the caption is fair.

data.caption: Average minutes per day spent reading by Thai teenagers (ages 13–18)
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. 2016: face-to-face survey of 2,000 students in 10 provinces. 2026: online poll of 380 followers of a Bangkok bookshop's page.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What does this data show, and would you use the caption in the assembly?
followUps: What counts as 'reading' in this survey, and what might be missing?
What are the limitations of how the data was collected?
Does this data show that social media caused the change? Why or why not?
What if a second survey showed that teenagers read more words per day than ten years ago, mostly on screens?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Printed book reading fell by almost half. Isn't the caption basically right?

keyPoints: Notes that printed book reading fell, but online reading and e-books/webtoons rose
Questions the narrow definition of reading and asks whether quality, length or type of text changed
Points out the different survey methods across years and the small sample in 2026
Explains that a trend over time does not prove social media is the cause; other factors include exam pressure, tutoring and cost of books
Suggests a more accurate caption or a more balanced message for the assembly
warningSigns: Accepts 'destroying our culture' as fact
Ignores the online reading and e-book rows
Does not notice the change in survey method

interviewee.doorPrompt: A tutoring school advert shows the table below with the headline: 'Choose the right faculty — or earn less for life!' It is being shared by parents in a school LINE group. You are asked to interpret the data and judge whether the headline is a fair conclusion.

data.caption: Average monthly starting salary, first job after graduation
data.smallPrint: Illustrative data for practice only. Data compiled by a tutoring school from a voluntary online form for its former students. Arts response rate: 12%. Medicine graduates' first jobs are mostly in a compulsory government service period.

interviewer.openingQuestion: What does this data tell us, and is the headline justified?
followUps: What is the difference between a starting salary and lifetime earnings?
Who made this table, and why might that matter?
What other information would you need before advising a student which faculty to choose?
What if data from five years after graduation showed the salary gap had almost closed?
interviewer.pressureProbe: Medicine graduates earn nearly twice as much. Isn't it simply irresponsible to choose arts?

keyPoints: Notes that the table shows only first-job salaries, not lifetime earnings or job satisfaction
Spots the very different sample sizes and the low response rate for arts
Questions the source: a tutoring school has a commercial interest in worried parents
Considers what is missing: employment rate over time, further study, people working abroad, freelance and self-employed income
Concludes that the headline overstates the data and that salary is only one factor in choosing a degree
warningSigns: Accepts the headline without questioning it
Rejects the data completely just because they want to study humanities
Ignores the response rates and who produced the table

interviewee.doorPrompt: Your aunt has forwarded this message to your family LINE group, and several relatives have shared it: 'BREAKING: Harvard scientists prove that teenagers who use TikTok more than 2 hours a day lose 10 IQ points!
